articles.title: Off to India, Marcos first PH leader to attend BRICS summit
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos will become the first Philippine leader to attend a BRICS Summit when he travels to India this week, joining the bloc’s annual gathering in his capacity as…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos will become the first Philippine leader to attend a BRICS Summit when he travels to India this week, joining the bloc’s annual gathering in his capacity as chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) for 2026.

Marcos will attend the 18th BRICS Summit in New Delhi on Sept. 12 to 13 at the invitation of Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, according to the spokesperson for the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Assistant Secretary Annalyn Ratonel, on Wednesday.
Manila sees the summit as a strategic opportunity to engage the major economies making up BRICS, which account for a major share of global output and trade.
Alternative to West

BRICS stands for Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa, the core members of the group. It’s expanded membership now stands at 11 after the inclusion of Egypt, Ethiopia, Indonesia, Iran, Saudi Arabia, and United Arab Emirates.
It currently has 10 partner countries: Belarus, Bolivia, Kazakhstan, Cuba, Malaysia, Nigeria, Thailand, Uganda, Uzbekistan and Vietnam.

The first BRICS Summit was held in 2009. All together, the grouping accounts for 49.5 percent of the world population, 40 percent of the global gross domestic product, and 26 percent of international trade.
BRICS is largely seen as offering emerging economies an alternative to Western-dominated alliances or institutions.
“Building a dialogue between Asean led by the Philippines and BRICS led by India could create significant geopolitical and economic support,” Ratonel said on Wednesday.
Making follow-ups
“This can create synergies between the priorities of Asean and BRICS that can lead to economic opportunities, trade diversification, regional security, and support for climate resilience,” she added.

According to the DFA, while Manila’s engagement with BRICS would be anchored on Asean centrality, “we recognize the value of working alongside international partners to address pressing global issues and challenges.”

The President will be accompanied at the summit by first lady Liza Araneta-Marcos, as well as Foreign Secretary Maria Theresa Lazaro, Information and Communications Technology Secretary Henry Aguda and Finance Secretary Frederick Go.
Engage when appropriate
He is scheduled to meet with Indian business leaders to strengthen economic relations and follow up on commitments made by Indian companies during his visit to India in August last year.
Following that trip, President Marcos announced $5.8 billion worth of investment pledges from Indian companies covering technology, health, energy and infrastructure.

Marcos is also scheduled to have a bilateral meeting with Modi to discuss the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership and review the implementation of the two countries’ Five-Year Plan of Action for 2025 to 2029.
Trade and investment, agriculture, climate change, defense and security, and science and technology are among the areas that could be discussed, Ratonel said.

Asked whether possible Philippine membership in the bloc would be discussed as well, Ratonel said the matter would require “further study” but that the country would continue to monitor developments and engage with BRICS when appropriate.
“We would also follow the experiences of our fellow Asean countries that are members (or partners) of BRICS,” he said, apparently referring to Indonesia, Vietnam, Malaysia and Thailand. /cb

articles.title: This is deep: Hungary’s grave-digging contest
articles.summary: NYERGESUJFALU, Hungary — Like death itself, this was no joke. A grave-digging contest in a Hungarian cemetery may sound like the opening line of a comedy sketch. It proved to be anything but as 38…

blocks.text: NYERGESUJFALU, Hungary — Like death itself, this was no joke.
A grave-digging contest in a Hungarian cemetery may sound like the opening line of a comedy sketch. It proved to be anything but as 38 competitors grabbed picks and shovels on Saturday.
The Hungarian Association of Cemetery Maintainers and Operators organizes the contest to showcase the grave-digging trade and its skills, and shake off death-related taboos.

The dry summer-baked soil in the public cemetery in Nyergesújfalu, northern Hungary, proved a worthy adversary for the 19 two-man teams. They huffed and puffed and sweated as they raced for the title of quickest-dug and most stylish grave.
‘Beautifully carved’
“Speed is the main thing here, not the beauty,” said Róbert Nagy, the victor with his teammate László Kiss.
“When you have to dig a grave for a funeral, you have to be very careful about the exact dimensions and to make sure that it is beautifully carved.”
Their winning time was 1 hour, 21 minutes, digging to contest specifications of graves 1.6 meters (5½ feet) deep, 2 meters (6½ feet) long and 0.8 meters (2.6 feet) wide.
They shared a cash prize of 200,000 Hungarian forints (about $640). /cb

articles.title: Government exempts interprovincial pipelines from review by impact assessment agency
articles.summary: The federal government is moving ahead with changes that will exempt a number of energy projects from a layer of its environmental assessment process.

image.caption: Workers lay pipe during construction of the Trans Mountain pipeline expansion in Abbotsford, B.C., in 2023. The federal government is exempting projects like interprovincial pipelines from a portion of its regulatory review process. (Darryl Dyck/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New
The federal government is moving ahead with changes that will exempt a number of energy projects from a layer of its environmental assessment process.
Projects will be reviewed by energy regulator as part of move to streamline approval

Projects including pipelines and transmission lines that cross international or provincial borders, as well as offshore renewable energy projects, will no longer be subject to an environmental review by the Impact Assessment Agency of Canada (IAAC), according to the new regulations published in the Canada Gazette on Wednesday.
Instead, those projects will be solely reviewed by the Canada Energy Regulator (CER).

"The CER has expertise conducting impact assessments that review a project's effects on a range of environmental factors, including air, water, soil, climate change, wildlife, species at risk and Canada's environmental obligation," a government news release said.
Certain oilsands extraction projects and fossil fuel-fired power generating projects are also being removed from the list of projects that will be subject to IAAC review, the news release said.
Major projects to get only one environmental assessment as Ottawa, Quebec strike deal
"These projects and facilities will continue to be subject to equally robust applicable provincial and federal assessment processes," the release reads.
Heather Exner-Pirot, director of energy, natural resources and environment at the Macdonald-Laurier Institute, said the changes are "great news" for industry.

"It does not mean these projects will not have environmental assessment — it means the [IAAC] will not duplicate some types of projects the provincial governments or the Canadian Energy Regulator (pipelines and transmission) are already assessing," she wrote in a post on X.
A 'wrecking ball' to regulations: environmental group
The changes come after Prime Minister Mark Carney promised to streamline regulatory approvals for major projects during the last election.

The Liberals, with the help of the Conservatives, passed Bill C-5 shortly after the 2025 election. That legislation allows the government to fast-track major projects it deems to be in the national interest. But these changes will impact the reviews for other major projects that don't receive that designation.
The government first proposed the changes as part of a suite of measures in May and subsequently launched consultations on the proposed reforms that wrapped up in July.

items: Danielle Smith wants to double Alberta oil production. Can she bring back the boom?
As Carney advances Metro Vancouver port expansion, environmentalists raise concern for at-risk species
Proposed changes to endangered species law would 'stab it to death,' says scientist

blocks.text: The report on those consultations was published on Tuesday, the same day the regulatory changes were announced.
"There was no forewarning of this decision," said Julia Levin of the Environmental Defence advocacy group in a statement.
"Prime Minister Carney has once again taken a wrecking ball to Canada's environmental safeguards and climate progress."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Darren Major is a senior writer for CBC's parliamentary bureau in Ottawa. He previously worked as a digital reporter for CBC Ottawa and a producer for CBC's Power & Politics. He holds a master's degree in journalism and a bachelor's degree in public affairs and policy management, both from Carleton University. He also holds a master's degree in arts from Queen's University. He can be reached at darren.major@cbc.ca.

articles.title: BARMM 2026 elections: Frequently Asked Questions
articles.summary: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will hold its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026.

blocks.text: The Bangsamoro Autonomous Region in Muslim Mindanao (BARMM) will hold its first parliamentary elections on September 14, 2026.
Here are the frequently asked questions that can help you understand the elections:
What is the relevance of the BARMM elections?
The election paves the way for the transition of the region's interim government under the Bangsamoro Transition Authority (BTA) to an elected regional administration.

President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. described it as the “fruition of an entire peace process that began in 1968, then to the Tripoli Agreement, and then the BARMM," as he called on Filipinos to protect and strengthen the gains of the country's peace process.
When will the Bangsamoro parliamentary election be held?
The first BARMM parliamentary elections will be on September 14, 2026.
The election period runs from July 16 until September 29, 2026.
Meanwhile, the campaign period is from July 30 to September 12, 2026.
How many registered voters are there in BARMM?
There are 2.393 million registered voters in the Bangsamoro region.
During the final command conference in Parang, Maguindanao del Norte, Commission on Elections (Comelec) chairman George Garcia said he is hoping for a 65-70% voter turnout in the BARMM polls.
How many voting precincts are there in the BARMM?
There are 5,212 voting precincts in 105 municipalities and two cities in the Bangsamoro Region.
To help voters locate their voting precincts, the Comelec launched its Precinct Finder on September 7.
They can locate their voting precinct by entering their full name, date of birth, and place of registration.
What time can voters begin to cast their votes?
Senior citizens, persons with disabilities, and pregnant voters will be allowed to vote as early as 5 a.m., while regular voting hours begin at 7 a.m.
Voting will continue until 7 p.m. to ensure all qualified voters can cast their ballots.
How many election areas of concern are there?
There are 108 election areas of concern (EACs) in the Bangsamoro region: Basilan, Lanao del Sur, Maguindanao del Norte, Tawi-Tawi, and special areas of concern.
Of the total EACs, 15 areas were placed in the Green category, 39 are under Yellow category, 27 under Orange, and another 27 under Red.
According to Comelec, areas under the green category have no security concerns or are relatively peaceful and orderly.

Areas under the yellow category are those with suspected election-related incidents (ERIs) in the last two elections, politically motivated ERIs during the current election period, intense partisan rivalry, or a history of being placed under COMELEC control.
Areas under the orange category meet two or more under the yellow category or exhibit serious armed threats.

Areas under the red category have one or more factors identified under the yellow and/or orange categories, along with serious armed threats or the existence of any ground for the declaration of COMELEC control.
How many seats are in the BARMM parliamentary government?
There are 80 seats in the Bangsamoro parliamentary government.
Of the total seats, 40 are designated for party representatives, 32 are for district representatives, and eight are for sectoral representatives.

There are nine seats for Lanao del Sur, five each for Maguindanao del Norte and Maguindanao del Sur, four each for Basilan and Tawi-Tawi, three for Cotabato City, and two for the Special Geographic Area.
For the sectoral groups, two seats are for non-Moro Indigenous Peoples, two for settler communities, abd one each for women, youth, traditional leaders and ulama.
In August, the NMIPs selected two representatives for the Bangsamoro Parliament.
The selected NMIP representatives are Jo Genna Jover from the Teduray indigenous peoples and Leticio Datuwata from the Lambangian indigenous groups.
They will be proclaimed along with the winning candidates after the elections.
How does the BARMM government work?
In the Bangsamoro region, the legislative power is vested in the Bangsamoro Parliament, while the executive power is given to the Chief Minister.

Meanwhile, the judicial power is excercised by in the Supreme Court, as well as in the Shari’ah and regular courts within the Bangsamoro territorial jurisdiction that form part of the Philippine judicial system. —Mariel Celine Serquina/LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Calvin Oftana, lone holdover from champion squad, joins Gilas in Japan
articles.summary: Coach Tim Cone weighed in on the pros and cons of tapping Calvin Oftana as a last-minute addition to Gilas Pilipinas for its defense of the gold in the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. While Cone can offer…

blocks.text: Calvin Oftana is a plug-and-play kind of standout, says national coach Tim Cone. —FIBA PHOTO
Coach Tim Cone weighed in on the pros and cons of tapping Calvin Oftana as a last-minute addition to Gilas Pilipinas for its defense of the gold in the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games.

While Cone can offer a lot of positives of having Oftana fill the final spot originally reserved for Justin Brownlee, he does acknowledge that the injuries that forced him to miss the last two windows of the Fiba World Cup Asian Qualifiers made them think twice at first.
“Calvin was always on the list to play, but we’re uncertain of his health status,” Cone said on Wednesday, two days ahead of Gilas’ opening assignment against Bahrain.
Oftana also missed the first phase of the PBA Governors’ Cup for TNT after dealing with injuries to his hamstring and undergoing minor surgery on his toe.
The last time he saw action was in June when TNT lost to Cone’s Barangay Ginebra in the Commissioner’s Cup Finals.
But the good news for Cone was that Oftana has recently taken part in TNT’s practices, thus opening the door for him to be given the call at the 11th hour.
“He has since returned to TNT’s practice and is good to go,” Cone continued.

With that concern now resolved, Gilas is banking on Oftana’s familiarity with Cone’s system, and even his experience playing in the Asiad, in hopes of retaining the gold the Philippines won three years ago in Hangzhou, China.
Oftana is the only holdover from that squad, as Gilas was forced to field a different squad compared to the roster that swept the recent fourth window of the Asian Qualifiers.
Gilas tapped 11 PBA players for the Asiad, headlined by Robert Bolick, Adrian Nocum, Zavier Lucero and Justine Baltazar, with Brownlee as its lone naturalized player.
But Brownlee, who missed the recent Fiba window, was ruled out for the Asian Games shortly after Gilas was beaten badly by South Korea in a two-game exhibition in Suwon.

In that series, Gilas was beaten by an average of 26.5 points, and the lack of familiarity with international play seemed evident. And that is perhaps why the addition of Oftana was taken into consideration.
“Because of the system we are running and his previous experience in the window teams, he’s a plug-and-play player and will fit right in,” Cone said.
Since Cone became the Gilas coach, Oftana has been a fixture on his shallow pool, appearing in 14 games across all Fiba competitions.

articles.title: Spanish intelligence warned of Ceuta mass crossing plans before surge
articles.summary: Declassified documents show Spanish and Moroccan authorities were alerted to social media calls for a mass migrant crossing the day before tens of thousands entered Ceuta.

blocks.text: Spanish intelligence services warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before tens of thousands of people entered the territory, newly released government documents show.
The revelations emerged in documents declassified by the Spanish government amid accusations it failed to give the full story of the migrant influx.
On 29 July, Spain's National Intelligence Service (CNI) told Moroccan and Ceuta authorities that social media groups were encouraging migrants to cross the following day.
Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez has insisted that the events of 30 July were impossible to predict, but opposition parties say the documents show the government misled Spaniards.
Sánchez had previously told parliament that there was "no information that conveyed the magnitude" of the "crisis we were going to suffer" on the last two days of July.
At least 72,000 migrants crossed from Morocco into Ceuta on 30 and 31 July. Most swam around a border fence and at least 100 people died during the crossing, according to figures from Ceuta's mayor.

Although most returned, as many as 5,000 remain in makeshift camps or are sleeping on the city's streets and beaches, leading to unrest in the autonomous Spanish city in North Africa. Locals have expressed safety concerns and some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.

In a note on 29 July, the CNI told Moroccan intelligence it had identified WhatsApp and Facebook groups promoting an attempt by migrants to reach the Spanish exclave the following day, "both swimming and via the [border] fence".

The CNI reported that around 180,000 people were receiving the messages, one of which read: "Whoever wants to cross has the last chance on Throne Day [30 July] at 8 the authorities will be distracted with the celebrations and parades".
It also warned, via text message, the central government's representation in Ceuta and the civil guard about the social media activity.

The messages are part of a tranche of more than 40 security documents linked to the Ceuta crossing that the government declassified following mounting pressure on Sánchez over his handling of the crisis and widespread allegations in Spain that Morocco had played a role in facilitating the crossings.
Earlier this month, a leaked Spanish police report seemed to implicate Moroccan police in the incident.
However, Sánchez has maintained that there is no evidence suggesting Moroccan complicity.
Shortly before the documents were released on Wednesday, he told Spanish television that "the mass arrival of migrants was not expected".
But opposition politicians said the newly released material contradict that claim.ed
"They had the information, they are directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died," said Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party.
Jorge Buxadé, of the far-right Vox, said on social media that the documents showed that Sánchez "and his band of criminals should be brought before the Supreme Court for treason and security crimes".
The government has continued to insist that it acted according to the information available.
Foreign Minister José Manuel Albares said he was "not aware of any report that might have forseen the magnitude of what happened on July 30".

A government source said the published documents "showed that the information available before the mass crossing did not make it possible to anticipate the scale that the crisis would reach or prepare with enough time the necessary response".
Miguel Ángel Pérez Triano, the central government's delegate in Ceuta, addressed the revelations about the text messages the CNI had sent to his office the day before the mass crossing.
"The Whatsapps from [July] 29 do not constitute an alert or a report," he said. "It is nothing more than an exchange of information."

articles.title: Que opens up four-shot lead in Lipa after flawless 66
articles.summary: LIPA—Angelo Que strode into the scorer’s area on Wednesday afternoon whistling a tune and wearing a wide smile, things he could well afford to do after a hot second round in the P2.5-million ICTSI…

blocks.text: Angelo Que: —CONTRIBUTED PHOTO

LIPA—Angelo Que strode into the scorer’s area on Wednesday afternoon whistling a tune and wearing a wide smile, things he could well afford to do after a hot second round in the P2.5-million ICTSI Summit Point Championship here.

“I am just hitting it so well that I am not worried one bit,” Que told the Inquirer after shooting a second straight six-under-par 66—this time bogey-free—for a 132 aggregate that had him opening up a four-shot lead over an equally hot Carl Corpus over the well-maintained layout.

“I have been hitting it good the past two weeks and whenever I do that and I can putt well, I can really go low,” added the 47-year-old, who had three straight birdies to start off his back nine—on No. 1—before capping his 32-34 with his sixth birdie on the par-5 ninth.
Que drained putts from as far as 30 feet, on No. 15 for birdie, and saved par the only time he was in trouble, a three-footer on No. 4.

First-round leader Justin Quiban had a different start to his homeward trip, signing for a wet double bogey 6 on the first that had him laboring to salvage a level 72 and be five back, in the company of Aidric Chan and Reymon Jaraula, who shot a 69 and 67, in that order.

Corpus played the first five holes of his back nine from the first at six-under after four birdies and an eagle, and practically leapfrogged the entire field, save for Que, to come into the third round in second spot.

Corpus is using this tournament to sharpen his game for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, where he will team up with Miguel Tabuena and Justin delos Santos in hunting for the country’s first gold medal since Yuka Saso won the individual and the women’s squad the team gold in the 2018 Jakarta edition.

“There won’t be a change in anything,” Quiban told the Inquirer in a separate interview when asked how he would play the third round now that he is five down. “I was just not as good off the tees today than I was (in the first round, where he shot a 65).”
“And I just struggled with the speed of the greens today. I was way off.”
Big-hitting Keanu Jahns fired a 67 to wheel into solid contention, just six shots off the pace, with the amateur Miguel Ilas shooting a 69 to be at 139.

Meanwhile, the accompanying P1-million ladies championship took on a different complexion late in the second round. Chanelle Avaricio shot a 69 to wrest the lead from Sarah Ababa and lead Apple Fudolin by a shot.

Avaricio now has a 144 aggregate heading into Thursday’s final round, where she will try to fend off Fudolin, who shot a 71 and Ababa, who returned a 75 to be two behind, tied with South Koreans Kim Seo-yun and Tiffany Lee, who shot 71 and 73, respectively.

articles.title: Ex-Doctor Who actor Noel Clarke charged with several sexual offences including assault, voyeurism
articles.summary: Noel Clarke, best known for his role in the sci-fi show Doctor Who from 2005 to 2010, has been charged with six sexual offences, including two counts of sexual assault, England and Wales’ Crown…

image.caption: British actor, writer and director Noel Clarke arrives at the High Court on March 7, 2025, in London, England. Clarke has been charged with six sexual offences, including two counts of sexual assault, that stem from allegations made by five women, U.K. prosecutors announced on Wednesday. (Getty Imag

blocks.text: Entertainment

Noel Clarke, best known for his role in the sci-fi show Doctor Who from 2005 to 2010, has been charged with six sexual offences, including two counts of sexual assault, England and Wales’ Crown Prosecution Service announced on Wednesday.
Charges stem from allegations made by 5 women against actor who was on BBC show from 2005-2010

Noel Clarke, best known for his role in the sci-fi show Doctor Who, has been charged with six sexual offences including two counts of sexual assault, England and Wales’ Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) announced on Wednesday.

The British actor and filmmaker, who is 50 and rose to fame after playing Mickey Smith on the BBC show from 2005 to 2010, also faces one charge of exposure and three charges of voyeurism. Under CPS, a voyeurism charge refers to when someone observes or records another person carrying out a private act without their consent, typically for sexual gratification.
According to CPS, the alleged offences involving Clarke took place between 2007 to 2016 and stem from allegations made by five women.

It also comes five years after a Guardian expose published sexual harrassment, groping and bullying claims made against Clarke by 20 women, including sources that alleged they were "sexually harassed or inappropriately" touched on set of Doctor Who — allegations the actor vehemently denied.
According to the Guardian, the recent charges were handed down after an investigation that began in September 2025.
Clarke is due to appear at Westminster magistrates court on Oct. 21.

The actor is also known for writing and starring in the teen crime drama films Kidulthood (2006), Adulthood (2008) and Brotherhood (2016), which explored drug abuse, bullying and violence on the streets of London. He also directed Adulthood and directed and produced Brotherhood.
His other on-screen credits include Centurion (2010), Fast Girls (2012), Star Trek Into Darkness (2013) and the TV series Bulletproof (2018-2021).
with files from Reuters

articles.title: After getting that Finals feel, NXLED ready to go all the way
articles.summary: Nxled got swept by Thailand’s EST Cola in its finals debut in the PVL Invitational Conference, 25-22, 25-21, 25-19, on Tuesday night at Smart Araneta Coliseum. But the Chameleons believe their best…

blocks.text: Nxled is all set for the All-Filipino tournament. —MARLO CUETO
Nxled got swept by Thailand’s EST Cola in its finals debut in the PVL Invitational Conference, 25-22, 25-21, 25-19, on Tuesday night at Smart Araneta Coliseum.

But the Chameleons believe their best is yet to come as they will play with a complete roster in the All-Filipino Conference next month, with three-time MVP Brooke Van Sickle returning from a shoulder injury.

“We are surely happy. I want to say a silver is a silver. But now, finally, we figured out how to enter a Final. Now we have to understand how to win it. So this is the next step,” said Nxled coach Ettore Guidetti after a lopsided finals loss.
“One hundred percent of my players will be available starting on the 14th of September, all of them,” he added.
The Italian coach admitted that his team couldn’t sustain their good showing in their first five games.

“They (EST Cola) really pushed us with their serves; we had problems in passing, and from that, I think that we didn’t really enter the game. So the block was working pretty [well], the defense was not bad, but our side-out didn’t express its full potential,” he said.
But Guidetti believes they are on the right track, with the champion players from the defunct Petro Gazz and the former Cignal duo Gel Cayuna and Jackie Acuña reinforcing the squad.
“I’m pretty sure that the continuous effort of the team will help us to figure out how to do it, to improve, and to have another possibility to take a title,” he said.
Despite missing their best player, the Chameleons made their presence felt during the Invitational.

“We’re really happy and blessed because our main goal this conference was to build our connection as a team, and that’s something you can’t develop overnight,” said Jonah Sabete-Escamillan in Filipino.
“Last conference, we were still trying to find our rhythm, even with Brooke with us, so being able to build that connection now means a lot.”

Nxled also had three All-Premier team awardees, with Cayuna winning her sixth Conference Best Setter trophy, MJ Phillips being named as the Best Middle Blocker and Escamillan earning her first PVL Best Outside Hitter award.

articles.title: Politics live: Kevin Rudd urges more multilateral diplomacy; UK hopeful Australia will join West Bank trade ban
articles.summary:
Follow the day’s news live

Don’t appease One Nation on migration warns Malinauskas

The wickedly popular South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas,…

blocks.text: Don’t appease One Nation on migration, Malinauskas warns
The South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, has iwarned the Albanese government not to join the “madness” of cutting migration to appease One Nation.

In a speech in Sydney last night, Malinauskas – whose grandparents migrated to Australia after the second world war – said the wave of populist politics has “more than arrived in Australia”, but the government should push back.

double quotation markAbove all else, [we must] preserve our strong migration program … The correct political response to anti-immigration politics and populists is not appeasement. More troubling is the prospect of mainstream politics entering a political race to the bottom for who can cut migration numbers the most. This is not unfortunate – this is madness. There could be no greater act of national economic self harm at this time than to slash migration numbers for political purposes.
He also warns against cutting international student numbers, calling it “crazy”.

double quotation markImagine if we did this to the mining industry, there world be an ad on every television station and mobile phone about how we’re killing the goose that lays the golden egg. It is crazy.

blocks.caption: Peter Malinauskas. Photograph: Sia Duff/The Guardian

blocks.text: Key events

items: 18m agoDon’t appease One Nation on migration, Malinauskas warns
42m agoAustralia should ‘put shoulder to the wheel’ on multilateral diplomacy: Rudd

blocks.text: ‘We need to explain Australia doesn’t have a migration crisis’: Malinauskas

Peter Malinaukas says he understands the concerns of Australians worried about migration and the housing shortage in Australia, but that the answer is politicians need to explain there is a housing crisis not a migration crisis happening.
He tells the ABC’s AM program that Australia will soon have more people over 65 than under 15 and migration will be essential to replace the ageing workforce.

double quotation markWe need to explain that Australia doesn’t really have a migration crisis so much as a housing crisis. If we have a housing crisis, we would do well to focus our skills policy on making sure that we’re bringing in the very workers that we require in the housing construction industry. You know, Australia’s got a massive shortage of almost every trade. Everyone, I think, accepts that it needs to be a well-calibrated, balanced migration program. My point is that we haven’t seen much evidence in the political discourse in this country in the last few years making the case for migration. Just to be seeing be a lot of culture wars being executed against migration. And I think that’s self-defeating, and we’ve got a responsibility to stand up against it.
But when asked what the magic number is for a well-balanced migration program, Malinauskas won’t say.

Instead of coming up with an arbitrary number and then cutting different parts of the migration program, Malinaukas says governments should work from the ground up, determining the skills shortages, and growth in regional areas and then coming up with a target.

blocks.caption: Krishani Dhanji

blocks.text: Krishani Dhanji
Good morning, Krishani Dhanji here with you for the final sitting day of the fortnight.

We’ll be hearing more on migration today with the South Australian premier, Peter Malinauskas, overnight warning the Albanese government not to join the “race to the bottom” against One Nation in cutting migration. The premier is doing the media rounds this morning.
Speaking of One Nation, the stoush between Pauline Hanson and Andrew Hastie continues – we’ll be following that closely.

And expect some more fight over the grants program that gave Labor seats a majority of funding, as well as the government’s digital duty of care bill, it’ll be an interesting issue for the Coalition – we understand there’s a pretty wide spread in opinion across their party room over the bill.
There’s plenty to get to, so let’s get stuck in!

blocks.caption: Adeshola Ore

blocks.text: Adeshola Ore
Victoria has highest rate of car theft and home burglary claims in ICA data
Melbourne recorded more insurance claims for stolen and broken-into cars than all other Australian capital cities combined, according to data analysis by the Insurance Council of Australia.

Property crime data released by the ICA on Wednesday night showed Victoria had the highest rates of car theft and home burglary claims in the country in the last financial year. Analysis of Insurance Statistics Australia (ISA) data showed that there were more than 12,300 claims – costing insurers $244m – lodged in the state for cars stolen or broken into.
In the same time period, every other state and territory recorded a decline.
The ICA’s chief executive, Andrew Hall, said in Victoria a car was stolen or broken into every 43 minutes while a home is broken into every two hours.
double quotation markThe insurance data shows Victoria has a crime problem, and it is being felt directly by households, businesses and communities.

Before the November state election, the ICA called for the next state government to reduce car theft and property crime through a statewide strategy and better intelligence sharing, improve disaster recovery by establishing centrally coordinated clean-up arrangements, and ease cost-of-living pressures by abolishing stamp duty on business, home and contents insurance products.
It also called for improving insurance affordability for healthcare professionals, community organisations and live music venues by “modernising civil liability laws”.
It was ‘hoped’ Australia would join UK trade ban on Israeli settlements in West Bank: Emily Thornberry
The head of the UK’s foreign affairs select committee says there was hope Australia would join the UK’s trade ban on Israeli settlements in the West Bank.

Australia is preparing another round of sanctions against Israel but has stopped short of joining the UK’s trade ban. On Tuesday, the UK government announced it would ban imported goods from illegal settlements in the occupied territories.
Speaking to the ABC’s 7.30, Emily Thornberry, the chair of the UK’s foreign affairs select committee, was asked whether she hoped Australia would join the UK’s trade ban decision:
double quotation markI think it was hoped that they might but, you know, all countries have their own decisions to make. We all want the same thing and nobody says this is easy.
Thornberry said she had a “a lot of time” for the foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong:

double quotation markI don’t know the basis upon which she’s made a decision not to be involved with us, but I’m sure that you know she believes that what she’s doing is in the interests of Palestinians and in the interests of justice.
She later added:
double quotation markI’m always happy to talk to my Australian friends and maybe even persuade them.

On Wednesday, Wong said she was concerned a blanket ban could have “unintended consequences” for Australian businesses, Palestinians and Israelis and reiterated the country would continue to protect the prospect of a two-state solution.

blocks.caption: Emily Thornberry in the House of Commons in London. Photograph: House of Commons/Reuters

blocks.text: Australia should ‘put shoulder to the wheel’ on multilateral diplomacy: Rudd

blocks.caption: Tom McIlroy

blocks.text: Tom McIlroy
Former prime minister Kevin Rudd is in Canberra for a round of high-profile speeches this week, marking his return to Australia after serving as ambassador to Washington DC.
Rudd spoke at the Australian Institute of International Affairs on Wednesday night and will be at the National Press Club today.

He said Australia must continue to push multilateral diplomacy, even as Donald Trump withdraws the US from a range of important global institutions. Australia, as a leading middle power, should promote the United Nations system, which has support across Asia and Europe, according to Rudd.

double quotation markThere remains an opportunity for Australia, in partnership with other middle powers around the world, to put our shoulders to the wheel in supporting those UN multilateral institutions which now find themselves under financial and institutional pressure as a result of the US withdrawing. Australia remains active in the UN, the IMF and the World Bank. We remain active in the G20 and in APEC. We remain active in major regional institutions, such as the Pacific Islands Forum, where the government has once again registered a remarkable series of foreign policy achievements.
Rudd said this kind of serious engagement would “put flesh on the bones” of the plan outlined by the Canadian prime minister, Mark Carney, at Davos earlier this year.

double quotation markAnd it would mark a deeply practical contribution to sustaining the multilateral rules-based system as America resolves its internal domestic debate on its future posture within it.
Good morning
Welcome to Guardian Australia’s live coverage for Thursday.
Krishani Dhanji will join us shortly.
Let’s begin.

articles.title: Filipino photog captures Alex Eala’s rise through US Open stints
articles.summary: To get to the USTA Billie Jean King Tennis Center, which hosts the US Open, Victor “Keats” London leaves his New Jersey home two-and-a-half hours before he needs to arrive at the famous complex…

blocks.text: Alex Eala —PHOTO BY KEATS LONDON

To get to the USTA Billie Jean King Tennis Center, which hosts the US Open, Victor “Keats” London leaves his New Jersey home two-and-a-half hours before he needs to arrive at the famous complex located in Flushing Meadows-Corona Park in Queens, New York.
“It only takes an hour and a half for the two train rides, but if you miss a connection, there can be quite a wait for the next train,” he said.
It’s almost an annual pilgrimage for the veteran photographer who has perhaps one of the most extensive photo collections of Alex Eala’s participation in the US Open.

He has been photographing Eala since 2021. He wrote a story that came out on the Inquirer’s front page in 2022, when the fast-rising superstar captured the US Open girls’ crown and became the first Filipino to win a Grand Slam singles title.
The current world No. 17 did not play at the 2023 US Open. She came back in 2024 and won her first women’s singles Grand Slam match in 2025.

There are perks to enjoy during the coverage, which happens at the tail end of hot New York summers: Freebies he gets to take home, high-end cameras he gets to test courtesy of popular brands and other things he gets to take home for his wife.
But the greatest perk is catching Eala in action and soaking in “Eala Mania,” which hit a new high in this year’s edition of the Slam.
“As a Filipino, born and raised, I feel proud that we have a Pinay who came out of thousands of qualifiers and made it all the way to the top 20 [in the world ranking],” he said.
There are challenges to the coverage: And it has more to do than the heat when staying under the sun and waiting for the perfect shot.

“I can bear the heat,” he said. “Sometimes, I shoot from where the sun is not bearing down on me. In fact, I love the sun when it provides a dark and bright side of the court. Very artistic when done right.”
The tougher challenge?

“I have to separate the me as a fan and me as the photojournalist,” he said. “As a photojournalist, we can’t cheer. Can’t even wear a shirt or hat that carries the name of a team or a person. Other photographers will call you out.”
But it’s a small price to pay for being able to watch history unfold from courtside.
“Eala is fun to shoot because she gives photographers energy, especially when she celebrates,” London said.

“I also love seeing Filipinos create ‘Eala Mania’ here. [This year], I saw more Philippine flags and shirts showing Eala even during practice rounds,” added London, whose photos appear on the Inquirer.

articles.title: Coming down hard on ‘Solar King’
articles.summary: Last January, the Department of Energy (DOE) showed some spine when it slapped a massive P24-billion penalty against the solar energy company of Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Leviste for failure…

blocks.text: Last January, the Department of Energy (DOE) showed some spine when it slapped a massive P24-billion penalty against the solar energy company of Batangas 1st District Rep. Leandro Leviste for failure to deliver on its commitment to produce some 11,000 megawatts (MW) of renewable energy.

But nine months later, Energy Secretary Sharon Garin admitted during the DOE budget hearing that the government had only managed to collect a measly P80 million out of the hefty fine on Solar Philippines Power Project Holdings Inc., a company that Leviste founded in 2013 which made him eventually a multibillionaire.

Yes, the DOE had taken measures to press Leviste’s company to pay the sizable fine by filing a criminal complaint with the Department of Justice (DOJ) and a civil case with the Office of the Solicitor General.

But the interminable delay in collecting on what is rightly due to the government has nevertheless reinforced growing pessimism and even outright dismissal of the government’s resolve to keep erring power companies in line.

Indeed, if power generators proven to have failed to honor their commitments to deliver contracted energy within the prescribed period go unpunished, then the entire energy development program is jeopardized.
Unequivocal message

Without an unequivocal message that these infractions will not be tolerated and that painful sanctions will be imposed, the DOE runs the danger of attracting power firms who are only interested in winning contracts for possible sale to other companies down the road and not on delivering the power.

Garin said as much when she justified the unprecedented fine against Leviste’s company. “Kung hindi natin gagawin ito, baka sumunod ang iba. Kukuha lang ng kontrata, maghihintay ng investor, laway lang ang ibebenta nila,” she said. (If we’re not going to do this, others would follow. They would get a contract, wait for an investor and just do some sales talk.)

Coming down hard on noncompliant firms, Garin added, was not meant to scare off investors but rather aimed to ensure that only “legitimate investors” with the necessary financial, technical, and legal capabilities will undertake energy projects in the Philippines.

Veering away from this right path is unacceptable and scams that should not be allowed to take root, especially at this time when the country urgently needs new energy sources to meet growing demand across the country, should not be tolerated.
‘Solar King’

Leviste indeed has much to answer for as of the 163 power supply service contracts that the DOE canceled from 2024 to 2025, Solar Philippines accounted for some 11,400 MW, about 64 percent of the total capacity.
Garin had said that Leviste was not being singled out in its sweeping crackdown on nonperforming power contractors, but the violations are just too big to ignore.

As much as Leviste has been hailed as the country’s “Solar King,” his group is in the government’s crosshairs for failure to live up to its end of the contract to deliver power by December 2025, although Leviste has consistently and vociferously denied that his company had failed to meet targets, claiming that many of them had not even been granted notices to proceed.

Leviste’s other company, Solar Para sa Bayan Corp., faces a similar complaint with the DOJ for “willful neglect and failure to fulfill the obligations” to install renewable energy-powered microgrids in remote and underserved areas across the country under a 25-year legislative franchise granted during the time of former President Rodrigo Duterte.

Over that time between winning contracts and DOE’s cases, Leviste has earned billions after selling some P24 billion worth of shares in SP New Energy Corp.—founded as Solar Philippines’ subsidiary—to the MVP Group’s Meralco PowerGen Corp. and other investors.
High price of failure
This means that as far as resources go, Leviste has more than enough to pay the fine if finally compelled by the courts.
It is indeed now up to the courts to promptly decide on the merits of the cases against Leviste that are increasing by the day, including estafa, graft, and even plunder.

But in the meantime, the DOE has to scramble for new investors that can be counted on to deliver the additional power to meet future demand and keep the power grids stable, and at the same time keep the country on track to meeting its goal of having renewable energy account for 35 percent of the total energy mix by 2030 from the current level of roughly 25 percent.

To the DOE’s credit, it has stepped up its crusade against violators by instituting clear sanctions against noncompliant power generation companies that will range from a formal warning to suspension and contract cancellation and corporate blacklisting after a third offense, a sanction that for Akbayan party list Rep. Chel Diokno should be meted out on Leviste’s company.
The DOE should keep up the pressure and take violators to task as Filipinos will ultimately pay the high price of failure in the form of expensive power rates and unstable energy supply.

articles.title: A different measure of success
articles.summary: The clearest evidence of humankind’s superiority over the rest of the animal kingdom lies in the fact that we are the only species on Earth that engages in pursuits beyond the necessities of…

blocks.text: The clearest evidence of humankind’s superiority over the rest of the animal kingdom lies in the fact that we are the only species on Earth that engages in pursuits beyond the necessities of survival. All other animals spend every single day of their entire lives exclusively searching for food, securing shelter, ensuring protection from predators, and engaging in procreation. In contrast, humans engage in a wide variety of passions beyond the bare necessities of life.

The wide range of pursuits that human beings get passionately interested in is astounding—astronomy, dance, architecture, biology, visual arts, botany, dental medicine, paleontology, to cite a few examples from the kilometric list of human interests. Our complex brain, which evolved and developed to be far more advanced than those of other animals, has enabled us to engage in pursuits beyond basic survival concerns. But what explains how everyone becomes intensely fascinated by one particular pursuit out of the many different fields of interest? Genes, parental influence, education, and life experience are obvious contributory factors. But why does the child of lawyers aspire to become an architect, for instance? Why does a successful accountant abandon her profession and put up a coffee shop in fulfillment of a lifelong dream? Why does the child of impoverished laborers possess a yearning for literature?

There’s not a single conclusive explanation as to why people possess an innate interest in particular fields to the point of developing them into lifelong passions if given the choice. These passions are elements of life that give every individual purpose, dreams, direction, and fulfillment. A society that thrives with an overwhelming number of its people pursuing their real dreams becomes vibrant with life.

How many of our people are pursuing their passions as their life vocations? How many of our countrymen are using their God-given talents in their trade, craft, or profession? How many of our people wake up happy and excited every day because they are living their dreams?
It’s starkly lamentable that the celebrated metric of success in our society is financial success.

It’s heartbreaking that so many of our children are forced to abandon their passions and are instead told to pursue professions that will put more zeroes in their bank accounts. So many of our children are forced to become nurses, police/military personnel, seafarers, and engineers because they’re told that they will have better chances of ensuring economic survival for their families if they pursue these professions. Our country is a wasteland of squandered talents.

It’s true that with financial security, people can afford to pursue their passions. But this means that passions become mere weekend hobbies instead of enduring careers. For most of their lives, people toil in jobs that drain instead of infusing life into their lives.

Our society’s reliance on economics as a measurement of success notwithstanding, we are constantly reminded that monetary success does not translate into contentment, fulfillment, and happiness. Despite material possessions and financial security enjoyed by people in affluent countries, they have their equal share, if not a higher share, of incidents of depression and more frequent occurrences of suicide.

In our country’s case, we may have recently attained upper-middle-income country status according to the World Bank, but what meaning and relevance does that have for the overwhelming majority of our people who toil every day in jobs and vocations that are totally detached from their passions?

I commune with friends and interact with clients whose lives range from the most destitute to the incredibly wealthy. The happiest and most contented family I’ve encountered consists of parents who are both dedicated and enthusiastic public school teachers with two kids who are attending a regional state university. They have not had the privilege of traveling abroad, but they talk of wonderful vacation memories in Baguio City and a summer beach trip not far from their province. They go out for lunch as a family on most weekends at fast food eateries. Their gatherings are filled with stories and laughter. The kids are voracious book readers pursuing courses dictated by their respective passions.

Experts should come up with a different gauge of a country’s success or failure by measuring the proportion of its people who are living and sustaining their lives through the pursuit of their talents and passions. A country may be teeming with people wallowing in wealth, but they lead nonhuman lives when they are detached from their passions. They’re no different from animals going through life entirely concerned with the bare necessities of survival.
Comments to fleamarketofideas@gmail.com

articles.title: At least one adult
articles.summary: As an extension of Suicide Prevention Month, I’d like to turn our attention to an often-overlooked protective factor against the risk of suicide and other threats to safety: having a reliable…

blocks.text: As an extension of Suicide Prevention Month, I’d like to turn our attention to an often-overlooked protective factor against the risk of suicide and other threats to safety: having a reliable relationship with an adult whom one can feel safe enough to turn to.

In our first year of clinical training, I was assigned to a community school. This was a school that received students who were kicked out of mainstream schools in the county. They weren’t just struggling with academics; a lot of them were involved in petty crimes and juvenile gang activity. Their neighborhood was infamous for having the highest murder rate per capita, with someone they knew being shot every day. This was the violent environment that the kids were growing up in. Their prospects of a nonviolent life were dim, with kids regularly recruited into gangs.

My supervisor, who has a background in social work, taught us about the principle of “at least one adult.” Studies show that having at least one stable and caring relationship with an adult helps develop resilience. For this particular neighborhood, it would mean improving their chances of breaking out of the cycle of violence. Such adults are not limited to parents or family. They can be a teacher, a neighbor, a family friend, or a community mentor. As such, the community-based organization I trained at firmly believed that by providing counselors at schools, they can ensure that there will be “at least one adult” who believes in the children.

The adult cannot necessarily change the child’s entire environment. (Ask any teacher or parent; I’m confident they will agree.) What a good relationship can offer, however, is to ensure that the child does not feel alone when they’re faced with obstacles and challenges. A problem can look very different, perhaps more manageable and feasible, when we know that someone is on our side. Resilience and courage are not found merely within us but also drawn from our stable relationships.

When we know that we do not have to struggle alone, or that someone understands what we are going through, this mitigates our sense of threat. A reliable relationship can help keep the fight-or-flight response at bay. As such, cognitive abilities such as contextual reasoning, critical thinking, long-term planning, problem solving, sound judgment, and emotion regulation remain accessible to us, allowing us to see and consider all our options. While desperation makes us feel that we are running out of options, the experience of a reliable relationship opens us up to more.

Experiencing a good relationship can be the counterevidence we need when faced with hopelessness and jadedness, both risk factors for suicide. Beck’s cognitive triad of depression theorizes that someone who experiences depression holds negative views about the world, the self, and the future. A stable and caring relationship can provide disconfirming evidence for such negative beliefs. When we lose hope about the world, our experience of a good relationship reminds us that good people still exist and that good people find us worthy of love.

Having the experience of someone accepting us for who we are without judgment can be the vaccine to clinical perfectionism and an intolerance of the mistakes and missteps we make along the way. Having someone have genuine faith in our potential, therefore not pressuring us to perform faster and better, can remind us of our capacity to grow, no matter how stuck or stagnant we feel our lives to be. Having faith in our potential also helps us ward off hopelessness about the future, remembering that life will not always be this way.

When we think of adults in a child’s life, we mistakenly think that the adult’s job is to tell the child what to do. We think of the rules to impose and the limits to enforce. We focus on correcting their mistakes. What optimizes an adult’s presence in the child’s life is not just the structure they provide but the relationship in which the child feels seen and understood. How they are reflected in this relationship determines how they begin to see themselves. If an adult loves them unconditionally, they begin to love themselves the same way. If an adult demonstrates patience and understanding when it comes to missteps and derailments, the child learns to be kind to themselves and trust that life will blossom for them eventually.

A stable and caring relationship needs time and effort to be built. It cannot be merely a reactive response to an acute threat to safety. True prevention starts at the beginning. We, as adults, can be that one adult for others. We may not be able to solve all their problems, but showing up for them can change the trajectory of their lives.
(I looked into that neighborhood again for this piece, almost two decades later. They just celebrated two years of no homicides. At least one adult.)
aatuazon@up.edu.ph

articles.title: Counting the poor: Realistic thresholds
articles.summary: With poverty incidence reduced to fewer than one in 10 Filipinos and the Philippines attaining upper-middle-income status early this year, are we finally moving beyond the economic struggles that…

blocks.text: With poverty incidence reduced to fewer than one in 10 Filipinos and the Philippines attaining upper-middle-income status early this year, are we finally moving beyond the economic struggles that have burdened the Filipino poor and middle class for as long as anyone can remember?

This is a tough question to answer because so many factors must be considered before anyone can say for sure that the worst of times are behind us and that we’re on our way to sustaining growth that truly benefits not just those at the top of the food chain—the country’s richest elites and the ruling political class (and their protegés).

Amid the onslaught of typhoons and floodwaters last month, a piece of good news offered a sliver of hope that things could get better down the road: the government has trumpeted the 2025 single-digit poverty rate of 9.7 percent as “historic” to show that its antipoverty efforts are working just fine despite continuing headwinds on the local and overseas fronts.

The latest poverty statistics are impressive, indicating that 6.5 million Filipinos were “lifted out of poverty between 2023 and 2025,” a relatively short period. Not only did the share of Filipinos living below the official poverty threshold fall to a historic single-digit rate, but the latest figures also show a rapid decline: 11.08 million people (9.7 percent) were considered poor in 2025, down from 17.5 million (15.5 percent) in 2023, and 19.9 million (18.1 percent) in 2021. The Philippine Statistics Authority (PSA) released these figures on Aug. 21, 2026.

“For the first time, fewer than one in ten Filipinos is living below the poverty line,” Secretary Arsenio M. Balisacan of the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development (DepDev) announced in a statement on Aug. 26, 2026. He said the government reached “this milestone ahead of schedule,” referring to the 9 percent poverty-reduction target by 2028.

Low poverty threshold. But if we look closer, the story is in the details: the government set the poverty threshold at P14,634 per month for a family of five in 2025, compared with P13,873 in 2023 and P11,998 in 2021. The P14,634-a-month poverty threshold—you’re not poor if you earn above this line—is based on the 2025 annual per capita poverty threshold of P35,121, or P96.22 per person per day.
The continued decline in poverty incidence was driven by changes in the poverty threshold and income during the same period. End of story? Not so fast.

The historic rate may not tell the whole story if the poverty threshold the PSA uses remains too low and outdated to reflect reality on the ground—the actual cost of meeting a family’s basic needs. “The issue [is] that PSA’s own chief statistician already admitted, back in 2024, that the food budget behind this threshold was too low to meet basic nutrition. PSA promised to fix it,” said Leonardo Lanzona, an economist (see “PSA: PH poverty hit lowest, single-digit level in 2025,” Headlines, 8/22/26).

Ibon Foundation raised another objection. Under government metrics, a person who spends more than P96.22 per day, or a family of five with an income slightly above P14,634 per month, is classified as “non-poor.” Ibon Foundation said the government’s standard for defining who is poor is “problematic, outdated, and very unrealistic,” because “the food threshold is based on a bare-minimum, least-cost basket” (see “Ibon: Gov’t poverty standard ‘outdated,’ ‘unrealistic,’” Nation, 8/26/26).

The P96.22 daily expense is highly unrealistic—a one-piece fried chicken value meal costs P99, and the poor also spend on nonfood items such as shelter, utilities, transportation, health and education, and clothing. Under this flawed methodology, medical and other emergencies are excluded.

Multidimensional poverty. But the DepDev explained that economic opportunities “expanded amid sustained GDP (gross domestic product) growth, moderating inflation, and generally favorable labor-market conditions.” Balisacan also praised the various ayuda, or targeted assistance, and government livelihood programs that “have helped narrow income gaps over the years” and “have made poverty reduction more responsive to economic growth.”

In apparent response to the stinging public rebuke, the PSA has recently released the first Multidimensional Poverty Index (MPI), revealing that 12.4 percent of Filipino households were classified as multidimensionally poor across education, health and nutrition, housing, water and sanitation, and employment.

“The MPI shows that poverty is not just about what people earn” but “whether Filipinos have access to essential services that allow them to live productive and dignified lives,” Balisacan said in a statement.

This is a better way to gauge poverty incidence because the MPI can assess specific deprivations beyond basic services and living conditions. Poverty is multidimensional, so government programs must be targeted and sufficient to address these deprivations.
For comments: lim.mike04@gmail.com

articles.title: High electricity costs: What can the Philippines do?
articles.summary: Electricity in the Philippines is expensive, and families and businesses feel it every month. Depending on consumption and billing period, residential electricity in Metro Manila can approach P15 to…

blocks.text: Electricity in the Philippines is expensive, and families and businesses feel it every month.

Depending on consumption and billing period, residential electricity in Metro Manila can approach P15 to P16 per kilowatt-hour (kWh). In Makati, where I live and work, many households effectively pay around P16.

We can debate why electricity in Association of Southeast Asian Nations neighbors appears cheaper. Some governments subsidize power; some have greater domestic energy resources. The Philippines imports much of its fuel and operates across an archipelago. These factors matter, but they do not lower anyone’s bill.
So the useful question is: What can we do about it?
After more than 25 years in renewable energy, I believe the Philippines can turn this challenge into an economic opportunity.

Start with what the Philippines has. The Philippines may not have abundant oil and gas, but it has sunlight. Solar has evolved from an expensive, subsidy-dependent technology into one of the world’s most competitive sources of new electricity, while battery costs have fallen substantially.

Awareness of solar and storage is growing among Philippine households and businesses. The question is increasingly how to make systems affordable and properly installed at scale. At today’s electricity prices, producing part of one’s own power increasingly makes economic sense.
Financing is emerging. Upfront cost remains the biggest obstacle. Many families cannot easily spend several hundred thousand pesos on a solar-and-battery system.

Pag-Ibig Fund, Social Security System, and Government Service Insurance System serve millions of Filipino workers and families. Their interest in affordable financing for solar and energy-saving investments is encouraging. Qualified households should be able to finance properly designed systems over long periods, with monthly payments ideally below their previous electricity bills. Instead of paying indefinitely, families gradually own an energy-producing asset.
Scale can lower costs. As interest in solar and storage accelerates, demand is testing installation capacity and costs—a sign of a market moving toward larger-scale adoption.

Technical Education and Skills Development Authority is already working with suppliers to train qualified installation and service teams. As Filipino installers gain experience, installation speed should approach that of more mature markets, while scale, competition, and efficiency reduce costs.

Lower system costs create a positive cycle: financing institutions can serve more families with the same capital, household returns improve, and monthly loan payments can fall further below existing electricity bills.
Installation, logistics, maintenance, and related services could also directly and indirectly create an estimated 50,000 to 100,000 jobs.

Build the supply chain here. If millions of Filipino families eventually install solar panels, batteries and inverters, such a large domestic market should be able to support a broader local supply chain.

The country already has an electronics base, industrial parks, export infrastructure and capable workers. My experience helping establish advanced solar-cell manufacturing in Batangas has strengthened my confidence that Filipino workers can operate sophisticated equipment to international standards.

Domestic demand can support competitive local manufacturing and assembly of modules, battery packs, inverters, and other components where localization makes economic sense—creating jobs, shortening delivery times, and strengthening local after-sales service.

Energy policy is industrial policy. Millions of solar homes would create distributed energy close to where electricity is consumed—particularly relevant for an archipelago of more than 7,000 islands. Solar and storage will not replace the grid or meet every requirement of large industrial users, but they can reduce demand, improve household resilience, and complement reliable large-scale generation.
Lower and more predictable energy costs can also strengthen the Philippines’ competitiveness for manufacturing investment.
From discussion to execution. One lesson from my years in renewable energy is consistent: technology, financing and policy matter—but execution determines the result.

The Philippines has sunlight, people, demand, and growing market awareness. Financing is emerging, training is underway, technology is ready, and local manufacturing capability is growing. The task now is to turn this momentum into scale—with strong standards, responsible lending, and qualified installation.

When I see electricity approaching P16 per kWh, I see not only a problem, but rooftops generating power, batteries serving families at night, local factories producing equipment, and Filipino technicians building a new industry.
High electricity prices are today’s reality, but they can become a catalyst for lower household costs, more jobs and a stronger, cleaner and more locally rooted energy industry.
Samuel Yang is an Australian renewable energy entrepreneur and chair of GBF New Power Group Inc.

articles.title: Impeachment languages and logic
articles.summary: Language diversity is hard for schoolchildren, and even for the adults in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial. The proceedings used Filipino, English, and Cebuano, but the participating…

blocks.text: Language diversity is hard for schoolchildren, and even for the adults in Vice President Sara Duterte’s impeachment trial. The proceedings used Filipino, English, and Cebuano, but the participating parties lacked a common level of proficiency in any one of them. The need to repeat questions and responses in different languages made the process tedious. Disputes over word meanings made the logic of arguments more difficult to follow.

Does translating “unconscionable” as kasuklam-suklam merit an objection for making the behavior sound more offensive to Tagalog speakers? Do large cash withdrawals from government accounts become more suspicious when described as “irregular” (hindi sa nakagawian) rather than merely “unusual” (hindi pangkaraniwan)? If done repeatedly within a short time span, can they be considered no longer merely unusual or acceptable? Or even more unusual, and perhaps deserve further scrutiny? Not trivial issues, but frustrating to viewers not fluent in the languages.

Viewers must contend with a second language problem. The administrative state and the legal profession speak their own distinct versions of English. Joint Circular No. 2015-01, a key document on confidential funds, uses fairly common words. Dependence on dictionary definitions may mislead. “Confidential and intelligence funds” cover activities involving sensitive security matters whose details cannot be publicly shared. But they function like technical terms, as defined by JC 2015-01 and related regulations.

The issue goes beyond language to the different focus of administrative/legal and managerial perspectives. Though “management” tends to be associated with senior, corporate jobs, it is a concern of carpenters, farmers, and anyone who wants a job done and cares about results. But bureaucrats and lawyers must also worry about how the job is done to protect against potential charges of violating established laws. Given possibly conflicting legal prescriptions and an increasingly litigious political and cultural environment, risk avoidance often raises the cost of meeting desired goals, a result unwelcome to the superiors whom subordinates wish to please.

Chief executives in effective organizations determine overall objectives and strategy but trust subordinates for the pencil-pushing and the vetting of potential problems. Less proficient bureaucracies often reverse the system. The bosses decide, and subordinates comply without question and provide the necessary paperwork. The testimony of Gina Acosta in the trial illustrates the pattern.

A career Davao local government official, Acosta had worked for some 20 years in the city administrator and budget offices when then Mayor Duterte chose her in 2019 as a special disbursing officer (SDO) for its confidential funds. Elected VP in 2022, Duterte gave Acosta the same responsibility for the larger, national job. But Acosta did not have the experience, training, or the security clearance for confidential operations. Hence, she gave the funds to Col. Raymund Lachica, head of the VP’s Security and Protection Group. She apparently believed her SDO accountability was fulfilled when she had faithfully reproduced the information provided by Lachica in the physical and financial plan (PFP) and later reports she had to file.

Unfortunately, the PFP, done by Acosta on Lachica’s information, lacked the required details to identify the confidential programs, activities, and projects, physical targets, and their allocated amounts. Since JC 2015-01 also established the PFP as the basis for subsequent disbursements, the deficiencies weakened a critical control document that would enable oversight authorities to check accomplishment reports on whether the funds were legitimately spent to implement the planned objectives.

Disbursement to final recipients was arguably part of program implementation, clearly not Acosta’s mandate. But JC 2015-01 did not permit her to entrust the funds to Lachica, who had not been bonded for this responsibility. She remained accountable for money over whose ultimate distribution she had no personal knowledge.

Acosta argued that she received explicit instructions from VP Sara to give the funds to Lachica. As she explained in court: “Ako your honor, nag-trust ako kay Colonel Lachica … kasi nag-trust po si VP Sara, kasi siya po ang gi-tudlo nga security officer … at saka ang gi-gastusan is confidential in nature your honor.” Acosta trusted VP Sara as the final authority on her SDO role.

Records may confirm procedural compliance with all the needed documentation for the deployment of confidential funds. Words matter, but don’t do magic. Calling a document a PFP does not make it a substantive plan. Completing required forms does not establish compliance if these lack the data for the necessary controls.
Acosta did some things wrong. The harder question for the impeachment court is determining the responsibility of those who designed, authorized, and approved what she was able to do.
Edilberto C. de Jesus is professor emeritus at the Asian Institute of Management.

articles.title: Living with water: Flood control is also a governance problem
articles.summary: Do not fool or fight Mother Nature. Mother Nature always wins. I am not an engineer, psychologist, or a sociologist, but I learned a lot from professor Randy David, a sociologist, when he discussed…

blocks.text: Do not fool or fight Mother Nature. Mother Nature always wins. I am not an engineer, psychologist, or a sociologist, but I learned a lot from professor Randy David, a sociologist, when he discussed the construction of an artificial island for Kansai International Airport (KIX) in Japan (see “Living with water,” Public Lives, 9/6/26).

He described the work of Japanese engineers, starting with rock and soil from the mountains as landfill down to the bed of the water. In spite of some natural flooding, the Japanese engineers controlled the sinking of the island by continuous observation and use of jacks and columns to keep the island afloat.

With the long-standing floods in Manila, Bulacan, and Pampanga, he mentioned the difference in the system management of KIX in Osaka Bay and flooded areas of Manila, Pampanga, and Bulacan. KIX, being an airport, is managed by one operator with a crew of engineers who work by the book. These flood-prone areas in the Philippines have no one body operating and managing them. In addition, houses and buildings in the past, and even recently, were built even on areas that are flood-prone. Even if there are building codes, almost nobody follows them completely.

David mentioned that “flood control is not merely an engineering problem but a governance problem that presumes institutional memory, continuous monitoring, and a reliable system of warning.“ We, in the Philippines, don’t have any of those, aggravated by systemic corruption in the government, especially in the Department of Public Works and Highways.
As an ordinary citizen, trying to do something about flood control, I would suggest the following:

1) Start with yourself by dividing the garbage we generate into organic for composting, recyclables, and general garbage for landfill. Try not to pollute the environment by cutting down on the use of plastics, shifting to old-fashioned leaves, regular paper, etc. Try not to dump garbage that will clog small canals. Teach this in schools and even in church. Global warming and climate change are here.

2) Establish some form of community boards, bigger and more powerful than the local barangays, to control permits and the construction of new houses and buildings or developments that can clog our waterways and destroy our environment. They have the last say on the approval of these constructions.

3) The government must come in by providing working pumping stations to dry out flooded areas (Manila had these before) and seek consultations locally and from other parts of the world with a history of flooding, like the Netherlands, for help and guidance. Pass strict laws on construction in low-lying areas prone to flooding.

4) The government and citizens must watch carefully the construction of flood control projects, and most importantly, their maintenance and upkeep. Citizens must report to government agencies any unusual activities in the construction, like unfinished projects caused by corruption.

David ended his article by stating “The engineers at Kansai Airport did not stop the sinking. Instead they provided for a system of continuous adjustment. That is the part we have not copied.” … AN EYE OPENER!
Ida M. Tiongco,
idationgco @gmail.com
For letters to the editor and contributed articles, email to opinion@inquirer.net
