articles.title: Barangay execs’ term extension slammed
articles.summary: he extension of the terms of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan officials is a violation of the 1987 Constitution, Kabataan party-list said yesterday.

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 12:00am
Kabataan issued the statement as the Senate passed on second reading the bill postponing the upcoming Nov. 2 BSKE and extending barangay and SK officials’ terms to five years.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — The extension of the terms of barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan (SK) officials is a violation of the 1987 Constitution, Kabataan party-list said yesterday.

Five senators opposed the measure – Senate President Pro Tempore Vicente Sotto III and Senators Kiko Pangilinan, Joel Villanueva, Bam Aquino and Risa Hontiveros – for denying the village voters’ right to choose their new barangay leaders this November.

“We pushed for the suspension of the barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan elections (BSKE) from 2026 to 2028 and extending the term of sitting officials for two years without providing sufficient basis. The Supreme Court (SC) said postponing elections needs to have a compelling governmental interest like protecting suffrage of a true emergency,” Kabataan Rep. Renee Co said.

“It should not be merely administrative convenience or seeking for continuity. It has not been a year since we passed a law that extends the term of BSK officials to four years, and yet we will extend their term again for another year?” she asked.
House Senior Deputy Minority Leader Leila de Lima of party-list Mamamayang Liberal also voted against the measure.

“Regular elections, held on time, remain the surest foundation of accountable governance at the grassroots level, because it is at the barangay where the impact of leadership, for better or worse, is felt most directly by ordinary Filipinos,” she said.

Rep. Sarah Elago of women’s group Gabriela also opposed the bill, saying “it will deny our citizens their right to choose their leaders. Because of the effect of postponement, they used term-fixing to push delaying BSKE this year.”
Sotto said fixing of their terms in office at five years from the current four can be done without postponing the upcoming BSKE.

“Considering that this is the eighth time that we have postponed barangay elections, it might give an impression to the public of how little regard we are giving to the unit of government closest to the people,” Sotto said yesterday.

Under the bill, barangay officials will be limited to two consecutive terms, while SK officials will continue to be limited to one term. Incumbent barangay officials already serving their third consecutive term will be disqualified from seeking the same position in the 2028 elections.
Election lawyer Romulo Macalintal has vowed to challenge the law before the Supreme Court.

articles.title: Mans Carpio’s bank records disclosure complaint junked
articles.summary: The Office of the City Prosecutor in Quezon City has recommended the dismissal of the complaint filed by Manases Carpio, the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, over the alleged violation of bank…

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 12:00am

Manases Carpio, husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, arrives with his lawyer at the Quezon City Prosecutor's Office to on Monday, April 27, 2026 to file charges over the alleged disclosure of bank records.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the City Prosecutor in Quezon City has recommended the dismissal of the complaint filed by Manases Carpio, the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, over the alleged violation of bank secrecy laws by several House members and government officials.
Based on the 23-page resolution, the Quezon City Prosecutor’s Office said the acts of the respondents were done in relation to their office, noting these “are not inherently immoral.”

“The issuance of a subpoena for the production of AMLC (Anti-Money Laundering Council) reports, the manifestations made during the impeachment proceedings against the Vice President of the Republic of the Philippines and the compliance with the subpoena – these acts were done by the respondents, public officers with Salary Grade 28 and higher, in relation to their office,” the resolution read.
“By no stretch of the imagination could we rule that these acts of the respondents were done in their private capacity,” it added.

Respondents are House justice panel chair Gerville Luistro, Senior Deputy Minority Leader Leila de Lima, Deputy Minority Leader Antonio Tinio, Akbayan party-list Reps. Percival Cendaña and Chel Diokno, Kabataan party-list Rep. Renee Co, Manila 3rd District Rep. Joel Chua and Bicol Saro party-list Rep. Terry Ridon.

State officials involved in the case are Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas Governor Eli Remolona Jr., Insurance Commissioner Reynaldo Regalado, Securities and Exchange Commission Chairman Francis Lim and AMLC Executive Director Ronel Buenaventura.
Carpio’s legal counsel Peter Paul Danao said they acknowledge the resolution and will review it once they receive a copy.
Meanwhile, Duterte appointed lawyer Paolo Panelo as her spokesman in the grave threats case she is facing before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court and the ongoing impeachment trial against her.
Panelo is the son of former chief legal counsel Salvador Panelo, who served during the administration of former president Rodrigo Duterte. – Bella Cariaso

articles.title: NBI discovers ‘double payments’ for SEAG cauldron
articles.summary: The National Bureau of Investigation claimed that the P55-million cauldron used in the 2019 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games was possibly overpriced after discovering a “double payment” while…

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 12:00am
The cauldron waits to be lit, signaling the start of the 2019 SEA Games at New Clark City in Tarlac in this file photo from November 2019.
Walter Bollozos

MANILA, Philippines — The National Bureau of Investigation claimed that the P55-million cauldron used in the 2019 Southeast Asian (SEA) Games was possibly overpriced after discovering a “double payment” while constructing the structure.

NBI Director Melvin Matibag revealed that two additional witnesses came forward last Monday with documents that would strengthen the bureau’s planned criminal case against listed officials of the Philippine SEA Games Organizing Committee (PHISGOC).
The NBI chief noted that the controversial cauldron should have cost only P30 million instead of P55 million.
“We saw that there’s a double payment,” Matibag told radio dzBB on yesterday.
He explained that payments for certain companies were logged twice in an undisclosed document.
Since the NBI needs to check the new documents, the filing of complaints against PHISGOC officials is delayed until next week.
Matibag earlier said the bureau has collected documents and testimonies to file multiple criminal charges against the PHISGOC board.
Sen. Alan Peter Cayetano introduced himself then as PHISGOC chairman, but his name was not listed in any of its corporate documents.
The committee, formed specifically for the conduct of the 30th SEA Games, continues to earn money to this day by sponsoring international sports events, according to Matibag.

articles.title: Up to 3 cyclones expected
articles.summary: Up to three tropical cyclones are expected to enter or develop inside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) this month, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical…

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 12:00am
PAGASA said the weather disturbances would be given the names Queenie, Rosal and Samuel once they enter or develop inside the PAR.
PAGASA

MANILA, Philippines — Up to three tropical cyclones are expected to enter or develop inside the Philippine area of responsibility (PAR) this month, according to the Philippine Atmospheric, Geophysical and Astronomical Services Administration.
This is lower than last month’s expected four tropical cyclones, which exceeded five when Pilandok entered the PAR in the last week of the month.
PAGASA explained that fewer tropical cyclones are expected in the upcoming months as the country begins to feel the effects of El Niño.
Fewer rains are expected this month, with rainfall expected to intensify by the last quarter of the year and possibly extend into the first half of 2027.
As of 4 p.m. yesterday, PAGASA was not monitoring any low-pressure area that could develop into a tropical cyclone.

Meanwhile, monsoon rains will be felt in Occidental Mindoro, while Metro Manila, Central Luzon, Calabarzon, the rest of Mimaropa, Pangasinan, La Union, Benguet, Nueva Vizcaya, Quirino, Camarines Norte, Camarines Sur, Albay, Catanduanes, Aklan and Antique will experience occasional rains due to the southwest monsoon.
Cloudy skies with scattered rains and thunderstorms will be experienced in the rest of Luzon, the rest of the Visayas, the Zamboanga Peninsula and Northern Mindanao.
The rest of the country will have partly cloudy to cloudy skies with isolated rainshowers or thunderstorms due to localized thunderstorms.

articles.title: Some senators want SC to decide on impeach vote threshold
articles.summary: Senators JV Ejercito and Raffy Tulfo want the Supreme Court to decide on the voting threshold to convict or acquit Vice President Sara Duterte amid a possible deadlock due to the continued absence of…

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Senators JV Ejercito and Raffy Tulfo want the Supreme Court to decide on the voting threshold to convict or acquit Vice President Sara Duterte amid a possible deadlock due to the continued absence of four senators.
They said allowing the SC to resolve the delicate threshold issue would unburden and save the senators from the difficulties.
“I would rather have the Supreme Court decide so we can avoid any conflict,” Tulfo said.
“Let the Supreme Court decide and save us the trouble. But it depends on what the impeachment court and the senator-judges would discuss on Sept. 23. We need to decide,” said Ejercito.
The Senate impeachment court is looking at tapping amici curiae or friends of the court as resource persons and speak in open court to help senators settle the issue.
Presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero said constitutional experts like former justices would speak on Sept. 16 before the prosecution and defense counsels hold oral arguments on Sept. 23.
On the same day, the impeachment court would vote whether or not to change Escudero’s ruling at the start of trial setting 16 votes to convict.
Escudero’s ruling was challenged by a motion by Sen. Erwin Tulfo on Tuesday questioning the phrase “all members” with respect to votes in convicting an impeached officer.
Tulfo asked whether “all members” strictly means 24 despite the absence of four senators, who are detained, at large or on leave and beyond the Senate’s coercive jurisdiction.

Tulfo pointed out that the chamber relies on the 1949 Supreme Court ruling Avelino v. Cuenco in determining a legislative quorum, which calculates the majority based only on members physically capable of attending.
Ejercito said Tulfo’s questions regarding the threshold are valid, citing the point raised by the other Tulfo that absent senators were unable to take part in the hearings.
“We will weigh things on Sept. 23 and decide what is best,” he said.
3 to 5 amici curiae
The impeachment court will invite three to five judiciary resource persons to educate the senators before they vote on the voting threshold, according to Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian.
But Gatchalian declined to name the “friends of the court” to be invited, but said he prefers former Supreme Court justices, legal luminaries and constitutionalists to educate them on Sept. 16.
“I don’t want to name names but they should be experts on the Constitution,” Gatchalian said.
Asked if the matter should instead be settled by the Supreme Court, Gatchalian said he doesn’t want to preempt the upcoming briefing with the amicus curiae and the oral arguments.
“It will depend on the explanation of the experts. We will all learn from them,” he said.

As to the requests of Sens. Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada to participate in the trial despite their detention for plunder, Gatchalian said the Senate should leave it to the Sandiganbayan to decide.
Gatchalian is hoping that the impeachment court could meet the timeline of finishing the presentation of evidence and rendering a verdict on or before December.
Duterte should testify
To face all the allegations against her and end the “trial by publicity” on social media, Duterte should testify in her impeachment trial, senators said yesterday.
The Tulfos stressed that the impeachment court is the proper forum for the Vice President to defend herself.
“Considering the so-called trial by publicity on social media, the impeachment court is the proper forum,” Erwin the younger senator said.
“This is the proper forum to explain your side, to give your side and if you have to deny it, then you have to deny it,” he added.
Raffy the older senator echoed this sentiment, noting that Duterte’s personal appearance would clear up lingering doubts.
“Ideally, yes. Let us hear it from the horse’s mouth. It is only the Vice President herself who can provide the answers,” he said.

But Erwin said the impeachment court would not compel the country’s second highest official to take the witness stand out of parliamentary courtesy, citing the precedent set during the impeachment trial of former president Joseph Estrada.
“But if she refuses, there’s nothing we can do. We cannot force her. Out of courtesy, we cannot subpoena her,” he explained.
Ejercito said impeached officers have the prerogative since they are already represented by their lawyers.
Palace press officer Claire Castro said it’s up to the impeachment court to decide whether the Vice President should take the witness stand.

“If that’s what the prosecution wants and if the Senate would allow it, let the Senate decide,” said Castro during a press briefing.?“And the prosecution is likely requesting this because the Vice President herself stated that she wanted a ‘bloodbath,’ and she had previously said she was ready to face allegations against her and clarify these issues,” she added.?“The decision rests with the Senate,” Castro said. – Marc Jayson Cayabyab, Helen Flores

articles.title: Ombudsman to oppose Martin’s bid for hospital detention
articles.summary: The Office of the Ombudsman will “strongly oppose” the bid of Leyte congressman and former speaker Martin Romualdez for continued hospital confinement as he faces detention for a…

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — The Office of the Ombudsman will “strongly oppose” the bid of Leyte congressman and former speaker Martin Romualdez for continued hospital confinement as he faces detention for a non-bailable P7.4-billion plunder charge.

“If his illnesses can be managed from outside of the hospital, the prosecutors will move that he be immediately transferred to the regular detention facility as all other accused in non-bailable cases,” Assistant Ombudsman Mico Clavano said.
He said prosecutors will ask a team of government doctors to assess Romualdez’s condition.
The Sandiganbayan Third Division issued an arrest warrant against Romualdez on Sept. 7 after his indictment, together with fugitive former congressman Zaldy Co and two others.
However, Romualdez’s camp said he had already been admitted to the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City when the arrest warrant was issued.
This prompted authorities to serve the warrant while he was in the hospital, clad in a hospital gown and hooked to medical equipment.
Romualdez’s lawyers claimed he suffered anxiety attack and a “cardiovascular event,” leading them to ask the Sandiganbayan to grant him “continued hospital confinement.”

In his motion, Romualdez has asked the court to allow him to remain at Cardinal Santos under lawful custody, saying he is suffering from hypertensive atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, unstable angina, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular ischemic disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and primary hypothyroidism.
Romualdez also noted that he underwent angioplasty surgery in October 2024 and has since required continuing cardiac monitoring and treatment.
He also claimed that he was confined at the same hospital in July this year as irregularities were found in his MRI scan examination.
As it is set to hear the motion today, the anti-graft court division has summoned four doctors of Romualdez to testify on his condition.
Romualdez is likewise directed to appear before the court “should his condition permit.”
The Sandiganbayan emphasized that custody of Romualdez belongs to the anti-graft court.

“If there are concerns regarding the accused’s medical condition, it is only this court that can determine whether such condition affects the implementation of the warrant, the confinement of the accused at a hospital or his commitment to a jail facility,” the order read.
No special treatment
An ordinary room awaits Romualdez at the Philippine National Police General Hospital (PNPGH), according to PNP chief Gen. Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr.

“The PNP assures the public that there will be no special treatment regardless of an individual’s position or status. Our duty is to uphold the rule of law and strictly observe the legal processes,” he said in a statement yesterday.

With Interior Secretary Jonvic Remulla declaring Romualdez a flight risk, police have beefed up security around Cardinal Santos hospital. Remulla said Romualdez owns two private jets, three helicopters and three yachts.

As critics slammed what they called double standard in the treatment of Romualdez, Malacañang said his doctors should be given the benefit of the doubt regarding their recommendation to let him stay in the hospital.

“The PNP or the leadership of the DILG (Department of the Interior and Local Government) cannot insist on bringing with them the accused if there is a certification that he should not be removed yet from the hospital,” Palace press officer Claire Castro said at a media briefing yesterday.

“It is up to the views of the doctors and doctors have to tell the truth. So, we will just give them the benefit of the doubt, the doctors who say that the accused is not feeling well... If he is in the hospital, maybe he will not be able to escape,” Castro said.

Asked to react to the move of the former House speaker’s camp to seek an extension of his hospital confinement, Castro said it would depend on the findings of his doctors. “For now, there is no discussion about hospital arrest,” the Palace press officer said.
“The administration will not meddle in that and we cannot second guess the feeling, the health condition of any accused,” she added.
Castro maintained that President Marcos, a first cousin of Romualdez, remains “neutral” with regard to legal processes, including the filing of charges against those accused of wrongdoing.

“We do not need to know the personal feelings of the President. What is necessary is to hold to account those who should be held to account. The feelings of the President are not likely to have an effect, whether happy or sad or whatever, it is not important,” she said.
“What is important is that justice is moving and if he needs to be held to account for any reason, it will be seen in the court. Let the court decide on this case.” – Alexis Romero, Emmanuel Tupas

articles.title: Marcos Jr. attending BRICS summit in India
articles.summary: President Marcos will visit New Delhi, India from Sept. 12 to 13 to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit.

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 12:00am

Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos (R) shakes hands with India's Prime Minister Narendra Modi during the ceremonial reception at India’s presidential palace Rashtrapati Bhavan in New Delhi on Aug. 5, 2025.
AFP / Sajjad Hussain
MANILA, Philippines — President Marcos will visit New Delhi, India from Sept. 12 to 13 to participate in the 18th BRICS Summit.

The President was invited by Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his capacity as this year’s chair of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN), according to Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA) spokesperson Analyn Ratonel.

Ratonel said the Chief Executive will have the opportunity to explain the Philippines’ key priorities as ASEAN chair to BRICS members. These priorities center on peace and security, people empowerment and prosperity.

BRICS was established as a grouping of Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa and has since expanded to include other major emerging economies. The group serves as a platform for cooperation on economic, political and development issues.

“Building a dialogue between ASEAN, led by the Philippines, and BRICS, led by India, could create significant geopolitical and economic support. Creating synergies with the priorities of ASEAN and BRICS can lead to economic opportunities, trade diversification, regional security and support for climate resilience,” Ratonel said.

“Through this visit, the President seeks to ensure that our modern partnerships remain open, resilient and capable of delivering prosperity to our people,” she said. BRICS economies account for a significant share of global economic output and trade and nearly half of the world’s population, the DFA official noted.

This year’s summit carries the theme, “Building for Resilience, Innovation, Cooperation and Sustainability,” focusing on global economic uncertainties, digital public infrastructure, innovation and collective climate action.

On the sidelines of the summit, Marcos is scheduled to meet with Modi to discuss progress on the Philippines-India Strategic Partnership and review implementation of the five-year Plan of Action for 2025 to 2029.
The two leaders are also expected to exchange views on economic issues affecting their respective countries and peoples.
The President will also meet with Indian business leaders.

The goal, Ratonel said, is to follow up on the pledges and commitments made by Indian companies last year. During Marcos’ visit to India in August 2025, Indian companies made investment pledges worth $5.8 billion covering various sectors.

articles.title: NCR tripartite board OKs P60 wage hike
articles.summary: The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board in the National Capital Region has approved an increase of P60 in the daily minimum wage.

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 12:00am
This undated photo shows an individual counting Philippine peso bills.
The Philippine STAR / Walter Bollozos
MANILA, Philippines — The Regional Tripartite Wages and Productivity Board in the National Capital Region (RTWPB-NCR) has approved an increase of P60 in the daily minimum wage.

The increase, contained in Wage Order No. 28, was disclosed by Department of Labor and Employment-NCR regional director Roy Buenaflor at Tuesday’s hearing of the House committee on appropriations on DOLE’s proposed P47.057-billion budget for 2027.
The implementation of the increase remains subject to review by the National Wages and Productivity Commission (NWPC) as a previous P85 wage hike remains under court injunction.
Buenaflor said the regional board approved Wage Order No. 28 Monday night through a 4-3 vote and forwarded it to the NWPC for the required review.
If upheld by the commission, the P60 increase would raise the daily minimum wage for non-agricultural workers in Metro Manila from P695 to P755.
Buenaflor said the wage order may be published as early as tomorrow, with the increase taking effect on Sept. 26 or 27, depending on the publication date.
The new wage order drew questions from lawmakers because the implementation of Wage Order No. 27, which granted a total P85 wage increase, remains suspended by the Pasig Regional Trial Court.
Deputy Speaker Raymond Mendoza questioned the basis for issuing a new wage order while the legal dispute involving Wage Order No. 27 remains unresolved.
Buenaflor said the regional board considered the new wage order as a way of immediately providing workers with the first tranche of the wage increase previously approved under Wage Order No. 27.
But Mendoza said the explanation was insufficient and raised concerns that the new order could cause legal complications.

Wage Order No. 27, announced by Labor Secretary Francis Tolentino in June, provided for a P85 increase in two tranches. The first P65 increase was supposed to take effect on July 25, followed by another P20 increase on Jan. 20, 2027.

Its implementation was initially stopped by a temporary restraining order issued by the Pasig RTC Branch 125 following a petition filed by two construction companies. The court later issued a writ of preliminary injunction, further preventing the implementation of the wage increase.
The Office of the Solicitor General has sought the lifting of the injunction and asked the Pasig court to resolve its pending motion for reconsideration.
Labor groups, meanwhile, criticized the issuance of Wage Order No. 28 and vowed to continue pushing for the implementation of Wage Order No. 27.
The Federation of Free Workers (FFW) and NAGKAISA Labor Coalition said they understand the position of the RTWPB-NCR and Tolentino but welcomed the move to provide workers with the P60 increase.
However, FFW president Sonny Matula said the groups would not abandon their legal fight for the full P85 increase under Wage Order No. 27.
“FFW clearly holds that a court that has no jurisdiction cannot erase July 25 with an injunction. And a new wage order should not erase July 25 with a ‘whereas’ clause,” Matula said.

“Give the P60 now. We welcome that. But don’t ask workers to exchange their possible July 25 arrears and P25 second tranche for it,” Matula said. “Plan B may move wages forward. It should not bury Plan A.”
Kamanggagawa party-list Rep. Eli San Fernando criticized the issuance of Wage Order No. 28, describing it as a reduction of the wage increase previously granted under Wage Order No. 27.

“Instead of standing by Wage Order No. 27, which was suspended by what I consider an illegal injunction issued by the Pasig RTC, the DOLE took a different course by issuing Wage Order No. 28,” San Fernando said.
Meanwhile, Malacañang assured the nation that efforts are underway to generate jobs and lure investments after the country’s unemployment rate rose to its highest level in four years.

The joblessness rate was at six percent in July, higher than the 4.9 percent posted in June and the 5.3 percent in the same period last year, according to the Philippine Statistics Authority. Last July’s rate is equivalent to 3.14 million Filipinos without job. It is the highest since June 2022. . - Alexis Romero

articles.title: 15 bank accounts of Sara, Mans match AMLC records
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel’s initial scrutiny of the bank accounts of Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio yielded positive results as 15 of them “matched”…

blocks.text: September 10, 2026 | 12:00am
Composite image shows Vice President Sara Duterte as seen in June 2026 and her husband, Mans Carpio, in April 2026.
The STAR / Miguel de Guzman; Philstar.com composite

MANILA, Philippines — The House prosecution panel’s initial scrutiny of the bank accounts of Vice President Sara Duterte and her husband Manases Carpio yielded positive results as 15 of them “matched” the details presented by the Anti-Money Laundering Council (AMLC).
“All (cross-checked) 15 matched the accounts that were identified by the AMLC,” Manila 3rd District Rep. Joel Chua, a member of the House prosecution team, said at a news briefing yesterday.
Chua, a lawyer, said they expect the defense to question former senator Antonio Trillanes’ credibility and the documents he provided by highlighting his prejudice toward the Duterte family.
But Chua maintained that the prosecution team would rely heavily on the authenticity of the AMLC documentary evidence.
“This cannot just be a say so of anybody, without any iota of evidence,” Chua said.
The prosecution is also expected, as mentioned by impeachment trial presiding officer Sen. Francis Escudero, to start presenting the unexplained wealth case of the Duterte couple on Sept. 14.

“This will be explosive, this will be exciting,” House Deputy Speaker Paolo Ortega V of La Union said as public and private prosecutors prepared the bank records and sought ways to shorten the next phase of Duterte’s impeachment trial.

He pointed to the large amounts moving through accounts as earlier discussed during the House committee on justice hearings, saying the financial records had drawn intense attention when they were first presented in 2025.
The prosecution, to be led by public prosecutor Rep. Chel Diokno (Akbayan party-list), is scheduled to begin its Article II (ill-gotten wealth) presentation on Monday.
The dates of Sept. 9 and 10 were set aside for marking more than 1,800 documents, including bank and insurance records, produced under court subpoenas.
During Tuesday’s hearing, Escudero directed Diokno to submit the prosecution’s witnesses for the following week and prepare for the scheduled resumption.
“So that we save on the court’s time and we will proceed as scheduled on Monday for the trial,” he said.
Escudero also announced full-day trial settings on Oct. 1 and 2, Oct. 5 to 9 and Oct. 12 to 15 before a suspension to give way to the Senate’s budget work.
25 witnesses
The House prosecution panel may present up to 25 witnesses to prove its allegations of unexplained wealth against the Vice President.
But Chua said the number will depend on whether the defense agrees to stipulate the authenticity of bank and other financial records of Duterte and her husband.
He said the prosecution submitted a request for admission, asking the Duterte camp to admit to the authenticity and ownership of certain bank accounts.
Chua said they are looking at 15 bank officials and if the defense agrees to stipulations, the witnesses “will be reduced by 10, more or less.”
“If they don’t agree, then we could have 20 to 25 witnesses,” he said.

Also lined up as prosecution witnesses are former senator Antonio Trillanes IV, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla or any representative of his office, as well as representatives from the Bureau of Internal Revenue, Securities and Exchange Commission and AMLC. – Daphne Galvez

articles.title: Iran tightens social control with crackdown on cafes
articles.summary: Authorities are keeping a close eye on cafes, fearing they could play a role in fostering anti-government sentiment.

image.caption: Tehran has seen a surge in the number of cafes over the past decade [FILE: April 23, 2026]Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Iranian authorities have launched a clampdown on cafes in the capital, Tehran, in recent months, suspecting them of fostering anti-government sentiment and facilitating protests.
According to the human rights organization HRANA, at least seven cafes and restaurants were shut down on July 19 alone for allegedly failing to comply with mandatory hijab rules.

Previously, some media outlets, including Javan, a newspaper affiliated with the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC), have described cafes as "gathering places for protesters" who, in their view, pose a threat to "national security."
Most recently, the "Vanak Park" cafes in Tehran were sealed, resulting in at least 200 people losing their jobs.
Crackdown on cafes
Authorities believe cafes, because of their widespread presence and popularity, could play a role in organizing mass protests.
The government's fears are rooted in the latest wave of protests in Iran, which began on December 28, 2025, and grew into the country's largest uprising since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.
Iranian women unveiled: A shift in hijab enforcement?

Saediniya, a well-known cafe chain with 10 branches in Iran, closed its branches on this day in support of calls for strikes. It was subsequently accused of engaging in "propaganda against the state."
Iran's Supreme Court has now upheld the sentence of Sadegh Saedinia, the owner of the cafe chain, to 12 years and six months in prison, along with the confiscation of his assets.
He was arrested over his support for the protests, and all branches of his cafe chain were confiscated and shut down by judicial order.

Other cafes, including "Lamiz" and "Voria," faced a broadly similar fate. Voria is owned by a prominent Iranian footballer. Both were sealed by judicial order because of their indirect support for calls to protest. Cafe closures have not been confined to periods of protest, however, and the practice continues.
The rise of the cafe culture
Tehran has seen a surge in the number of cafes over the past decade, rising from around 300 in the early 2010s to as many as 4,000 now, according to various estimates.

Some experts attribute the growing number to changes in urban lifestyles in recent years. They see this as more than the expansion of a particular type of business and describe it as a sign of wider social and cultural changes within Iranian society.

"The explosive growth of cafes in society can, to some extent, be seen as a social response to living in a state of chronic crisis," Saba Alaleh, a clinical psychologist and psychoanalyst whose work focuses on political and social issues, told DW's Persian service.
"In such circumstances, people are not simply looking to consume or be entertained. They are looking for a place to temporarily distance themselves from the pressures of everyday life," she said.

"In this sense, the cafe becomes a third space. It is neither home nor the workplace, but a space between the two where people can briefly step away from their everyday roles and pressures, connect with others, and feel that life is still somewhat manageable and normal."
Can Iran survive Trump's new sanctions?
The cafe trend has become particularly popular among Gen Z, who are bearing the brunt of runaway inflation and steep living costs in Iran.

"The young people who gather in these cafes do not necessarily come from affluent backgrounds," Nasser, a cafe owner in Tehran, told DW. "In many parts of Tehran, young people from the middle class also meet at cafes, and many of our customers belong to this group."
The political role of cafes
Even before the latest bout of nationwide protests that began at the end of last year, shutting down cafes was common practice for the Iranian government.
Most of these crackdowns and closures, however, were carried out under the pretext of enforcing compulsory hijab.
The protests that began in late December 2025 changed that, with cafes becoming the target more often and for varied reasons.
"They shut down our cafe on the pretext that we had served customers who were not wearing the hijab, but that is only an excuse," Nasser said.
"Outside, on the streets of Tehran, women and girls have effectively abandoned the compulsory hijab, yet the government expects us not to allow them into the cafe," he added.

blocks.caption: The cafe trend has become particularly popular among Gen Z, who are bearing the brunt of runaway inflation and steep living costs in Iran [FILE: April 5, 2026]Image: Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto/picture alliance

blocks.text: Maintaining control over social spaces
Alaleh said the issue is no longer simply about cracking down on women for not wearing the hijab.

"Authoritarian governments generally seek to control the flow of information, social interactions and the organization of citizens," she pointed out. "Any space beyond the direct supervision of those in power that allows trust, dialogue and social ties to develop can weaken part of the government's monopoly over the social sphere."
The expert said the crackdown on cafes and cafegoers is part of the government's efforts to preserve its monopoly over social spaces.

She underlined that to a security apparatus, even a group of young people casually sitting together can represent the emergence of an independent social network outside the formal structures of power.
"The broader and more deeply rooted these independent networks become, the more difficult it is for the government to maintain exclusive control over the public sphere," added Alaleh.

The average asking price for a rental unit in Canada in August was $2,035, down 4.8 per cent compared with a year ago.

items: Why N.S. rents are still increasing far faster than we saw historically for decades

blocks.text: Average asking rents have now fallen year over year for 23 consecutive months, with prices down seven per cent compared with 2024.
Rents were essentially flat on a monthly basis, down 0.1 per cent from July after four consecutive monthly increases through the spring and early summer.

Urbanation president Shaun Hildebrand says the escalating trade war between Canada and the United States is emerging as a new uncertainty for the rental market. Asking rents for purpose-built apartments fell 3.3 per cent year over year to an average of $2,038 last month, while asking rents for condominium apartments decreased 7.7 per cent to $2,050.

articles.title: John Malkovich cancels Israel trip over fabricated solidarity quote
articles.summary:
The Wild Horse Nine actor had been due to appear on stage in The Music Critic in Tel Aviv – but pulled out over PR firm’s ‘unacceptable and untenable’ attribution of statement

John Malkovich…

blocks.text: John Malkovich has cancelled a planned trip to Israel next year to appear on stage after a PR firm hired by the show attributed quotes to the actor that the company had written.

Malkovich, who is a leading Oscar contender for his role in Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine, was due to appear in The Music Critic, a theatrical-musical satire composed by the Jewish violinist Aleksey Igudesman, in Tel Aviv’s Charles Bronfman Auditorium on 13 April.

A press release circulated on 5 September quoted Malkovich as saying he was “thrilled to return to Israel” and looked “forward to meeting the warm Israeli audience once again, to whom I feel a strong closeness and solidarity”.

The actor, 72, was alerted to the quotes after reading them in the Hollywood Reporter, who picked them up from the Jerusalem Post. In a statement to the Hollywood Reporter on 8 September, Malkovich said that a “PR company hired by the Israeli promoter drafted a quote for the article that was attributed to me, though I never made the statements that were quoted, nor was I consulted before they were printed.”

He added: “I did not utter these phrases, and they most certainly are not approved by me, nor do they reflect my feelings. The fact that they were printed as direct quotes from me is unacceptable and untenable. For this reason, I have decided I cannot participate in the Tel Aviv performance.”

The PR firm admitted the error, releasing a statement apologising for “incorrectly” attributing the quotes to Malkovich. “Mr Malkovich did not make, provide, authorise or approve this statement, nor was it approved by his representatives,” said the firm. “We sincerely apologise to Mr Malkovich and his representatives for the incorrect attribution and regret that this occurred.”
In his lengthy statement to the Hollywood Reporter, Malkovich went on to distance himself from any implied endorsement of any country’s political actions.

“Throughout my long career, I’ve been lucky to perform across a quite wide swath of the world – in countries with governments whose values or culture I do not share and in front of audiences of many differing faiths and ideologies,” he wrote. “Travelling to places whose view of the world may not align with mine has given me a chance to observe and to listen and learn and to share my idea of what makes good storytelling and what makes beautiful music and how they can complement each other and illuminate the human condition.

“My appearance in any country, even my own, does not constitute approval of said country’s policies, nor actions, nor its elected or unelected leaders. My appearances would also not condone nor mean that I am in supposed ‘solidarity’ with any particular political cause, nor with the killing of innocents, nor with any acts of terrorism, nor any other kind of barbarity.”
Malkovich last visited Israel in 2013 when he appeared on stage in The Infernal Comedy: Confessions of a Serial Killer; five years previously he was guest of honour at the Jerusalem film festival.

In 2011, he told an interviewer he was not a “political person”, lacked “an ideology”, and hadn’t voted since 1972. In 2002, speaking at the Cambridge Union, Malkovich said the two people he’d most like to kill were journalist Robert Fisk and politician George Galloway.
The actor did not elaborate on his comments, but some speculated they concerned the then-MP’s call the previous month for people in Scotland to boycott goods from Israel.

The actor’s statement to the Hollywood Reporter closed with a caution, saying: “I look forward to continuing to exercise my artistic freedom, come what may. However, only playwrights, novelists and screenwriters can put words in my mouth, and even then, only in the service of storytelling, and no one else should think they can do that without my consent and without the resultant consequences.”

In Wild Horse Nine, Malkovich plays a terminally ill CIA agent who travels to Easter Island with colleague Sam Rockwell in the mid 1970s. The film, which premiered at Venice earlier this month, is widely expected to land the actor his third Academy Award nomination.

articles.title: Ethiopia's constitutional reform: What does it mean — especially for Abiy?
articles.summary: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed stands to benefit from a planned constitutional reform in the country. A new presidential system would reshape political power — and could give him a more powerful…

image.caption: After the National Dialogue: Is Ethiopia heading towards a new presidential system?Image: Ethiopia National Dialogue Commission

blocks.text: Since 2018, Abiy Ahmedhas been the most powerful man in Ethiopian politics, governing the country during some of its most trying days in recent history. From the Tigray war to a feeble but lasting peace with neighboring Eritrea, Abiy has actively shaped and reshaped Ethiopia's role in Africa and indeed the world.
Soon, he might even get to consolidate more power and influence in his office, as Ethiopia's political system might fundamentally change in the future.

Following weeks-long consultations, there are indications that the offices of prime minister and president could potentially be merged. This would mean that the largely ceremonial presidency could thus become the center of political power in the country.
While details about the precise re-designing of the system remain unclear, local reports say that the consultations indeed resulted in a positive recommendation to create a stronger presidency.
For Abiy, that would likely be a remarkable prospect.

blocks.caption: For Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, a constitutional reform could mean greater powers.Image: Office of the Prime Minister-Ethiopia

blocks.text: Support for a new office

During a drawn-out national dialogue with around 4,000 delegates in Addis Ababa in recent weeks, participants discussed some of the country's key political conflict, including: the overall structure of the state, ongoing ethnic tensions, the rule of law and human rights — as well as the role of the prime minister.
Abiy did not take part in these meetings but could benefit significantly from their endorsement of a presidential system.

One key element for any constitutional reform to be pushed through parliament is already in place: Abiy won June's parliamentary elections with a massive majority, which could help him and his party with advocating for a presidency with broader executive powers.
Benefits of a stronger presidency
Supporters of a stronger presidency see it as a way of bringing Ethiopia's ethnically and regionally fragmented society closer together.
A president representing the country as a whole could help strengthen a national political identity.

Befeqadu Hailu, an Ethiopian civil rights activist and political commentator, told DW that this might be a strength of the proposed new system, and that a president directly elected by the public would have a stronger mandate to govern.

Hailu believes that in future elections, a presidential candidate would have to convince "more than one ethnic group and more than one religious group" to win an election, which could help strengthen democratic processes.
At the same time, he issued a warning that "[p]residential systems are more prone descending into dictatorship."

blocks.caption: Ethiopia's National Dialogue concluded on August 22, 2026, in Addis AbabaImage: Ethiopia National Dialogue Commission

blocks.text: How much more power is there to take?
But the key question is not who would become presiden but rather what powers this office would have — as well as who would be tasked with holding the president to account.
Ethiopia already has a powerful executive branch and since taking office in 2018, Abiy has consolidated more and more political power.

The creation of the Prosperity Party in 2019 under his leadership out of a number of coalition partners has already considerably reshaped the country's political system, significantly limiting the role of the opposition.
Abiy already controls the military and security apparatus, with little less power left to grab under a new system.
For British journalist and Ethiopia expert Martin Plaut, the proposed reform is therefore less of a transfer of power to one person that an act of "formalizing the situation that currently exists."
What Addis Ababa voters said about Ethiopia's elections
'Legal does not mean legitimate'

The proposed reform also raises a fundamental question about democratic processes: Can such a concentration of power be viewed as the will of the people if it is enacted through legal procedures in parliament? Or should there perhaps be a plebiscite on the proposed changes?

In this context, civil rights activist Hailu highlights the importance of distinguishing between procedural and popular legitimacy. In Ethiopia, he says, existing political institutions have "procedural legitimacy" to enact such changes while they lack broad "popular legitimacy."
Hailu says bluntly that "no one believes that Ethiopia has ever had democratic elections," referring to the most recent parliamentary election, which took place under difficult conditions:
Voting was not possible in several conflict-ridden regions of the country, while opposition parties reported instances of restrictions and repression.
It is therefore unclear to what extent the result of the poll can be regarded as democratically legitimate — yet it is seen as the official result.

This is why Hailu believes that parliament may have the formal authority to amend the constitution and introduce a presidential system while still being only partially representative of the voting populace.

blocks.caption: Members of the Tigray community and other Ethiopians held a demonstration to protest mandatory military service in the Tigray region. Location: Addis Ababa, on july, 18th, 2026Image: Solomon Mucie/DW

blocks.text: Who was actually included in the process?
Another issue is not only what was recommended by those participating in the national dialogue but also who exactly took part in it — and who didn't.

The composition of the dialogue, which eventually issued the recommendation to change the current system, is a major concern, as opposition parties boycotted the process, while influencial armed groups with strong political aspirations were equally not represented.
Despite certain valid reservations about some of these movements, the result was that some of the major political forces most directly involved in Ethiopia's current conflicts therefore were absent.
Plaut says this leaves only one conclusion: "Without the opposition parties and armed factions, the process lacks the backing of groups that feel alienated by the current system, he explains
"I'm sure that the Prime Minister will get what he wants," Plaut says, describing the dialogue as merely a "rubber-stamping exercise."

Hailu also shared some critical views on the lack of political inclusion of opposing groups, arguing that it was ultimately aimed at implementing changes "based on the vision of the Prosperity Party itself."

blocks.caption: Ethiopia's Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed, Eritrea's President Isaias Afwerki and Tigray People's Liberation Front leader Debretsion Gebremichael have managed to reach a tentative peaceImage: Office of the Prime Minister-Ethiopia

blocks.text: No resolution in sight for Ethiopia's neverending conflicts
Ethiopia's biggest challenges meanwhile are unlikely to be solved with a different style of leadership.

Armed conflicts continue in Oromia and Amhara; the 2020-2022 war in Tigray left deep political and social divisions, with many political and territorial issues remaining unresolved despite promising peace initiatives. And nearly half the population continue to live below the poverty line.
Plaut thinks that a new system of government will hardly address these problems; he believes that the proposed reforms amount to little more than "sticking a plaster on what is a gaping wound."

The relationship between centralized power in Addis Ababa and Ethiopia's more than 80 ethnic groups remains unresolved, he argues. Previous attempts to ease tensions between the center and the periphery have failed.
In Plaut's view, the underlying tensions between the central government and Ethiopia's various ethnic and regional groups have to be resolved first.

articles.title: Apple expected to unveil pricey folding iPhone in its 1st major overhaul in a decade
articles.summary: Apple is widely expected to unveil a pricey folding iPhone at a launch event on Wednesday at its Cupertino, Calif., headquarters.

image.caption: A person uses a phone to capture iPhones on display during Apple's event at the Steve Jobs Theater in Cupertino, Calif., on Sept. 9, 2025. Apple is expected to unveil its new folding iPhone on Wednesday. (Manuel Orbegozo/Reuters)

blocks.text: Business·New
Apple is widely expected to unveil a pricey folding iPhone at a launch event on Wednesday at its Cupertino, Calif., headquarters.
Event will be the first with new CEO John Ternus at the helm

The event, the first with new CEO John Ternus at the helm, will be the most noticeable overhaul of Apple's flagship product since it removed the physical home button from the iPhone X in 2017. The iPhone brought in $209.6 billion US ($288.8 billion Cdn), or slightly more than half of Apple's sales, in its most recent fiscal year.

The keynote address will also be the first extended commentary from Ternus, who previously served as Apple's hardware chief but has kept a low public profile aside from a handful of product introductions and sustainability initiatives.

It will fall to Ternus to persuade Apple's customers that they need a foldable device that could cost more than $2,000 US (about $2,755 Cdn), a new high for a global brand that has defined mass luxury.

The first iPhone in 2007 mainstreamed touch-screen technology, years after it was developed. Now Apple is betting its first foldable phone can do the same for a format stuck in a niche despite years of efforts from Samsung and Chinese rivals like Huawei.
Even with a steep price tag, analyst firms such as IDC expect Apple will sell every foldable iPhone it can produce and secure a 40 per cent share of the lucrative niche by the end of next year.

items: John Ternus is replacing Tim Cook as Apple CEO. But he faces a big challenge in AI
Shocked by how much she used her smartphone, a tech reporter switched to a flip phone instead

blocks.text: Analysts also expect Apple to benefit from its late entry into the folding phone category by mastering key engineering challenges such as creating an elegant-but-sturdy hinge that can survive repeated opening and minimize how much of a crease shows where the screen folds.

One key remaining challenge could be how well the devices resist dust and water, an area in which Google's most recent Pixel 10 Pro Fold bested Samsung's offerings with what is known as an IP68 rating, meaning the device is dust-tight and can be dunked in a metre of water.
Wednesday's event is also expected to mark a major change in Apple's annual product schedule.

While analysts expect Apple to show off new watches, they anticipate the company will hold off on updates to its more affordable iPhone models until next spring and instead focus only on the new folding device and its iPhone Pro and Pro Max lineup.
The move is aimed at smoothing out Apple's annual sales cycle, which typically shows a large bump in revenue during the year-end holiday quarter for the U.S. and Europe.

Despite attracting attention with their large screen size, foldable phones have only secured a single-digit percentage share of the overall global smartphone market due to trade-offs — including inferior cameras, a shorter battery life and an awkward crease at the screen centre once the handsets are unfolded.

articles.title: Tens of thousands line the streets as Norway bids farewell to King Harald V
articles.summary: Europe’s royals and global political figures attend ceremony that brings 13 days of national mourning to a close

blocks.text: Norway has observed a minute’s silence as it takes leave of King Harald V in a series of ceremonies, bringing to a close 13 days of ​national mourning that followed the popular monarch’s death last month at the age of 89.

Tens of thousands of people lined the streets of Oslo and foreign heads of state and government converged on the Norwegian capital for the funeral of the late king, a light-touch and unassuming reformer who ruled for more than three decades.

With the king’s casket carried on an artillery carriage, draped in Norway’s red royal banner and topped with white flowers, the funeral cortege made its way on foot along Oslo’s main avenue from royal palace to the cathedral, as a 21-gun salute rang out from the Akershus fortress.

blocks.caption: Norway’s Prince Sverre Magnus, King Haakon VIII, Crown Princess Ingrid Alexandra, and Princess Martha Louise walk behind the coffin of King Harald V. Photograph: Ole Berg-Rusten/EPA

blocks.text: King Haakon VIII, who succeeded his father on Harald’s death, and other royal family members walked behind the coffin, with Harald’s widow, Queen Sonja, 89, and Haakon’s wife, Queen Mette-Marit, who is recovering from a lung transplant in June, following in a car.

blocks.caption: Despite its recent scandals, the monarchy remains broadly popular. Photograph: Cornelius Poppe/NTB Scanpix/AP

blocks.text: The procession was followed by a church ceremony attended by royals including the Britain’s Prince William and Princess Anne; Spain’s King Felipe and Queen Letizia; ‌Sweden’s royal family; Denmark’s King Frederik and Queen Mary; the Netherlands’ King Willem-Alexander and Queen Maxima; and Japan’s Crown Prince Akishino.

Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and political leaders and dignitaries from more than 20 countries were at the service, at which the speaker of Norway’s parliament, Masud Gharahkhani, recalled a monarch who was “not afraid to meet his people with his rubber boots on”.

blocks.caption: The Prince of Wales and Princess Anne leaving the funeral service. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

blocks.text: The prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, said Harald “struck a balance between being stately and being down-to-earth. He made Norway greater. He spoke of a ‘we’ in Norway where everyone is there for each other.”

After the service four F-35 fighter jets flew over the cathedral, one breaking away to symbolise the king’s passing. The casket was then carried to the Akershus fortress where it was due to be lowered into the royal crypt, next to Harald’s parents and grandparents, in a private ceremony.

blocks.caption: A painted portrait of Norway’s King Harald V is displayed among flowers and Norwegian flags at a makeshift memorial outside the royal palace in Oslo. Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Norwegian police said securing the funeral had been the largest planned operation in the force’s history. More than 46,000 Norwegians have filed past the king’s casket in the past week and schoolchildren were allowed to miss ⁠classes for the occasion.
after newsletter promotion

Harald’s death came at a time of numerous crises for the Norwegian royal family, with Mette-Marit, 53, in particular coming under heavy criticism – including from the prime minister – for her association with the late US sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

blocks.caption: Marius Borg Høiby leaves the funeral service. Photograph: Dylan Martinez/Reuters

blocks.text: The new queen’s son from a previous relationship, Marius Borg Høiby, who is under house arrest and wearing an ankle monitor pending his appeal against a conviction for rape and domestic violence, was given permission to attend the funeral and was a pall-bearer during the transfer of Harald’s coffin to the royal chapel.

Despite its recent scandals, however, the monarchy remains broadly popular: 72% of Norwegians support it, while 20% favour a republic or another form of government, according to a poll for the public broadcaster NRK.

blocks.caption: The casket of King Harald V leaves the royal palace for Oslo Cathedral. Photograph: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP/Getty Images

articles.title: Uganda pulling out of Prince Harry's Invictus Games, says military chief
articles.summary: The decision, announced by the chief of defence, comes just two months after Uganda said it would participate.

blocks.text: The Ugandan military chief's announcement follows a letter sent this week on behalf of the King which made clear that Prince Harry and Meghan, who have now returned to the UK, were not working royals.
A report in The Times newspaper quoted the general's concerns about the "Harry-Meghan nonsense", suggesting this was the background to the decision.

"In order not to be construed as being opposed to His Majesty King Charles III of the United Kingdom, whom we deeply revere, Uganda hereby withdraws from the Invictus Games," said the general in an overnight post.
"We shall not participate in anything that does not have His Majesty's approval."
However, royal sources have said that the King encourages all projects which support wounded service personnel.
A spokesman for the Invictus Games said they had not received any official information about a potential withdrawal and have been seeking clarification from their contacts in Uganda.
Among other posts on X from General Kainerugaba on Thursday was one that read: "I consider myself the most handsome, most daring and glorious Commander who ever lived."
There was also a series of angry messages about other generals who had danced without his permission.

The participation of Uganda in the next games, to be held next year in Birmingham, was announced in July, when Prince Harry was in London promoting the sports event, which celebrates the resilience and rehabilitation of wounded military men and women.
Uganda had become the 26th country to take part in the games.

articles.title: The RBA hoped this year’s three interest rate rises would tame inflation – but nothing is going their way
articles.summary: The breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, rising oil prices and the explosion in data centre investment are making the central bank’s task harder

blocks.text: For five years the Reserve Bank has been trying to wrangle inflation back to its 2.5% target, and for years it has essentially failed.
The result is a cost of living crisis that has generated intense community grievance.
The RBA’s deputy governor, Andrew Hauser, acknowledged as much on the ABC’s 7:30 report on Tuesday.
“People are furious about inflation,” Hauser said.
“Inflation has been above target for a long period of time and at some point we will have to say, ‘That is long enough’.”
Are we at that point? Not yet, said Hauser, even as he hinted we are getting closer every day.
The RBA’s nine-member board had hoped this year’s three interest rate hikes would be enough to bend the arc of inflation slowly back to reach 2.5% by the end of next year.
But nothing is going their way.
The latest blow is the complete breakdown of the US-Iran ceasefire, with escalating tit-for-tat strikes on oil tankers and infrastructure in and around the strait of Hormuz.
The global oil benchmark has risen above $US100 a barrel for the first time since July. Fuel prices are tracking higher once again, with unleaded approaching $2.10 a litre and diesel passing $2.50.

Then there is this year’s sudden explosion in datacentre investment. That has heaped pressure on a construction sector already struggling to get the materials and labour it needs to build the massive pipeline of work to build homes, roads and rails.
Households are complaining a lot and feeling depressed, but there’s still a surprising lot of spending happening, which is keeping consumption growth ticking along.
Meanwhile, Australia’s productivity performance – the thing that could make it easier for the economy to grow without pushing inflation up – remains flat.
Investors and an increasing number of economists believe we are approaching that point when the RBA has to say “enough is enough” and act more aggressively to get price rises back under control.
Financial markets are pricing in more than a 70% chance of another rate hike on 29 September, and even the chance of a second by the end of the year.
after newsletter promotion
“Of course we could raise interest rates sharply,” Hauser said.
“We could do it tomorrow. We could no longer take seriously the full employment part of our objective [and say] we’re gonna bring inflation down come hell or high water.”
Here Hauser is pointing out that the RBA has not been asleep at the wheel, but has been making a conscious calculation.
Since mid-2021, annual inflation has only been below 3% for one year.
On the other hand, unemployment has been below 5% for almost all of that time – a labour market record unmatched in modern Australia history.
“The reason as a board we have decided to take it slowly is to preserve as many jobs in this country as we could,” Hauser said, and not for the first time.
But the balance is starting to shift.
“We have one big problem, and that’s inflation,” he said.
“Inflation is too high, that’s why we raised interest rates three times at the beginning of this year. The question now, frankly, for us is have we done enough, or is more needed.”

articles.title: ‘I fear the price could be high’: Inside the German state where the far-right surged
articles.summary:
After the AfD’s landslide win in Saxony-Anhalt, people in the state capital share what they make of the result – and what comes next

•

blocks.text: Asking residents in a city where a seismic political event has just taken place ‘How do you feel?’ demands chutzpah – this struck me as I walked around Magdeburg, Germany on Monday. The night before, the far-right populist, anti-immigrant, pro-Kremlin party Alternative für Deustchland (AfD) had landslide 44% win in Saxony-Anhalt’s state elections, sending shock waves to Berlin, across Germany and way beyond. Regardless of how people in the capital voted, it felt like a bit of an affront to probe. Given the radical plans of the victors, a party classified by domestic intelligence as “rightwing extremist”, that is what I wanted to know. But from the 21-year-old Guinean-German paramedic I met at the central bus station, collecting donations for a local hospice, to the elderly couple returning to their apartment after a stroll down the Elbe river, almost everyone I met opened up to me warmly.

Judith, 88, was initially reluctant to talk, but shared some of her life story. Her experience as an eight-year-old refugee, forced to leave Poland in 1946 and eventually ending up move with her family in Magdeburg, had shaped her outlook on life, her successful career as a project engineer – as well as her politics. The news that AfD had not only won the election, but by such a wide margin, was “heartbreaking”, she said.

Huy, from Vietnam, who runs a newsagents in the city centre, was also reticent, but laughed and rolled his eyes as he sold the last copy of that day’s local paper, Die Volksstimme, and pointed to the headline that read: “Landslide in Saxony-Anhalt”. Shaking his head, he said: “44%!” “I don’t want to think what it might mean … but maybe it will all be OK?” His question hung in the air.

A glance at the AfD’s manifesto, in particular its pledge for the first 100 days, focuses the mind. Top of the list: challenging Germany’s post-war memory culture (which it says stands in the way of national pride) – so, “more Bismarck, less Hitler”, as they put it. “From the first minute”, they say, the party will start the deportation of what it refers to as “irregular migrants”.

I met Franz-Josef, a 71-year-old retired mechanic and Green voter, on holiday from a small west German town. He called the election a “catastrophe”, particularly in the light of the country’s Nazi past.

Luisa, a 34-year-old bank teller told me she hopes “those who voted for the AfD thought about what they were doing”. It was one thing, she said, to “deliver a kick in the shins” to Berlin, over its failure to pull the German economy out of the doldrums. And maybe the AfD would fail to push through its promises in government. “But we cannot know, and I fear the price could be high.”
Fragrance of power

It remains unclear how precisely the AfD, led by charismatic former fragrance salesman Ulrich Siegmund, might take the reins of power in Saxony-Anhalt, if at all. He lacks an absolute majority by a whisker.

There have been rumblings for days – even prior to the election – of an AfD charm offensive to try to lure members of chancellor Friedrich Merz’s Christian Democrats, to make up the necessary numbers. The CDU denies any defections are expected.

Some AfD members have brazenly appropriated Ronald Reagan’s appeal to the Soviets to “tear down this wall”, from his 1987 speech in West Berlin. They are calling on mainstream parties to “tear down the firewall”, a reference to the Brandmauer, or refusal to ever coalesce with the AfD in an effort to prevent the far-right populists from coming to power. Yet an increasing number doubt that the firewall will hold much longer. Especially now that almost one in two of those who cast their votes on Sunday have opted for the party. Turnout at 78% was a record for the state.
after newsletter promotion

Whatever the outcome, we can expect weeks, even months of wrangling. Expect stasis in the meantime on the federal government front, as we’re close to elections on 20 September in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern and Berlin, where the AfD is also expected to do well. Merz will be wary of doing anything that might drive more voters away. At the same time politicos in Berlin are debating how long he has in the job. In the Bundestag today, Merz accused the AfD of seeking “ethnic cleansing”.

No wonder Maryam, 16, whom I met as she returned from work experience at a retirement home, said she and her family were on edge. The Syrian teenager, whose father arrived in Germany in 2015, followed by her and her mother, told me she couldn’t stop thinking about what this vote might mean for her family. She wished, she said, for a return to the days of Angela Merkel, the German chancellor who welcomed in a million migrants including Maryam’s father, resentment over which turbo-charged support for the then-fledgling AfD.

Across the road, Doreen, a cleaner, who reluctantly admitted voting for the AfD, said: “What on Earth is there to thank Merkel for? It’s owing to her that we are in the state we’re in.” She recalled an attack near the Christmas market in the city centre in 2024, where six people were killed when a Saudi doctor drove a car into the crowd, an incident that helped fuel support for the AfD. “That attack is symbolic for a whole lot of misery, the decision to open our doors to strangers has brought us,” Doreen told me. “I say, good on the AfD for promising to clean up the mess.”
For such a small state, home to 2.1 million people, Saxony-Anhalt has managed to create a political maelstrom, the ramifications of which will be felt across Europe.

articles.title: Oil prices rise above $100 a barrel for first time since July as Iran war escalates
articles.summary: Brent crude up by more than 3% after latest fire between US and Iran in Gulf and Houthi attacks on Saudi cities

blocks.text: The price of oil has risen above $100 a barrel for the first time since July as the escalating conflict in the Middle East threatens further disruption to global supplies.
Brent crude, the international benchmark for oil prices, rose by more than 3% to top $101 after tensions increased in the Gulf amid the latest tit-for-tat exchange of fire between the US and Iran.

The US military said it had “destroyed” multiple Iranian tankers, after Tehran attempted to strike a US navy warship with ballistic missiles. The previous nightm Iran-backed Houthis attacked four cities in Saudi Arabia, wounding more than 70 people and setting oil installations ablaze.

UK and mainland Europe gas prices also soared on Wednesday. The benchmark Dutch gas contract rose by almost 4% to €78.73 a megawatt hour, the highest since January 2023. Meanwhile, the British contract rose by 7.77p to 196.57p a therm, the highest since December 2022.

On Tuesday, the Bank of England governor, Andrew Bailey, said the latest rise in oil prices was putting pressure on inflation and interest rates. “The risks, I’m afraid, are on the upside,” he told MPs. “And that’s really the risks coming from energy prices.”
The oil price has jumped by a quarter since early August as hopes for a permanent resolution to the six-month-old war faded.
The climb in costs has hit UK motorists, with petrol at the pump reaching an average of 166.2p a litre on Tuesday, the highest level in four years, according to the motoring body the AA.
The AA said diesel hit an average of 187.7p, a price it last reached in May. Prices for a litre of petrol have risen 4.4p since the August bank holiday, with diesel up 4.1p.

Households will face further pressure on their bills when Ofgem’s energy price cap rises by 4% in October. Andrew Goodwin, the chief UK economist at the consultancy Oxford Economics, has predicted that the cap could now rise by a further 13% in January.
“Wholesale prices are currently well above the level of the previous observation window, and our commodities team expect them to remain high in the near term,” he said.

The energy companies BP, Shell and the British Gas owner, Centrica, were among the top performers across the FTSE 100 on Wednesday morning, with their shares rising by at least 1% on the back of the higher oil price. The index was down by 0.5% overall.
Brent is up more than 60% this year, and has risen above the $100 mark for three periods so far in 2026.
China, the world’s largest importer of crude, has increased purchases in recent days, after a hiatus that had been a factor keeping oil prices somewhat in check in the early part of the conflict.
after newsletter promotion
Giovanni Staunovo, a commodity analyst at UBS Global Wealth Management, said: “For the direction of crude prices, we are also monitoring Chinese crude imports as a key indicator.

“Chinese crude imports recovered to nearly 9m barrels per day in August, up from the June low of 7.15m, but still lower compared to the [pre-conflict] February imports of 12.6m. It looks like the recovery trend could continue.”
Oil prices have fluctuated in the six months since the start of Tehran’s block on the strait of Hormuz prompted what many feared would be the greatest energy supply disruption in history.

In the first weeks after the first US-Israeli attacks on Iran in late February, oil prices soared past $100 a barrel. The oil price peaked at $126 in April but later fell back amid hopes of a ceasefire. The price then began to climb again after the memorandum of understanding between the US and Iran fell apart and hostilities restarted.

The rise in energy prices has stoked fears about inflation and the prospect of higher interest rates this year. In the US, economists are expecting at least one interest rate rise from the Federal Reserve by the end of the year.
