articles.title: Burnham sees sanctions against Israeli settlements as an electoral asset
articles.summary: While a survey found Labour, Lib Dem and Green voters to be the strongest backers of such a ban on trade, even Tory and Reform voters were in favour overall

blocks.text: There was a time when placing Israel under strict trade sanctions would have been a politically risky thing for a British prime minister to do. Andy Burnham, however, considers it an electoral asset.

As Kemi Badenoch attacked him over defence spending at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, Burnham deliberately turned the topic to the trade ban on illegal settlements which he had announced on Tuesday.

With the foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, sitting to his left, the prime minister said: “In this difficult and dangerous world Britain has to stand for something, Britain has to show leadership, Britain has to stand for fairness against injustice.

“Where people are being bullied out of their homes and intimidated, we will always stand with the underdog and take what action we can to support them. That, Mr Speaker, is leadership on the world stage: Britain being true to what it’s always been about.
“That is what the British people expect of us and that is what this government will do.”

Under the new sanctions announced on Tuesday, goods produced in illegal settlements in occupied Palestine will be banned from being imported into the UK and those who help build or finance settlements will face sanctions.
The measures drew a sharp response from the Israeli government, which announced the closure of the British consulate in East Jerusalem.
Domestically, the opposition has been led by Badenoch, who has long been a staunch ally of Israel.
In a piece in the Jewish Chronicle, the Conservative leader warned that the prime minister risked “fanning the flames of antisemitism here at home”.
“For all Labour claim to have rooted out antisemitism internally, the degree of anti-Israel hatred means that Labour’s approach to many of these issues is Corbyn in all but name,” she added.
Others in her party, however, have struck a less aggressive tone.

On Tuesday, the shadow foreign secretary, Tom Tugendhat, said: “None of us here rejects the government’s stated aim that we must do everything we can to end the circle of violence and support the Abraham accords and the two-state solution.
“What we reject is performative politics, acting alone, that leaves our envoys irrelevant and our voice weaker.”
Some senior Conservatives even backed the government.

Edward Leigh, who as father of the house has held his seat longer than any other MP, told the Commons on Tuesday: “I am proud to say that I absolutely and fully support what he is doing today, because it is about standing up for freedom, for morality and for justice for all people in this world.”
The government has reason to believe it is on strong electoral ground with this decision.
A poll by YouGov earlier in the summer found 50% of British voters supported a ban on trade with West Bank settlements, while only 16% were opposed.
While Labour, Liberal Democrat and Green voters were the strongest backers of such a move, even Conservative and Reform voters were in favour overall.
Labour officials hope the announcement may help them make up ground with progressive and Muslim voters who have moved away from the party since the 2024 election.

Many say they remain angry about an interview given by Keir Starmer soon after the Gaza war began in which the then prime minister said he thought Israel had the right to withhold water and electricity from Palestinians.
The disillusionment among Muslim voters was particularly important in the Green party’s victory in Gorton and Denton.
Meanwhile Labour lost a large part of its broader progressive base during the local elections, in which the Greens took a number of councils and mayoralties in central London.

Zack Polanski, the leader of the Greens in England and Wales, tweeted on Tuesday: “Ed Miliband’s statement on Israel is only a first step. We need to go further: a full ban on goods, services & investment.”
Labour and the Greens are now again locked in battle, over the Holborn and St Pancras seat, which Starmer has vacated.
Though the policy was in train long before that byelection was called, it could prove an important campaign tool for Labour canvassers looking to reassure their core voters.

articles.title: Oil prices rise as Middle East conflict escalates
articles.summary: The price of oil returned to triple digits in US dollars, as conflict in the Middle East threatens supply chains and puts a strain on global reserves.

image.caption: Brent crude rose above $100 a barrel for the first time since JulyImage: Maxim Shemetov/REUTERS

blocks.text: Oil crude prices topped $100 ($86) a barrel on Wednesday for the first time since July amid concerns over oil supplies due to the conflict in the Middle East.

"The move towards and back above $100 Brent is reflecting a market that increasingly must change its view on how long the Middle East crisis will continue to curb supply from the region," said Ole Hansen, head of commodity strategy at the Danish Saxo Bank.
The attacks on Saudi energy facilities by the Iranian-backed Houthisthreaten oil shipments on the Red Sea. This has been a key alternative route to the Strait of Hormuz path.

Meanwhile, the US attacked Iranian oil tankers in the Gulf of Oman and in the Strait of Hormuz. "Iran has used the tankers as part of a multibillion-dollar shadow network that funds the IRGC and its regional proxies," CENTCOM said in a statement.
Runing out of stock
Since the conflict in the Middle East started, oil exports have been reduced significantly, making some countries turn to their reserves.

The US has reported its lowest oil reserve since 1982, holding 289.7 million barrels. Former US President Joe Biden and President Donald Trump have used the reserve to cushion consumer prices amid the crisis.

The new price of the barrel is still below the peak reached early this year. In April, Brent jumped to $126 a barrel. Experts believe this is a big risk to a market with little room for capacity to absorb new disruptions occasioned by the war.

articles.title: Peter’s farm is on ‘flood country’. As Australia’s sea levels rise, safe land is vanishing and costs are huge
articles.summary:
Climate Council forecasts more than 267,000 coastal properties will be damaged by flooding by 2100, costing hundreds of billions of dollars

  • Get our

blocks.text: When grazier Peter Lake moved to the Clarence Valley in the New South Wales northern rivers region in 2007, he knew was “buying in flood country with … eyes open”.
His cattle farm, about halfway between Yamba and Grafton, borders the Coldstream River and has flooded five times since 2009.

“Out of 130 acres … in a major flood we would have maybe 15 acres that were flood-free,” he said. Lake has systems in place to prepare for such events, including moving cattle to the dry paddocks, where they would also store fodder to feed the animals.

But the amount of safe ground is shrinking: in the historically big flood in 2022, “we only had just a few acres of flood-free land”. Because of both drought and frequent floods, “we just haven’t been able to successfully grow a fodder crop for some years”.

“If we’re going to have more frequent and more severe major events … we need to change the way we think about how we manage,” Lake said. “If rising sea levels impact on us, it’ll just this make property less and less viable.”

blocks.caption: Grazier Peter Lake on his Clarence Valley cattle farm. Photograph: Peter Lake

blocks.text: Agricultural damages are among $855.1bn in economic losses projected Australia-wide by the end of the century due to coastal flooding, according to a Climate Council report released on Thursday.
The report forecasts that more than 267,000 coastal properties and 2m hectares (4.9m acres) of Australian land will be damaged by flooding by 2100 as sea levels rise.
Queensland (93,157 properties), NSW (71,210) and Western Australia (51,366) are the three states with the greatest number of homes at risk.
The Gold Coast, Brisbane and Melbourne are the metropolitan areas expected to be worst affected.

blocks.caption: Coastal areas around Brisbane and the Gold Coast are at significant risk, the Climate Council says. Illustration: Climate Council

blocks.text: The Gold Coast, the country’s most exposed urban area, faces $84.4bn in projected economic losses, while in Melbourne, losses are concentrated in low-lying areas around Port Phillip Bay and the Yarra River.

The Climate Council report is based on mapping coastal flooding by 2100, taking into account both sea level rise and storm surges under the climate scenario known as RCP4.5 – which projects a 2.7C increase in global temperature by the end of the century, similar to expected heating based on current policies worldwide.

blocks.caption: Coastal areas around Port Phillip Bay are vulnerable to rising seas. Illustration: Climate Council

blocks.text: It was co-authored by Prof Tom Kompas at the University of Melbourne, whose modelling of the economic impacts was also published in the peer-reviewed journal Scientific Reports and drew upon localised projections at 239 hotspots around Australia.
after newsletter promotion

Kompas said the costs – an estimated $274.3bn in property losses and $580.7bn in land use damages – were a conservative estimate, and did not take into account the additional impacts of coastal erosion or significant ice sheet melt.
He said due to the scale of agricultural losses, there was a food security issue potentially coming as well: damage is projected to affect 619,713 hectares (1.5m acres) of farming land.

blocks.caption: A map showing coastal areas at risk in NSW and the projected economic damage. Illustration: Climate Council

blocks.text: Sea levels have risen, on average by more than 22cm globally since 1900, with human-caused global heating the dominant cause of the rise since 1970. An additional 14cm rise is expected in Australia by 2050, increasing the frequency of permanent inundation and tidal flooding.
Kompas said that while reducing greenhouse gas emissions to limit global heating was of paramount importance, “we have to start planning and responding and adapting now”.
“The nice thing about the work is it shows where the hotspots are and what … assets will be impacted. So we can start to plan for how to deal with that.
“The first thing, of course, is not to build on flood plains, which is common still.”

articles.title: RentTech companies asking tenants for personal details ‘completely outside’ new Victorian laws
articles.summary:
Some rental platforms encourage hopeful tenants to share ‘excessive’ amount of information, Consumer Policy Research Centre review finds

  • Get our

blocks.text: So-called “RentTech” companies may be circumventing new Victorian laws designed to protect tenants’ personal data by asking for information outside the rental application process, a review as found.

The Consumer Policy Research Centre (CPRC) identified rental platforms that encouraged hopeful tenants to share an “excessive” amount of personal information, or asked them questions that were “completely outside” the new rules.

RentTech platforms are increasingly used by real estate agents in Australia for people applying for rental properties to submit applications and supporting documentation, meaning they store sensitive data.

An Australian Housing and Research Institute report released in January found while providing personal information is necessary for rental agreements, the “over-collection of data poses significant risks to renters’ data security and privacy”.

In addition to potentially putting people’s privacy at risk, RentTech companies continued to use controversial tools such as screening tests and “rewards” schemes, the CPRC found in its report on the sector, released on Thursday.

As part of its report, the CPRC reviewed Victoria’s rental reforms which, in March, established a new standard rental application form designed to limit the information real estate agents can request from renters.
Victorian rental providers and agents can now only ask for the information set out in the standard form, which covers the details needed to confirm a renter’s identity and ability to pay rent.
The CPRC’s deputy chief executive, Chandni Gupta, said while there had been improvements in Victoria, these had not extended to other parts of Australia.

For example, in other jurisdictions, rental platforms were still asking more invasive questions of prospective tenants and charging people third-party fees for background checks or to process their applications and rental payments.
“Big tech will move the needle just enough and will narrowly follow, but likely won’t offer that same service outside of where there’s no obligations to do so,” Gupta said.
In New South Wales and South Australia, RentTech companies are banned from charging prospective tenants for background checks, but they are still allowed to request them.
after newsletter promotion

Between November 2025 and March 2026, the CPRC reviewed six RentTech platforms used for submitting and processing rental applications, payments and end of lease arrangements, as well as managing property maintenance.

Its findings were based on several “mystery shops” – mock rental applications on three of the major platforms – as well as interviews with Victorian renters and industry experts and reviews of the company’s privacy policies.

Even though real estate agencies may simply use personal information for rental applications, the data had the potential to be shared with a “wide variety” of entities including debt collectors and the providers of financial products, the CPRC found.

“It’s really difficult to ascertain how that data will be used for or against you and whether it might exclude you from the actual rental process, or whether it might even [expose you to] personalised particular products and services outside of that,” Gupta said.
“There’s a power imbalance between renters and the platforms they have to use because pushing back or finding an alternative is not an option.”
In April, the privacy commissioner found that one of Australia’s most-used RentTech platforms had collected unnecessary personal information from consumers via unfair means over a five-year period.

articles.title: Several senators want SC to resolve impeachment vote threshold
articles.summary: Several senators said they want the Supreme Court (SC) to settle the matter of the threshold vote required to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment case.

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 10:00pm
Several senators said they want the Supreme Court (SC) to settle the matter of the threshold vote required to convict Vice President Sara Duterte in her impeachment case.

The issue was raised by Sen. Erwin Tulfo, who questioned how the 16-vote threshold could be reached when not all of the senators have consistently attended the trial, especially with several of his colleagues missing from the proceedings.
Sen. JV Ejercito said that it would be less work for the Senate if the SC steps in.

“Ako, kung gusto ko sana sa Supreme Court na para hindi na kami mahirapan din. Pero depende kung anong gusto ng impeachment court, ng judges. Depende mapag-uusapan on September 23. We may just have to make the decision kung sakasakali,” Ejercito said.

(Me, I would prefer it if it is with the Supreme Court so that we do not have a hard time. But it depends on what the Impeachment Court judges want. It depends on what we will talk about on September 23. We may just have to decide the case.)
On September 23, the Senate impeachment court will hold a hearing with amici curiae, or "friends of the court”. There, they will consult experts regarding the threshold requirement.
Erwin Tulfo’s brother, Sen. Raffy Tulfo, would also prefer that the SC resolve the matter.
“Kung ako, sa sarili ko, iakyat na sa Supreme Court para matapos na, let the Supreme Court decide. Para matapos kami,” Raffy Tulfo said.
(If it were me, for myself, we could raise it to the Supreme Court to have it done; let the Supreme Court decide. So that we could be done.)

Meanwhile, Senate President Sherwin “Win” Gatchalian did not disclose his own views on the matter, saying that it was difficult to preempt the court, and it would depend on what is discussed in the amicus curiae.
“Marami tayong matutunan dyan at marami tayong malalaman dahil sila pinag-aralan ito, marami rin dito ay mga experts pagdating sa konstitusyon,” Gatchalian said.
(We will learn a lot of things there and we will know more since they have studied this; we have a lot of experts when it comes to the Constitution.)

In a separate interview, Erwin Tulfo clarified that he did not want to have the threshold lowered, but he did want clarity on the matter, especially with the impeachment trial expected to end earlier after the prosecution withdrew 15 witnesses, opting to have Duterte herself attend the trial.
The younger Tulfo said that it would be better to hear from experts through the amici curiae.

“These are what I heard. Pag-uusapan pa rin namin na dalawang Chief Justice, dalawang Associate Justice, and later I will suggest na baka pwede na rin nating isama yung constitutional ng mga ika nga convenor,” Erwin Tulfo said.
(These are what I heard. We are talking about two Chief Justices, two Associate Justices, and later I will suggest that maybe we can include constitutional conveners.) —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Syria arms depot explosion kills at least 14
articles.summary: The explosion struck near the Syrian city of Sarmada in Idlib province in the northwest. The Defense Ministry said the weapons and remnants from the war were being stored temporarily at the site…

image.caption: The large explosion led to secondary explosions and fires that it took several hours to controlImage: Moawia Atrash/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Syrian authorities reported that at least 14 people were killed and another 11 wounded on Wednesday as a result of an explosion at a temporary site used to store weapons and remnants of the country's long-running civil war.
The explosion took place near the city of Sarmada in the northwestern Idlib province.

blocks.caption: Emergency services and Red Cross workers rushed to locate and if possible rescue victims potentially trapped beneath the rubble Image: Moawia Atrash/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: What do we know about the explosion?
Syria's Defense Ministry said the weapons and war remnants were being stored termporarily at the site before being transported elsewhere. It said that some of its personnel were among those wounded.
The explosion in an area full of volatile materials led to secondary explosions and fires that hampered the emergency response. Smoke billowed from the blast site for some time on Wednesday.

"The toll from the explosion in a temporary storage for collecting weapons and war remnants near the city of Sarmada ... registered 14 killed and 11 injured in a preliminary count," the Idlib health department said.

blocks.caption: Firefigthers battled to bring the primary and secondary fires under controlImage: Kasim Yusuf/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: Authorities have not yet said what caused the explosion.
It was the second fatal incident of its kind in Idlib province this month. On September 1, five people were killed and others were wounded when a vehicle carrying ammunition exploded in Binnish.

Syria only recently emerged from more than a decade of civil war, when forces loyal to new President Ahmed al-Sharaa ousted Bashar Assad and took control of Damascus. Idlib was one of the hardest-hit regions in the country during the war.

blocks.caption: Idlib province is still awash with ordnance after fierce fighting from 2011 until late 2024Image: Kasim Yusuf/Anadolu/picture alliance

articles.title: How Belarusians still find hope in a silenced country
articles.summary: The documentary "Letters From the Silenced Country" depicts the ongoing repression under the authoritarian regime. Director Andrei Kutsila talked to DW ahead of the film's Venice premiere.

image.caption: The film 'Letters From the Silenced Country' also features animated sequencesImage: DW/ZDF/Arte

blocks.text: When Belarusians took to the streets in 2020 to protest against the disputed results of the presidential election, hopes were high that the regime of autocratic ruler Alexander Lukashenko would end, and that Belarusian society would find freedom.
But authorities responded with an unprecedented campaign of repression that continues to this day. All forms of dissent have essentially been silenced.
It's in this context that filmmaker Andrei Kutsila directed a new documentary that depicts the state's system of repression.
His film, "Letters from the Silenced Country," was co-produced by DW and premieres at the Venice Film Festival on September 9.
A silenced country
Like the 300,000 to 500,000 Belarusians who now live in exile, Kutsila realized that he had to leave his home country amid the state's crackdown on free speech.

While he was completing his previous film — the award-winning "When Flowers Are Not Silent" (2021), on the state's brutal suppression of demonstrations — different colleagues around him were arrested, he says.
Many of them have since been released, "but at the same time, new prisoners are found to keep filling the cells. The situation is not changing; it's even worse now," Kutsila tells DW.
As the film points out in a postscript card, the human rights organization Viasna has documented at least 65,000 politically motivated arrests and detentions in Belarus since the 2020 protests.

"From the outside, people live their normal lives, but the streets have become quiet and conversations are reduced to whispers," says Kutsila. Those who remained in the country can get arrested and sent to prison simply for posting Belarusian symbols of freedom and resistance online, notes the filmmaker.
That was one of the reasons that motivated him to make "Letters from the Silenced Country."
Returning to Belarus and to physically meet and film protagonists in his home country was not an option, so he searched for an alternative way to portray their situation after the protests.
Letters to prisoners served as a starting point to Kutsila's film project: "I read thousands of them," he says.
He then picked stories of individuals — political prisoners, exiles and underground activists — who embodied different aspects of the situation.

blocks.caption: Footage from Belarusian prisons exposes harsh conditions for political detaineesImage: DW/ZDF/Arte

blocks.text: Vitold Ashurak died in prison
Belarusian opposition activist and environmental campaigner Vitold Ashurak is one of the film's protagonists.
Sentenced to five years in prison for participating in the protests, Ashurak's fate is portrayed through his correspondence with friends and family during his imprisonment.
Letters from a friend include meticulously selected photographs. Ashurak finds brief moments of mental freedom in these pictures, while the same images are also poetically embedded in the film.

But CCTV footage showing prison guards beating inmates brings viewers back to the brutal reality: Vitold Ashurak died under suspicious circumstances while in custody. His name is remembered as a symbol of the state's repression.
Between resignation and hope
The film also includes animated sequences, based on drawings created by the young student Kasia Budzko, who was sentenced to 2 1/2 years in prison for participating in protests.

Another protagonist in the film is Andrei Ostapovich, a former criminal investigator. In August 2020, he left his position, writing a letter of resignation in which he denounced the police officers' brutality against protesters.

blocks.caption: In the film, Ostapovich describes the sadistic tendencies he saw among the police forceImage: DW/ZDF/Arte

blocks.text: As one of the first security officials who publicly and categorically opposed the Belarusian regime, Ostapovich fled the country — facing many perilous detours.

In one scene of "Letters from the Silenced Country," Ostapovich is asked if, after everything he's been through and witnessed, he still believes in a free Belarus. After much hesitation, his only response is a sigh of resignation.

Filmmaker Andrei Kutsila shares this ambivalence: "Of course, it's in a way my perspective too, as I tried to express my feelings through my protagonists." But, Kutsila focuses on long-term progress, as he adds, "history is the foundation on which we can build a free country."
"You know, 200 years ago Belarus didn't even exist on a map," he points out. There have been struggles to free the country ever since: "So from this long-term perspective, there is a lot of hope."

"No matter how awful the situation is, the only thing that can empower and give us hope is solidarity, connection between people and love. So these are the things giving us hope," notes Kutsila. "And the film, I think, shows this."

The arraignment of Vice President Sara Duterte for three counts of grave threats is set for Friday, September 11, 2026, before the Quezon City Regional Trial Court (QCRTC).
According to a report on "24 Oras," Duterte’s lawyer, Michael Poa, said they have yet to discuss the arraignment with the Vice President.

The court held the oral arguments on Duterte’s motion in late August.
Duterte previously said her remarks were "maliciously taken out of logical context."
The vice president's alleged grave threats against Marcos are also the basis of one of the Articles of Impeachment against her in the ongoing trial before the Senate impeachment court.

articles.title: Why we're still looking for dark matter
articles.summary: When physicists said they may have spotted evidence of dark matter almost 100 years after it was proposed as a theory, the internet lit up. Here's why we're searching for the thing that holds…

image.caption: Dark matter: the thing that glues everything else in the universe together Image: Peopleimages Com/peopleimages.com/IMAGO

blocks.text: On September 1, 2026, scientists at a dark matter detector called LUX-ZEPLIN (LZ) reported they had observed an event, a particle interaction, that they were unable to explain.

The team, based in South Dakota in the US, said the event resembled what they think a dark matter particle should produce when it collides with liquid xenon, one of a range of materials used for detecting dark matter.
They stopped short of calling it the discovery, or proof of dark matter, that many in the field have been hunting for almost 100 years.
The term "dark matter" was coined by physicist Fritz Zwicky in 1933 as a means to describe unseen matter that would explain fast-moving galaxies.

The LUX-ZEPLIN observation came just days after the release of the second season of Dark Matter, a sci-fi thriller starring Joel Edgerton and Jennifer Connelly. Both events pushed the term "dark matter" back into people's minds.
Here's what you need to know, with the science separated from the series.
What is dark matter in simple terms?
Dark matter is often described as an "invisible" substance. But it may be better described as "transparent" because it can be seen, or detected, by the gravitational attraction it exerts.
That said, it neither emits nor reflects light, and has never been observed directly. So, in that sense, it is invisible.
Is it true that 95% of the universe is invisible?
Yes, roughly.
Ordinary matter — everything that can be seen or touched — accounts for about 5% of the universe.
Dark matter accounts for about 27%, and dark energy, a separate force linked to the accelerating expansion of the universe, about 68%. Together they account for about 95%.
A different figure of 85% is dark matter's share of matter alone.
But does dark matter really exist?

The strongest evidence that dark matter exists comes from the so-called Bullet Cluster, which formed when two galaxy clusters collided. The collision produced hot gas clouds that interacted. This interaction showed revealed mass in the gas clouds that distributed differently from the gas. Researchers said that mass could be dark matter.
Earth spins at 1,670 km/h: Why don't we feel it?
How do scientists search for dark matter on Earth?
Scientists use detectors like the LUX-ZEPLIN that passively wait for interactions between naturally occurring particles and detect radiation.
They tend to be buried deep underground, where the surrounding rock blocks cosmic radiation that would otherwise distort signals.
They are built from materials chosen for their very low levels of trace radioactivity, so a genuine detection is not lost in background noise.

The LUX-ZEPLIN detector specifically works by watching for a faint flash of light and pulse of electric charge released when a passing particle strikes a liquid xenon particle. Liquid xenon, a noble gas, has good properties for detecting radiation.
What is dark matter made of?
The leading candidate particles are:
WIMPs, or weakly interacting massive particles, are the longest-standing theory. They are heavy and interact only rarely with ordinary matter.
Axions, which are lighter and behave more coherently than WIMPs. A team at Kyoto University, Japan, say data from Earth's magnetic field could be used to search for axions.
What does dark matter do to humans?

Dark matter passes through the body constantly, without measurable effect. Billions of candidate particles cross through a person every second, but only about ten strike a nucleus in the body over a year.
The resulting radiation exposure is far lower than what people receive from radon or cosmic rays.

articles.summary: Louie Alas leads the Ateneo Blue Eagles in such delicate times, taking over as interim coach for the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament following the resignation of former head coach Tab…

blocks.text: NEW COACH. Ateneo Blue Eagles interim coach Louie Alas during the UAAP Season 89 press conference.
UAAP

Louie Alas leads the Ateneo Blue Eagles in such delicate times, taking over as interim coach for the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament following the resignation of former head coach Tab Baldwin

items: Coach Louie Alas takes over as interim coach for the Ateneo Blue Eagles following the tragic deaths of two student-athletes, Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili.

Alas, who previously coached the Letran Knights to three NCAA championships, embraces the challenge despite the pressure and aims to keep the team focused amidst backlash over their UAAP participation.
The Blue Eagles are dedicating their season to Baterbonia and Adili, wearing memorial patches on their jerseys, and are focused on healing and mental fortitude as they prepare for the competition.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – Guiding an embattled Ateneo team still reeling from the tragic deaths of Rene Baterbonia and Divine Adili is no easy task, but coach Louie Alas is up to the challenge.

Alas said he never shies away from pressure as he leads the Blue Eagles in such delicate times, taking over as interim coach for the UAAP Season 89 men’s basketball tournament following the resignation of former head coach Tab Baldwin.
It will be Alas’ first head coaching stint in college since he called the shots in 2012 for the Letran Knights, a team he steered to three NCAA championships.

“When the incident happened, I was ready to go because of command responsibility,” said Alas, who was hired in 2024 as a deputy. “But when one of the priests approached me and asked me if I was open to being a temporary coach, I said, ‘Father, it is not in my personality to back down from challenges.’ When I saw the players, how could I leave them?”
Alas, 62, did not join the team building in Dipaculao, Aurora, where Baterbonia and Adili drowned during a seawater activity on June 8, and in turn, did not get punished by the UAAP.
Those in attendance were penalized, with the UAAP slapping Baldwin with a lifetime ban and handing assistant coaches Dean Castaño, Sandro Soriano, and Jon Jacinto indefinite suspensions.

“I was ready to go and ready to retire, but with that situation, I think no coach would leave. I guess I’m destined to be here. I was fine with being an assistant, I no longer wanted to be a head coach. But this is what the Lord gave me and I’m ready to accept the challenge,” said Alas.

And the challenge includes keeping his wards locked in as the Blue Eagles deal with the backlash over their UAAP participation, with many fans believing Ateneo should have been suspended for at least one season given the gravity of the incident that claimed the lives of two student-athletes.
Jeers from the crowd during the games are also likely, but Alas trusts that there is enough security at the venues to keep things in order.
“Our concentration is on the UAAP itself. I hope nothing untoward happens,” said Alas.
The Blue Eagles are coming off a promising run in the Pinoyliga Cup, where they reached the semifinals before losing to eventual champion UST Growling Tigers.

Alas’ son, rookie guard Kieffer, showed the way for Ateneo in the preseason tournament where it beat Our Lady of Fatima University, St. Benilde, and Mapua with an average of 18.3 points, 5.3 rebounds, and 2.5 assists.
Travis Roberts backstopped the younger Alas with 12.3 points and 4.0 rebounds, while third-year guard Jared Bahay produced 6.5 points, 3.3 rebounds, and 3.3 assists.
Alas, though, knows the competition in the UAAP is on a whole ‘nother level.
“We have no expectations because we want to take care of our mental [fortitude] first. But we’ll make sure that we’re ready when we go into a game,” said Alas.
“Of course, this is part of our healing. And winning would make it easier for us to heal.”

Ultimately, the Blue Eagles are not just playing for victories or school pride as they offer the season to Baterbonia and Adili, with the men’s and women’s basketball teams wearing memorial patches with the initials “RB” and “DA” on their jerseys.
“Ever since the accident happened, the first thing on their mind is to dedicate this year to [Baterbonia and Adili.] They are in the players’ hearts,” said Alas. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Cambodia's floating schools hit by rising fuel costs
articles.summary: The Iran war has sent fuel prices higher in Cambodia, squeezing families who rely on fishing and boats for their livelihoods. For children living on Tonle Sap, rising fuel costs pose yet another…

image.caption: For children living around Tonle Sap, access to education is increasingly under threat as an indirect consequence of rising fuel pricesImage: Action Education/Education Above All Foundation

blocks.text: Every morning, 12-year-old Soksan Set faces a journey most children his age never have to think about. Outside his home, there is no road, only water.

Soksan lives in Prek Toal, a floating community on Tonle Sap, Southeast Asia's largest freshwater lakewhere boats are the main means of transport. A Grade 4 student at the local primary school, he travels several kilometers on water to attend class and sometimes helps younger children along the way.

But increasingly, the biggest obstacle between Soksan and his classroom is not distance. It is fuel. His family, like many others in the commune, depends on fishing for their livelihood. When fuel prices rise, they are forced to make difficult choices.

"When gasoline prices go up, we don't have enough money to take our children to school regularly," said Soksan's father, 41-year-old Set Soeum. "We don't catch enough fish, and we need around three liters of gasoline a day to travel long distances for fishing. Because of this, Soksan often has to miss school."
For families living on the water, rising fuel costs can quickly become a barrier to education.

blocks.caption: Remote schools also depend on boats to transport teachers, textbooks, classroom materials, food and maintenance suppliesImage: Action Education/Education Above All Foundation

blocks.text: Why rising fuel costs hit Cambodia's poor the hardest

Cambodia relies heavily on imported fuel, leaving households exposed to global price shocks and regional supply disruptions. The 2026 Iran war has driven up energy costs, making transport to remote communities more expensive. Around Tonle Sap, this has hit students and their families.
Gasoline prices rose 45% and diesel prices more than 70% in March, the largest single-month increase since 2008, according to the World Bank.
Gasoline currently costs 5,700 riel ($1.41) per liter, up 26.7% from 4,500 riel ($1.11) a year ago, according to Global Petrol Prices.

Although Cambodia does not depend directly on the Strait of Hormuz for most of its fuel imports, it is exposed to higher global oil prices and supply disruptions affecting regional suppliers. Cambodia imports all of its petroleum products and has no domestic refining capacity.
For Soksan's family, the pressure is felt both on the fishing boat and the school boat. Some days, they borrow money to buy gasoline. Other days, they cut back on food, clothing or school supplies.

"Five students collect money to buy gasoline, sometimes just one liter at a time," Soksan said. When they cannot afford even that, they row themselves. "We row the boat ourselves. It can take up to an hour, but we still try to go to school," he noted.

On the Tonle Sap, 12-year-old Siyien Ly walks more than 30 minutes to school during the dry season. When flooding makes the roads impassable, she relies on an aid-supported school boat. Some of her classmates have stopped attending because their families cannot afford the cost of transport.
"Even though fuel prices are rising, we still keep trying to come to school because education is important for our future," Siyien said.
Siyien's family of six has four children in school. Her mother, Kunthea Chin, now sells sugarcane juice after Siyien's father developed serious hearing problems following a water-related accident.

Kunthea said that her daily income has fallen from about 80,000 riel ($20) to around 40,000 riel, while the cost of supplies has risen. The family spends around 600,000 riel ($150) a month on fuel, which they need for both the children's transport and her business.
Cambodia's floating schools face brunt of climate crisis
Taking risks to reach the classroom
Families also try to reduce costs by traveling together and sharing fuel expenses. Some have returned to traditional rowing boats. But saving money can come at the cost of safety.
When several children share a small boat, it can become crowded. During storms and heavy rain, parents worry about their children's safety on the water.
"My mother worries when too many students ride together," Siyien said.

Remote schools also depend on boats to transport teachers, textbooks, classroom materials, food and maintenance supplies. Higher fuel prices can therefore increase the cost of delivering education itself.

"For children living in floating and remote communities, access to education depends not only on having a school, but also on being able to reach it," said Samphors Vorn, country director of Action Education in Cambodia.

"When fuel prices rise, the cost of that journey rises with them. For families already living with very limited incomes, this can turn transportation into a barrier to attendance and, ultimately, to a child's right to education."
The Cambodian government has introduced measures to cushion consumers from international fuel-price increases, including fuel discounts, tax reductions and zero customs duties on fuel imports.
But subsidies at the pump cannot fully shield families whose incomes remain low and unpredictable.
Climate and economic shocks deepen education woes

Last year, DW reported from the region on how climate change was disrupting children's education. Rising and falling water levels, extreme weather and the dangers of traveling by boat were making it harder for children in floating communities to reach school.
The challenges have since deepened.

blocks.caption: Increasingly, the biggest obstacle between Soksan and his classroom is not distance, it is fuel.Image: Action Education/Education Above All Foundation

blocks.text: Today, 14-year-old Nary is no longer in the classroom. She has been unable to return because of persistent headaches following health complications linked to suspected long-term meningitis.
Her younger sister, 11-year-old Naren, continues to attend Grade 2. She relies on a school boat and pays around 500 riel ($0.12) for the return journey.

For their family, even small costs matter. Their father, Tit Sarin, earns around 30,000 riel ($7.50) a day from traditional fishing. But traveling farther across the lake to find fish can require about six liters of fuel, costing roughly $6.60.
"When we cannot afford fuel, we have to find other work," he said.
The family then works as day laborers, picking chilies for as little as 1,000 riel ($0.25) per kilogram. For families like Nary's, climate change and rising fuel costs are now a double burden.
Nary hopes to return to learning. Her father is saving to buy a boat dedicated to shuttling his children to school and back home.

articles.title: Marcoleta insists on voting power as senator-judge despite detention
articles.summary: Senator Rodante Marcoleta insists that he still has a voting capacity as a senator-judge in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte despite being detained for plunder charges.

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 8:35pm
Senator Rodante Marcoleta insists that he still has a voting capacity as a senator-judge in the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte despite being detained for plunder charges.
This was disclosed in a 16-page letter dated July 20 but released to the media on Wednesday, Marcoleta had written to Escudero and Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian while he was in detention.
“There is no impairment to my legal capacity to vote as a Senator-Judge for I am not under preventive suspension,” Marcoleta wrote.
Marcoleta maintains he was not issued a preventive suspension, neither has he resigned or incapacitated.

“I have been charged and arrested for the crime of Plunder on the basis of a politically-motivated administrative determination of probable cause by the Ombudsman. I have presented myself to the custody of the PNP- CIDG (Philippine National Police Criminal Investigation and Detection Group). However, these circumstances do not cause my office as Senator to be vacated,” Marcoleta said.

The detained senator also voiced his objection to Escudero as the presiding officer of Duterte’s impeachment, saying that it should be the Senate President. He said that the general rule applied that the Senate President, who oversees all Senate proceedings, should also preside over the trial.
The Senate should not distort the meaning of the Constitution, Marcoleta said.

Healso reiterated his support for the 16 vote threshold to convict Duterte, as this was already agreed upon when Escudero set the rules for the impeachment proceedings on July 3. Marcoleta was arrested three days later on July 6.
“For the foregoing reasons, I vote in favor of the ruling on the 16-vote requirement to convict the impeached Vice-President,” the lawmaker said.
Marcoleta is currently detained at the Quezon City Jail for plunder after he allegedly received P75 million in undeclared campaign donations. —RF, GMA News

articles.title: For GCash’s early private equity backers, record IPO will be ultimate payday
articles.summary: GCash's blockbuster IPO could turn years of paper gains into billions for its early private equity backers. For the retail investors buying in now, the question is how much growth still remains.

blocks.text: GCash's blockbuster IPO could turn years of paper gains into billions for its early private equity backers. For the retail investors buying in now, the question is how much growth still remains.

items: GCash is preparing for an initial public offering (IPO) that could be the largest in Philippine history, allowing ordinary investors to participate in its success and providing early backers with a significant exit opportunity.

The IPO will involve the issuance of up to 1.61 billion new shares and the sale of 6.42 billion shares from existing shareholders, with 80% of the shares being secondary, indicating that most proceeds will benefit early investors rather than raising new capital.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

GCash has become so ubiquitous that its blue QR codes are just as easy to find in sari-sari stores as they are in malls. Its upcoming initial public offering (IPO) now promises to give ordinary investors a chance to own a piece of that success.
And for some of GCash’s earliest financial backers, an IPO poised to become the largest in Philippine history also offers the kind of exit private equity (PE) investors spend years hoping for.

Bow Wave Capital, Warburg Pincus, Insight Partners, and LGVP invested in Mynt — the parent company of the e-wallet giant — long before it commanded anything close to the valuation it’s seeking today. They helped bankroll its rise from fast-growing fintech to profitable household name. Now, the IPO could allow them to turn what has so far been paper gains into cash.
And this is no small liquidity event.

Under the latest offer structure, Mynt will issue up to 1.61 billion new shares, while existing shareholders will sell up to 6.42 billion shares. Another 1.20 billion shares available under the overallotment option will also come from existing owners.

That means only 20% of the firm offer is primary, while 80% is secondary. In other words, most of the shares being sold will come from existing shareholders rather than from new shares issued to raise fresh capital for Mynt.

By the time the bell rings, the vast majority of the IPO proceeds will be going to shareholders selling down stakes accumulated years earlier, giving some of GCash’s earliest backers the ultimate payday.
The institutional sellers are mostly early financial investors. At the P10 ceiling and assuming the overallotment option is fully exercised, the prospectus shows:

items: Bow Wave Capital, through ASP Philippines – could sell about P27.04 billion worth of shares, cutting its stake from 6% to around 1.82%
Warburg Pincus, through Lion Fintech Investments – could sell around P12.18 billion, bringing its stake down from 2.70% to around 0.82%
Insight Partners, through Insight PHP Holdings – could sell about P8.53 billion, reducing its stake from 1.89% to around 0.57%
Advanced New Technologies, an Ant International-linked company – could sell about P25.18 billion, reducing its stake from 6.22% to around 2.30%
LGVP, through its three investment vehicles – could sell around P2.66 billion combined, cutting their combined stake from about 0.59% to roughly 0.18%

blocks.text: These are investors deeply familiar with fintech.

Bow Wave is a relatively specialized private equity fund whose mandate centers on online and mobile payments. It first backed Mynt in 2020, when GCash’s pandemic-era growth was taking off and Mynt was valued at close to US$1 billion, meaning it has been invested for around six years. Bow Wave has also backed Ascend Money, the company behind Thailand’s TrueMoney Wallet, another Southeast Asian digital payments success story.

Warburg Pincus, meanwhile, is one of the world’s most prominent private equity firms and has plenty of experience betting on digital finance in emerging Asian markets. Its portfolio has included MoMo, Vietnam’s largest e-wallet, Indonesia’s GoTo Group, which combines Gojek, Tokopedia and GoTo Financial, and Advance Intelligence Group, whose businesses include buy-now-pay-later platform Atome. Warburg joined Mynt’s 2021 funding round, giving it roughly a five-year holding period by the time of the planned IPO.

Insight Partners came into Mynt in the same 2021 round. The New York growth investor has an extensive fintech portfolio that includes payments company Checkout.com, digital bank N26, Indonesian payments firm Xendit, Flutterwave, and financial infrastructure company Tink.

blocks.caption: [Finterest] GCash, Maya IPOs in 2026? What this means for potential investors

blocks.text: But the sell-down doesn’t mean GCash’s most important strategic owners are heading for the exits. Globe Capital Venture Holdings, Mynt’s single biggest shareholder at 33.84%, along with Ant International Technologies (21.44%), Ayala-Mitsubishi vehicle AM 50 Ventures (13.02%), and MUFG Bank (8.05%), are all staying put.
Nor should the PE (private equity) sell-down automatically be read as a vote of no confidence in GCash.

“It is fair to say that the IPO provides a liquidity or partial exit opportunity,” FirstMetroSec vice president and digital solutions and investor engagement division head Andoy Beltran told Rappler, adding, “but I would be careful about interpreting that as them losing confidence in GCash because those are two very different things.”

After all, exiting is part of the private equity playbook. Unlike strategic investors such as Globe or Ayala, PE and growth funds generally don’t buy stakes with the intention of holding them indefinitely. They invest, help a company scale and multiply in value, then eventually sell some or all of their stakes so they can return capital and profits to their own investors.

The timing is hardly unusual either. Recall Bow Wave first invested around 2020, while Warburg Pincus and Insight came in during 2021, putting them at roughly five to six years in Mynt by the time of the IPO. From my own experience consulting on private equity deals — including fintech investments — that’s the exit window that funds look for.
That may be the more important question for retail investors taking their place.

GCash is already operating at enormous scale. Mynt posted P79.7 billion in adjusted revenue and P17.25 billion in net income in 2025, while GCash reached 41.5 million monthly active users by June 2026, equivalent to nearly 56% of Filipino adults.

Growth, however, has cooled from its earlier breakneck pace. Adjusted revenue in H1 2026 only rose 9.8%, while net income grew 7.3%. DragonFi equity analyst Jarrod Tin argues that GCash has already deeply penetrated its core wallet market, with competition from Maya, MariBank, and other financial apps making the next leg harder.
However, Beltran still sees a growth story, with more runway in lending, savings, investments and other financial services, but cautions investors not to expect the old growth rates indefinitely.
“The question is how much of that future growth is already being priced into the IPO,” he said. – Rappler.com

articles.title: EU proposes more restrictions for Airbnb, holiday rentals
articles.summary: The European Union wants tighter rules on short-term rentals to tackle housing shortages in tourist hotspots.

image.caption: Protesters in Malaga call for Airbnb to be 'out of our neighborhoods' [FILE: June 2024]Image: JORGE GUERRERO/AFP

blocks.text: Airbnb and other companies providing short-term home rentals could face tighter restrictions after the European Commission proposed new rules on Wednesday to help tackle housing shortages in tourist hotspots.

A surge in short-term holiday rentals has contributed to a shortage of affordable housing and a spike in housing prices in many of Europe's most popular tourist destinations, prompting residents to protest in recent years .
What do we know about the EU's affordable housing proposal?

The EU's executive branch unveiled the measures as part of an "affordable housing" package, which will allow local authorities to limit short-term rentals to address what European Commission vice-president Teresa Ribera described as a "terrible crisis."
"When the market fails to deliver something as fundamental as an affordable home, public authorities have a responsibility to act," the Spanish politician said.

The measures seek to harmonize rules across the bloc, after attempts to crack down on Airbnb-style rentals by authorities in cities such as Paris, Berlin and Barcelona, among others, were met with legal challenges by rental and tourism companies.

The European Commission's Affordable Housing Act — which still needs to be approved by EU legislators and EU member states — would provide cities with legal support by clarifying when local authorities can act against housing companies without breaking EU single market rules.

Under the proposal, city and local authorities would be allowed to limit short-term and holiday rentals as well as curb the purchase of property for short-term letting in areas considered to be "under housing stress," the European Commission said.
Spain: Tourism boom worsens housing crisis
For an area to be defined as "under stress," certain parameters — including the ratio between local housing prices and incomes — would have to be met.
Before restrictions can be introduced, cities would have to show that holiday rentals have had a major negative impact on the affordability or availability of housing for at least three years.
The proposed legislation will not impact landlords renting out their primary residence for short-term periods.
The Commission also recommended that authorities free up land for more housing and modernize planning and construction of new homes to address housing shortages.
How have rental companies reacted?
CCIA Europe, a lobbying group that represents Airbnb, among others, said the EU's measures fail to address the need for independent assessment of the restrictions.

"Europe will not solve its housing crisis by giving cities an EU framework to restrict short-term rentals and then letting them police their own ​compliance," CCIA's head of ⁠policy Alexandre Roure said in a statement.

"Without independent scrutiny or effective redress, this proposal will remain a paper tiger, leaving disproportionate restrictions ⁠in place and undermining ​the legal certainty the Affordable Housing Act is meant to provide," Roure added.

articles.title: PDP-Laban: Lowering 16-vote threshold for conviction violates Constitution
articles.summary: The PDP led by its president Baste Duterte said Wednesday that the lowering the existing 16-vote threshold for a conviction in the Senate impeachment court will violate the Constitution.

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 8:18pm

The Partido Demokratiko Pilipino (PDP)—led by its president, acting Davao City Mayor Sebastian "Baste" Duterte—said Wednesday that the lowering the existing 16-vote threshold for a conviction in the Senate impeachment court would violate the Constitution.

The party issued the statement a day after the possibility of lowering the threshold was raised during Day 23 of the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte, sister of Sebastian, since four of the 24 Senators are not participating in the ongoing proceedings.

Senators Jinggoy Estrada and Rodante Marcoleta are detained on separate plunder charges, while Senator Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa is in hiding amid an arrest warrant from the International Criminal Court.
Senator Loren Legarda, meanwhile, has not been attending the trial for weeks now due to health concerns, specifically a lung problem that she is having treated overseas.

“(PDP-LABAN) views with great alarm, the efforts of certain members of the Senate to once again bend the law to the breaking point, by attempting to tamper with the evident intent of the framers of the Constitution in setting a threshold of 16 votes of all the members of the Senate, in order to convict an impeachable officer, in order to stave off the acquittal of a Vice-President due to weak evidence and a less than competent prosecution panel,” lawyer Ferdinand Topacio, PDP-Laban national spokesman, said in a statement.

“The Constitution is a sacred document that should be placed above the swirling winds of political expediency. The yardstick of sixteen was specifically formulated to insulate the Senate, sitting as an Impeachment Court, from political manipulation and interference, such as what is happening now,” Topacio added.
Topacio said the 16-vote threshold is an “immovable standard” supported by debates in the Constitutional Commission and by ruling case law.

“The present administration, with its evil plan of lowering the threshold, is showing its panic and desperation in the face of the impending defeat of its vile efforts to unseat and disqualify the clear choice of the people for Vice-President and for President in 2028,” he said. — BM, GMA News

blocks.text: The White House has taken down a Tetris-style game on its website called "Build The Wall", days after The Tetris Company raised concerns over its use of the game's likeness.
The game, which saw players stack blocks to build a wall to "protect the border" is one of five arcade games which have appeared on the White House website.
On 4 September the official Tetris account on X posted, external the firm was "not involved in the creation" of the game and it took "copyright infringement very seriously".
The White House has not responded to requests for comment from the BBC or given an official reason for the takedown.
"At Tetris we believe in the power of connection and building people together, not dividing them," the firm said in its initial response to the game.
"To our fans everywhere: we love you, we see you, and we're grateful to have you in our community."

The Tetris Company has had previous success in suing firms for infringing on its copyright - settling for an undisclosed fee with the makers of the iPhone game Mino in 2012, which it claimed stole the look and feel of the block-builder.
Four other arcade games still remain on the mini-game section of the White House website.
"Flappy Bill", a clone of the 2013 viral hit Flappy Bird sees players fly a bald eagle and dodging monuments from the National Mall.
Meanwhile in Rio Run, players must "patrol the line along the river", with gameplay reminiscent of the classic phone game Snake.

articles.title: German chancellor accuses far-right AfD party of seeking ‘ethnic cleansing’
articles.summary: Friedrich Merz says Alternative für Deutschland is ‘dividing our society’ after party won nearly 44% of vote in Saxony-Anhalt state election

blocks.text: Germany’s chancellor, Friedrich Merz, has accused the far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) of seeking “ethnic cleansing” with its “remigration” drive, after the nativist party’s seismic weekend victory in a state election.

In his first public confrontation with the AfD since Sunday’s shock outcome in Saxony-Anhalt, Merz said at a raucous parliamentary debate that the far-right party would take an axe to one of the pillars of the German economy with a racist campaign of mass deportations.
“The term ‘remigration’ is nothing but a synonym for ethnic cleansing based on origin and skin colour,” he said on Wednesday to applause from the other parties in the Bundestag lower house.
In a fiery speech addressed to the AfD parliamentary group, which repeatedly interrupted him with loud taunts and heckling, Merz said millions of working immigrants were crucial to German society.

“If those working in Germany have to leave the country again because you are championing ‘remigration’,” Merz said, “then the skilled trades in Germany will no longer be able to function: not a single care home will remain open, not a single hospital in Germany will remain operational, and not a single restaurant in Germany will be able to stay in business.”
He said the AfD’s rhetoric, which propelled it to the strongest showing for a far-right party in a German state since the Nazi period, “is precisely what is dividing our society so deeply”.

Support for Merz, a conservative Christian Democrat, has plummeted in the 16 months since he took office at the helm of a coalition with the centre-left Social Democrats, amid disappointment over slow progress on economic growth and the cost of living.
He has adopted a hard line on border policy in a faltering bid to win back AfD supporters, and acknowledged Germany still had “problems in the area of migration”.
“We still have many people in Germany who should not have permanent residency. This is consensus in the [ruling] coalition, that we need to deport more people,” he said on Wednesday.

“But we make a careful distinction between those who work in Germany, who contribute to our prosperity, and who are welcome here, and those who do not have permanent residency in Germany and who must leave our country. Unlike you [the AfD], we take great care to make this distinction.”

blocks.caption: (From l to r) AfD party co-chair Tino Chrupalla, Ulrich Siegmund and Alice Weidel a day after the Saxony-Anhalt state election. Photograph: Clemens Bilan/EPA

blocks.text: The AfD won nearly 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt but fell three seats short of an absolute majority. Its chief candidate, Ulrich Siegmund, is seeking potential supporters among the other parties to elect him as state premier.
after newsletter promotion

Merz, who has acknowledged that his unpopularity played a role in the halving of support for his party in the state, tried to put a brave face on the rout. “Fifty-six percent of voters in Saxony-Anhalt didn’t vote for you,” he told the AfD.

He accused Siegmund, whose party is classed as rightwing extremist by domestic intelligence, of “electoral fraud” by already breaking a campaign promise not to seek to govern the state if he failed to win an absolute majority.
“And you won’t manage that in Germany either” at the federal level, Merz told the AfD co-leader Alice Weidel. “Nowhere in Germany will you get a majority. You are and remain a destructive force.”

Merz also attacked the AfD for its opposition to military assistance for Ukraine, and accused it of making common cause with Russia, which Berlin has alleged is mounting a sabotage and disinformation campaign on its soil.

He said that despite “clear evidence” a failed drone bomb attack at Leipzig airport last month “had been planned in Russia for months and was specifically directed against Germany”, the AfD had remained silent on it.
Earlier from the podium, Weidel savoured her party’s resounding election victory, saying the CDU had been “pulverised” and calling it a referendum on Merz’s leadership.

Attacking the government’s migration policy and blaming it for crime and other security problems, Weidel said: “Your time is up. The public want a change in policy, and they will get it,” reiterating her party’s aim to form a federal government in the foreseeable future.
Polls show Merz’s fractious coalition would not have a majority in a general election, which is not scheduled until 2029.
The AfD is polling in first place at 28% to 29%, with the wind at its back before another two state polls this month, in Berlin and Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania.

articles.title: Sherwin Gatchalian: Court to decide Marcoleta, Estrada impeachment attendance
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Wednesday said detained senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada would have to seek permission from the Sandiganbayan to attend Senate sessions, including…

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 7:49pm

Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian on Wednesday said detained senators Rodante Marcoleta and Jinggoy Estrada would have to seek permission from the Sandiganbayan to attend Senate sessions, including the impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
In an interview with reporters, however, Gatchalian said both senators are in the custody of the courts.
"By process, they will have to ask permission there if they can attend the session or the impeachment. In the past, it was like that,” Gatchalian said.
Asked if he would write to the Sandiganbayan, Gatchalian said the senators themselves would have to ask for permission.
“So, the court will decide if there is justification for them to attend even a session or the impeachment,” Gatchalian said.

Estrada and Marcoleta are currently detained over plunder charges. Marcoleta has reportedly written to Gatchalian and impeachment presiding officer Sen. Francis “Chiz” Escudero, saying there was no impairment to his capacity to serve as a senator-judge.
Estrada, however, has already petitioned the Sandiganbayan to allow him to attend the impeachment trial. The anti-graft court denied the plea for lack of merit.
In July, Marcoleta also publicly asked the Senate to find ways to allow him and Estrada to participate in the impeachment trial.
Marcoleta’s request was again raised when the Senate impeachment court discussed the voting threshold for convicting Duterte.
With four senators unable to attend the impeachment proceedings, questions were raised over how many votes would be needed to convict her.
The Senate impeachment court is set to consult legal experts on the matter through amici curiae.

Aside from Estrada and Marcoleta, Sen. Dela Rosa has also been unable to attend the proceedings as he remains in hiding amid an ICC arrest warrant over alleged crimes against humanity linked to the Duterte administration’s drug war.
Legarda, meanwhile, has missed the proceedings after leaving the country and has sought an extended absence, reportedly due to health reasons.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: N Korea has built two-storey uranium enrichment facility, says watchdog
articles.summary: The International Atomic Energy Agency's says the facility is cause for "serious concern".

blocks.text: North Korea has built a new two-storey uranium enrichment facility, the head of the world's nuclear watchdog said this week, calling it a cause for "serious concern".
The new building is part of the main Yongbyon nuclear complex, and reportedly capable of housing up to 28 centrifuge cascades used to enrich uranium.
In a report published late last month, the International Atomic Energy Agency said Pyongyang has also begun operating an expanded annex at another enrichment site.

These findings point to a steady expansion of the North's sancitoned nuclear infrastructure. The agency, which has no inspectors in North Korea since it was expelled in 2009, relies on satellite imagery for assessments.

"The continuation and further development of the DPRK's nuclear programme are clear violations of relevant UN Security Council resolutions and are deeply regrettable," IAEA director Rafael Grossi said in a statement earlier this week.
The IAEA first referred to the existence of the building in June, although Grossi had mentioned the possibility earlier in the year.
In June, the agency said that North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited a "newly inaugurated nuclear materials production factory" on 3 June, which it identified as the Yongbyon enrichment facility.
Kim had praised the country's "greatly expanded production capacity", adding that this would "offer the possibility of carrying out larger plans", according to the agency's report.
Despite running one the poorest countries in the world, Kim spends millions each year developing a secretive nuclear arsenal. A 2022 report by a non-proliferation think-tank put this figure at $640m.

"What makes North Korea's nuclear programme so concerning is that many of its facilities are unknown, concealed, and thus difficult to target," Edward Howell, a lecturer at the University of Oxford told the BBC.

"Beyond Yongbyon, we know that other facilities exist: Kangson, for instance. The embeddedness of North Korea's nuclear doctrine within its foreign and domestic policy means that we should expect there to be more concealed production sites."

The agency also said there were indications that operations had started at another enrichment facility in Kangson, near the capital Pyongyang, in January this year. An annex had first been constructed in Kangson in 2024, it said.
It had said in April that North Korea appeared to be stepping up its ability to make nuclear bombs, saying they were monitoring the apparent expansion of Yongbyon.

The North's nuclear programme has accelerated under Kim, who has overseen a record number of missile tests. The country has fired has numerous intercontinental ballistic missiles (ICBMs) since it began testing its long-range system in 2017.
The country has conducted six nuclear weapons tests so far, the last of which was in September 2017.

articles.title: Syria: How the 'house of sisters' threat split society
articles.summary: Rumor has it that the 'house of sisters' is where kidnapped women from other Syrian sects are forced to convert to Islam. Nobody knows if it really exists, but it's being used to create communal…

image.caption: Protest about abducted Syrian women: Another example of the kinds of rumors circulating is that women from minority communities are being sold as sex slaves Image: Elisa Gestri/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: A knock on the door, a muted threat and then they made the decision to leave the country, says Layla, a math teacher and mother-of-three in her 40s.

Until recently, Layla — who didn't want DW to use her full name for security reasons — was living in Damascus, Syria's capital. She and her family are Alawites, the same religious sect as former Syrian dictator Bashar Assad, who are often targeted because they're seen as Assad's allies.

"But we never supported him, his father killed members of my family. We hated him actually," she told DW. Still, she describes feeling fearful when rebel groups entered Damascus in 2024 for the first time after the fall of the Assad regime, calling them "extremists."
At first, she and her husband decided to stay in Syria. But then a stranger came to the door.
"He told me 'we know your daughter plays piano and has dance lessons. You should stop that. If you don't, maybe we will take her to the house of the sisters," Layla recounts.

In conservative Islamic circles, women playing music and dancing for an audience is frowned upon. And Layla had heard about the so-called "house of the sisters" — she had read online it was a place where Syrian women from other sects were forced to convert to Islam. A few days later, the family decided to leave the country. They are now in Lebanon.
"I just don't want my children to grow up that way," Layla explains.
What is the 'house of sisters'?

Headlines about the "house of sisters" first really made waves in Syria in May after an Alawite university student Batoul Alloush, 21, was reported missing by her family, possibly kidnapped, only to turn up later wearing religious clothing and saying she left her family in order to convert to Islam.
There were already other stories of missing women, including from the Alawite minority.

Reham Suleiman, a psychologist who works for the United Nations and with the Alawite community, told DW she has firsthand knowledge of several cases of kidnapping. "And it’s not just one incident or coincidence," she says. It is clear some of women were kidnapped for ransom money, revenge or forced marriage.

But other cases were apparently resolved when, for example, the women said they had been visiting friends, wanted to escape their families or had run away to a lover. Alloush herself said she wished to convert to Islam and leave her family. Her parents insist she's been drugged or coerced.
Organizations like Amnesty International and the UN's Commission of Inquiry on Syria say the cases — which number between 40 and 60 ­­— have not been fully investigated.
A political football

Syrian authorities did look into the "house of sisters." A spokesperson for Syria's Minister of Social Affairs, Hind Kabawat, told DW that the ministry has not licensed any facility with that name and that any unlicensed centers of this nature would be shut down.
Syrian fact-checking organizations like Verify-Sy found that pictures of the supposed "house of sisters" building were created with AI.

"A constant stream of unverified claims circulates on a daily basis concerning alleged kidnappings and killings, arrests and cases of torture in detention facilities," a spokesperson from Verify-Sy told DW.
"Verifying many of these is challenging when evidence available through open sources is scarce, contradictory or otherwise insufficient."

So whether the "house of sisters" exists in some form is unclear. But real or not, some groups appear to have instrumentalized it for their own agenda anyway, independent media outlet Shaam News Network, or SNN, wrote recently.

"Despite the absence of any physical evidence … social media platforms and pages began circulating 'the house' as an established fact," SNN wrote. "And it gradually became the focus of broader narratives about the 'organized kidnapping' of Alawite women."
International influencers

A private organization called the Syrian Investigation Mechanism, or SIM, founded in May 2026, links the "house of sisters" to a Muslim organization that proselytizes to gain new converts. SIM claimed the missing women were coerced into converting and held in "the house."

In an interview on YouTube, SIM director Yasser Shalati, who is based in Brandenburg, Germany, claims this is evidence of "demographic engineering." SIM did not reply to DW's requests for further comment.

blocks.caption: Christian neighborhood in Damascus: There have been reports of more attempts to convert others to Islam since the fall of the Assad regime, which treated proselytizing as a threat to national security Image: Mohammad Bashir Aldaher/imageBROKER/picture alliance

blocks.text: A Berlin-based organization, the Union of Syrian Alawites in Europe, or USAE, has also repeatedly posted about the "house of sisters."

On his personal Facebook page, Muaiad Ibrahim, who is listed as USAE's deputy director in official court documents, regularly criticizes the new Syrian government and recently expressed support for Syria's highest religious scholar under the Assad regime, Ahmed Hassoun. In late August, Hassoun was sentenced to life in prison after being convicted of inciting civil war and complicity in intentional killing.

Other recently founded overseas organizations — including some that claim they have a network of millions of human rights advocates but link to incomplete websites — have also repeatedly disseminated stories about the "house of sisters."
Arab investigative journalism outfit DARAJ notes some of these organizations have been criticized for their apparent support of the Assad regime.
The damage done?

"This kind of information ebbs and flows, but it does have a real impact and its quite powerful," says Gregory Waters, a senior fellow at the Atlantic Council, who's traveled extensively in Syria and monitors events on his site, Syria Revisited.

"It has the political intent to isolate Alawites, to make them fearful and keep them from engaging with the government, with [Syrian] Sunnis, and maybe to some extent, pull them towards insurgent [anti-government] networks."
Online propaganda feeds on real events within minority communities, adding to their existing fears, he says.

Verify Sy conducts a monthly audit of online disinformation, and researchers there say incitement is the second most common objective. Waters says Syrian authorities have been trying to rein in local influencers who spread disinformation, although obviously they can't impact those based overseas.

blocks.caption: Syrians are still finding mass graves after 14 years of a civil war that has resulted in polarized opinions among localsImage: Ugur Yildirim/DIA/IMAGO

blocks.text: Like anywhere else in the world, you'll get a wide spectrum of opinions within every Syrian community, Waters notes. "There are there those who will insist that there's a program of ethnic cleansing, and there are others who say life is fine, we are fully integrated into the state."
Although it depends which part of the country you're looking at, he doesn't think relations between different communities are getting worse.

"In Syria, everything is unique to its local environment," Waters explains. "So in some places, we could say that walls between communities have hardened over the past two years and little progress has been made in reducing that. But even so, the walls are not getting higher."
Stabilization first

"Right now, generally speaking, the government in Damascus is busy establishing institutions, taking control of the security situation and trying to stabilize the country," argues Naseef Naeem, research director at the Berlin-based Candid Foundation, which consults on Syrian affairs. But sooner or later, Syria is going to need more of a national dialogue between different community groups, he says.
In the meantime, both he and Waters believe the Syrian economy, devastated after years of war, could hold the key to better relations.

blocks.caption: Every summer, Latakia's beaches in western Syria are a popular destination for thousands of Syrian holidaymakers Image: Elisa Gestri/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: "As soon as the economic recovery really gets underway, many of these phenomena will gradually disappear," Naeem told DW.
For example, Waters says, over summer, a lot of domestic tourists, many of them Sunni, made their way to the Syrian coast, an area where many Alawites live.

"There was a massive tourism boom," Waters explains. "Everybody's interacting and I've heard from friends there that there wasn't harassment, no violence. The government and security authorities really emphasized supporting the tourism industry in coastal areas this year and it's had a really positive impact."
Those kinds of inter-community contacts in real life "help reduce the impact of disinformation campaigns and the level of fear," he concludes.
