articles.title: Germany's Merz attacks AfD in stormy debate after far-right election win
articles.summary: Germany's chancellor clashes with AfD leader Alice Weidel, saying her migration policy amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images/Reuters
Merz and Weidel faced off for the first time since Sunday's AfD election victory
ByPaul Kirby
Europe digital editor

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz has clashed with AfD leader Alice Weidel in parliament, calling her party a "destructive force" with a migration policy that amounts to "ethnic cleansing" for skilled workers.

Merz was addressing the Bundestag in the aftermath of the anti-immigration party's sweeping victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt where it won almost 44% of the vote, while the chancellor's conservatives saw their vote halved.
Weidel told MPs that voters had shown that Merz's coalition with the centre left was a total failure and his time was up.
Merz hit back saying the AfD had harmed German interests by backing Russia, and its "remigration" policy would affect millions.

It is not yet clear whether the party will be able to form a government or not in Saxony-Anhalt, having fallen three seats short of an outright majority. No far-right party has won power in any of Germany's 16 states since World War Two, and Merz has admitted the "seismic" result has changed Germany.

The AfD's success has been praised by US President Donald Trump, who said "the Populist Party in Germany just had a really big night", linking the victory to "absolutely horrible immigration rules and regulations".
The AfD in Saxony-Anhalt has been labelled as "right-wing extremist" by German domestic intelligence and the party has promised a "deportation and remigration" offensive targeting irregular migrants.

Repeatedly heckled by AfD MPs, the chancellor told Weidel that one in six skilled workers had a migration background, and if her party had its way then its policy would amount to "nothing other than an ethnic cleansing in the skilled trades based on skin colour and origin".
While the government understood some deportations were needed, he said it make a careful distinction between those who contributed to German prosperity and those without permanent residency.
Disruption by AfD MPs became so loud that at one point Bundestag President Julia Klöckner threatened to start expelling people from the chamber: "We are not on a football pitch."

Weidel said mass migration had left Germans with daily knife violence and attacks on trains and in stations, but Merz warned that the AfD's plans would mean that no single care home, hospital or restaurant could function.

blocks.caption: Map of eastern Germany highlighting the state of Saxony-Anhalt in white. Key locations marked include Magdeburg (the state capital), Querfurt and Leipzig within or near the highlighted area, and Berlin to the northeast. Poland is shown to the east and the Czech Republic to the south. An inset map…

blocks.text: As leader of the main opposition party in the Bundestag, Weidel opened the session by telling Merz his Christian Democrats had been "pulverised" in Saxony-Anhalt, after winning 17.2% of the vote, and she accused his government with the Social Democrats of driving Germany towards bankruptcy.
Merz said her party had not won an outright majority in Saxony-Anhalt and it would not achieve one in Germany.

"You are and will remain a destructive force," he said, accusing the party of cheating the voters by saying before the election that their candidate for premier, Ulrich Siegmund, would only rule if he won a majority, but hours after the vote deciding to go and find one.
The AfD has opened the door to working with another party, perhaps the left-wing populist BSW, as long as it backs Siegmund to be state premier.

Siegmund's number two in Saxony-Anhalt, has even suggested that Merz's CDU could work with his party, if it abandons the so-called firewall (Brandmauer), under which no mainstream party will work with the far right.

articles.title: SWS: 48% of Filipinos expect quality of life to improve in next 12 months
articles.summary: Forty-eight percent of Filipinos aged 18 and above believe their quality of life will improve in the next 12 months, according to the latest survey by the Social Weather Stations (SWS).

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 7:23pm
Forty-eight percent of Filipinos aged 18 and above believe their quality of life will improve in the next 12 months, according to the latest survey by the Social Weather Stations (SWS).
The poll classified the 48% of respondents who expected improvements in their quality of life as “optimists.”
Meanwhile, 31% said their quality of life would remain the same, while 8% or the “pessimists” expected it to worsen.
The remaining 12% did not give an answer.

These figures resulted in a net personal optimism score of +40, computed by subtracting the percentage of pessimists from the percentage of optimists. SWS classified the score as “excellent,” according to SWS.
The June 2026 score was 17 points higher than the “high” +23 recorded in March, the survey firm said.
“The 17-point increase in the national Net Personal Optimism score between March and June 2026 was due to gains in all areas,” SWS said.
Net Personal Optimism rose from “high” to “excellent” in Balance Luzon, increasing by 27 points from +22 to +49.
The score also rose from “high” to “very high” in Metro Manila, up by 8 points from +28 to +36; in the Visayas, up by 6 points from +27 to +33; and in Mindanao, up by 11 points from +20 to +31.

The non-commissioned survey was conducted from June 20 to 29 and interviewed 1,200 adults face-to-face: 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas and Mindanao, and 600 in Balance Luzon, or Luzon outside Metro Manila.
The sampling error margins are ±3 percentage points for national percentages and ±6 percentage points each for Metro Manila, Balance Luzon, the Visayas and Mindanao.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: The problem with replatforming Alfred ‘Krip’ Yuson
articles.summary: Publishing house Exploding Galaxies announces that it will no longer republish and circulate Yuson's novel 'Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café'

blocks.text: Publishing house Exploding Galaxies announces that it will no longer republish and circulate Yuson's novel 'Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café'

items: Filipino author Alfred 'Krip' Yuson has faced multiple allegations of sexual misconduct and a plagiarism case, raising concerns about the ethics of republishing his work, particularly his novel 'Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.'

Despite initial support for the republication from Exploding Galaxies, backlash from the literary community led to a reconsideration of its decision, highlighting the complexities of promoting literature by controversial figures.

The situation has sparked broader discussions within the literary community about the moral implications of supporting works by authors with problematic histories and the responsibilities of publishers in such cases.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

MANILA, Philippines – Filipino literature and the classics that have come out of it always deserve to be known, and it’s often made possible by efforts like republishing and circulating physical copies to make them accessible to even more readers. But when the author behind one of these books has caused more harm than good, it becomes an entirely different story.
Case in point: Alfred “Krip” Yuson and his 1988 novel Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.

The book was supposed to have been given new life by Exploding Galaxies — with the publishing house even standing by its initial decision to republish the book despite drawing backlash from members of the literary community. Here’s what went down.

Yuson, a Carlos Palanca Memorial Awards for Literature Hall of Fame inductee, has been accused of sexual misconduct on several instances by different individuals. His latest published work was the 2022 book The Mountain That Grew.

“Why re-platform a man who’s responsible for the harassment and suicide of women? I do not care how brilliant you think his book is. I DO NOT CARE. And I will NEVER understand,” writer Katrina Stuart Santiago said in a Threads post on August 26.
Santiago further attested that she knows of young female writers who have had their own share of “horrid” experiences at the hands of Yuson.

“I remember when writers were being ‘cancelled’ left and right for everything from minor indiscretions to horrible mistakes to bad decisions, my question then was: when do we talk about the dirty old men of the literary establishment? Because THAT is a list. And it also has a list of victims. Re-platforming one of them by reprinting his book seems like [a] signal, doesn’t it. Of many things, including that people think we forget who these men are. We do not. We cannot. WE SHOULD NOT,” she said in another post on August 27.
Santiago added that literary workshops fuel Yuson’s predatory behavior, given the power dynamics that exist in these spaces between mentors and their mentees.

In response, Exploding Galaxies had initially attempted to discredit Santiago’s commentary, stating that while sexual harassment isn’t something they take lightly, the allegations that have been thrown at Yuson “have not been proven or independently corroborated.”

“We republished Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café for its well-established literary merit, and we stand by our decision to publish the book,” Exploding Galaxies wrote in its first public statement on September 5.

“We also stand firm against dishonest and unfair attempts to discredit this republication, especially as it is coming from a person who has expressed a longstanding personal grudge against the author, and who has, over the years, leveled serious public accusations against others,” it added.

Other figures in the literary community were quick to weigh in on the matter, with award-winning writer Jose “Butch” Dalisay Jr. pondering on the topic of art being created by questionable individuals.

“Does moral or political purity translate to some kind of elevated prose, or more honest and insightful poetry?” he wrote in a Facebook post. “Can someone please put together a library of vetted literature (or otherwise a new Index Librorum Prohibitorium) to spare us the process, and so we can keep to the straight and narrow, and enjoy reading without guilt or shame?”

Dalisay had followed it up with another post apologizing for appearing to trivialize the plight of sexual harassment victims — adding that the phenomenon of enabling a culture of harassment in workshops was something he would take up with the UP Institute of Creative Writing.

“There was a specific context to my remark that sexual misconduct and plagiarism were “low-hanging fruit.” It was not to dismiss them but to suggest that they were, among human evils, among the most visible and most common (which makes them no less painful to those concerned). I was talking about the possible crimes writers and artists have been accused of, which include murder and treason, and other offenses that injure not just one but many,” Dalisay said.

“I apologize to those victims of sexual harassment who may have seen my remarks as dismissive; they were not meant to be. It is a serious problem we are confronting not only in literature but in society at large.”
But sexual harassment isn’t the only serious issue that Yuson has found himself involved in. Writer Jaemark Tordecilla had accused him of plagiarism in 2011.

Tordecilla noticed that Yuson lifted several paragraphs from sportswriter Rey Joble’s piece about former PBA commissioner Rudy Salud. Joble’s story was published under GMA News Online, while Yuson had passed off his own version of it to Rogue Magazine.

Yuson was serving as GMA News Online’s editor-at-large then, and was in charge of copyediting Joble’s draft. He explained that since he had rewritten portions of Joble’s work, he thought he was considered to at least be part-author.

While he apologized for his actions, Yuson had merely attributed them to his old age, being overworked, and the pressure of having to meet deadlines. He still continued to write more after, and had even published several more works, like Islands of Words & Other Poems (2015), The Music Child & The Mahjong Queen (2016), and In the Footsteps of St. Ignatius of Loyola (2017), among others.
On September 7, Exploding Galaxies eventually announced that it would no longer push through with promoting or publishing Great Philippine Jungle Energy Café.

“We hear you all. We are sorry for the hurt this has caused our community. We are no longer promoting or releasing this book. As a publisher, we will do better. Thank you for speaking up,” the publisher said.

Exploding Galaxies also promised to “do better” in its mission to put works of Philippine literature back into circulation. But this still begs the question: How can publishers and literary circles do their part in discerning whether or not it is appropriate to promote a piece of work when the individual behind it has caused hurt to many others in the past?
Yuson has yet to comment on the matter himself. – Rappler.com

articles.title: LIV Golf in financial turmoil: what's next for the sport?
articles.summary: Six months after Saudi Arabia pulled funding from the breakaway organization, LIV Golf have filed for bankruptcy protection. Several of the world's best players signed on to LIV, so where does that…

image.caption: Bryson DeChambeau is owed an estimated $5.7m by LIV GolfImage: Jerod Ringwald/IMAGN Images/REUTERS

blocks.text: What has happened to LIV golf?
The breakaway golf tour, launched with much fanfare, billions of dollars of investment and a string of the world's best players, in 2021. But on Tuesday it filed for bankruptcy protection in the US.

Bankruptcy protection is a way of keeping a company alive while it restructures its debts. In this case, LIV would be moving from being financed by Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund (PIF), which pulled out in April, to being supported by BC Partners, a British investment firm.
"This process gives us the structure and time to pursue a landmark transaction and begin the next chapter of LIV Golf," said the chief executive, Scott O'Neil.

According to documents related to the filing, LIV Golf has between $500m (€430 million) and $1bn in estimated liabilities to at least 1,000 creditors. This includes an estimated $45 million to a group of top players like Bryson DeChambeau ($5.7m), Jon Rahm ($7.5m) and Dustin Johnson ($5.7m).

O'Neil added that LIV intends to move towards a "player-first ownership model" but detail is thin and there is currently no schedule in place for 2027. Most of LIV's staff were laid off earlier this year.
What has caused LIV golf to go bankrupt?

The sudden withdrawal of the PIF, which had invested an estimated $5 billion in LIV Golf, is the over-riding reason. At the time, the PIF said that LIV Golf was "no longer consistent with the current phase of PIF's investment strategy."

This was considered evidence of the project's failure to overthrow the established PGA Tour or make much in the way of money or impact. While the huge prize money on offer lured away several big names, many more remained with the PGA Tour.

While Tuesday's legal move may buy LIV time, the withdrawal of Saudi funding was so key to its business model that it gives O'Neil few options. To survive, it seems, they must keep at least some of their big-name players while slimming down dramatically.
Why is Saudi Arabia investing billions in sports?
Is this further evidence of Saudi Arabia pulling out of sport?

It certainly seems that investment in golf is a thing of the past for the oil-rich, Gulf state. There have also been withdrawals of funding for tournaments, clubs or organizations in snooker, women's tennis, rugby and football. Saudi Arabia also backed away from its commitment to host the 2029 Asian Winter Games.

Sport was a key part of Vision 2030, a pet project of Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman that aimed to diversify the Saudi economy and, in the eyes of many, also help launder its reputation through sport and other cultural assets.

blocks.caption: Saudi Arabia is scaling back many sporting plans, including for World Cup 2034Image: Fayez Nureldine/AFP

blocks.text: The uncertainty caused by conflict in the Middle East has meant even the vast wealth of the Saudi ruling class has taken a hit while projects like the resort of Trojena, set to be a key resort in those Winter Games, have been scaled back.

The same is true of Neom, a proposed World Cup venue for 2034. Planned as an entirely new type of city - 500-meter-high, built in a straight line and powered by renewable energy, Neom's construction has been significantly scaled back. The Guardian reported in late 2025 that several proposed World Cup stadium architects have been asked to rethink their plans to cut costs.
What will happen to the LIV golf players now?

That too is unclear. The PGA Tour and LIV Golf have always had a frosty relationship. Any player leaving to join LIV was immediately suspended from the PGA Tour, which runs all golf's major championships.

The 'returning member program', used by US golfer Brooks Koepka earlier this year to return to the PGA, briefly offered a potential pathway. It was designed as a "route back to elite performers who no longer have contractual limitations preventing them from complying with PGA Tour rules and regulations."

However it is was only open to players who left the PGA Tour at least two years ago and have won the The Players Championship or one of the four majors. DeChambeau, Cam Smith and Rahm were, therefore, the only players that qualified. But with that door now seemingly closed even to them, a return looks complex.

"I'm not part of the discussions but I'm pretty sure they aren't going to be welcomed back straight away," said Rory McIlroy, a six-time major winner who has been consistently critical of LIV, in August.

"They were offered this returning member program back in February, the one Brooks [Koepka] took, but that has come and gone and I think it was said at the time that the deal they get going forward if they decide to come back would not be as good at the one Brooks got. So I'd say it will be a tough road back."

articles.title: Norway's King Harald V laid to rest in state funeral
articles.summary: Heads of state from around the world came to Oslo to pay tribute to the late monarch.

image.caption: Harald reigned for 35 years, eschewing the modern tradition of abdicating in old ageImage: Jonathan Nackstrand/AFP

blocks.text: A 21-gun salute rang out over Oslo on Wednesday afternoon as the coffin of Norway's King Harald V left the royal palace for the city's Lutheran cathedral.
Thousands of people lined the streets to say goodbye to the king.
Norway then observed a minute of silence to start the funeral service.
The procession and funeral will bring an end to 13 days of national mourning following the death of the well-liked and down-to-earth monarch at the age of 89.

blocks.caption: King Haakon (second from left) walked alongside his children and sisterImage: Ole Berg-Rusten/NTB/REUTERS

blocks.text: Who is attending the funeral?

The funeral is being attended by heads of state and government from all over the world. This includes the UK's Prince William and Princess Anne, Japan's Crown Prince Fumihito and his wife Princess Kiko, Spain's King Felipe and Queen Letizia, as well as fellow Scandinavian royals from Denmark and Sweden.
Other leaders such as Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Germany's President Frank-Walter Steinmeier are also attending.
Harald's son King Haakon VIII will be there alongside his mother Queen Sonja and his wife, Queen Mette-Marit.
Controversially, Mette-Marit's son from a previous relationship is also expected to be at the funeral.
Marius Borg Hoiby's participation in an earlier part of the official mourning drew an outcry in Norway, as he was recently convicted of rape and domestic violence and is under house arrest.

articles.title: Serbia dissolves parliament as snap elections called
articles.summary: Serbia will head to the polls in late October after President Aleksandar Vucic dissolved parliament following growing pressure from protesters demanding political change. However, Vucic plans to…

image.caption: Aleksandar Vucic has signaled his ambition to run for prime ministerImage: Marko Dimic/ZUMA/picture alliance

blocks.text: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic signed an order on Wednesday calling for an early election after dissolving parliament.
"Elections will be held in Serbia on October 25. I believe that, after the elections, we will finally emerge from this crisis," he said.
"We have had … huge turbulences," Vucic said in an televised address. "We need election results that will clearly show the will of the people and the direction where Serbia is going."
Since November 2024, student-led protests have demanded Vucic step down, alleging corruption ⁠and authoritarianism.
The protests emerged after the collapse of a railway station in the northern city of Novi Sad, which left at least 16 people dead. Protesters say corruption led to shoddy construction work.
Initial calls for a transparent investigation then turned into demands for snap elections.
Nationalist leader Vucic has held power as both president and prime minister for more than a decade.
He is not allowed to run for another presidential term, but he has said he plans to run for prime minister instead.
More to come...

articles.title: Colombia's new president loosens gun control rules
articles.summary: President Abelardo de la Espriella has lifted a decade-long suspension on permits to carry legal firearms.

blocks.text: Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has signed a decree which eases restrictions on people carrying legal firearms in public.

De la Espriella, who during his campaign for the presidency promised to take an iron-fist approach to crime, said it was "not right that criminals are armed to the teeth while decent people can't defend themselves".
The decree lifts a suspension that had been in force for a decade, which meant that even those in possession of a permit to carry guns could not do so without additional authorisation.
De la Espriella insisted that the decree would not create a free-for-all and that tight controls over who can own a gun would remain in place.
While signing the decree, the president said he had made good on his campaign promise: "A man's word is his honour, and I have honour, that's why I keep my word."

The restriction on carrying legal guns in public was brought in by the then-President Juan Manuel Santos in December 2015. It was originally meant to be a temporary measure, aimed at improving security during the Christmas and New Year festivities.
But the suspension was extended yearly by Santos and two subsequent presidents from opposing sides of the political spectrum: conservative Iván Duque and left-wing Gustavo Petro.
Under the law, even those with a permit to carry a gun could not take it out of their homes unless they applied for - and were granted - additional authorisation.
De la Espriella has insisted that his decree has removed a restriction which had never been meant to be permanent.
According to Spanish newspaper El País, the decree will affect almost 700,000 people in Colombia who are already in possession of a legal permit to carry a gun.
They will now be able to take their registered gun out of their home, provided their permits remain up to date.
Green Alliance Party Senator Ariel Ávila described the move as a "grave error", arguing that legally held guns would end up in the hands of criminals.
Ávila insisted that it created an ethical dilemma, as it should only be state forces that carry guns and act as guarantors of people's security.

De la Espriella insisted that the measure would not negatively affect security in the country and said forces were targeting those holding illegal guns and had seized more than 15,000 firearms so far this year.
Most of them, according to de la Espriella, belonged to members of breakaway factions of the Farc rebel group and the Gulf Clan criminal gang.

articles.title: 'Hunted,' 'shattered,' 'scared': How victims say Canada's most prolific voyeur has altered their lives
articles.summary: CBC News has spent months going through court records and speaking with victims in the largest case of voyeurism ever reported in Canada. Victims say it has left them feeling shattered, hunted and…

image.caption: 'It doesn't devalue who you are … you didn't do anything wrong to put yourself in this situation, and none of it was your fault,' one woman tells others who are victims of a prolific voyeur. (Mike McArthur/CBC)

blocks.text: The 15-year-old wore her school uniform, unaware a stranger followed as she walked with her mother and brother through Victoria's Mayfair Shopping Centre.
A cellphone video would later show a voyeur trailing the family, before getting close enough to slip a camera beneath the girl's pleated skirt.
When police told the girl's mother, she faced a dilemma: tell her daughter, or keep it to herself?
"Learning my daughter's image had been taken and posted on child pornography websites was devastating," she wrote in a victim impact statement read in court earlier this year.
"I have carried significant stress over how I want to tell her and how she will cope with the information once she learns the truth."
The teen is one of 652 women and children filmed in what officials claim is the largest case of voyeurism ever reported in Canada.

Yin Yeung Derek Chan spent six years secretly recording victims throughout communities on southern Vancouver Island, filming through house windows and prowling malls and well-known stores in the heart of downtown Victoria.

In the year prior to Chan's 2024 arrest, the voyeur was creating more than a video a day, uploading footage and photos of victims to social media, porn sites and a personal website that had over a million views before it was taken down.
Chan was sentenced to four-and-a-half years in prison in May — but many of the photos and videos remain online. Only a fraction of the victims have been identified.

items: B.C. attorney general says potential victims of Saanich voyeur have 'right to know' key details from police

blocks.text: Despite wide reporting of the sentencing, many questions remain about the police investigation and the impact of Chan's crimes.
CBC News has spent months gathering court records, listening to audio of courtroom proceedings and reaching out to Chan's victims.
In her victim impact statement, one woman said watching the video Chan took of her "shattered" her sense of safety.
"Seeing myself through the eyes of someone who had been hiding, watching, deliberately capturing me without my knowledge or consent — it made me feel hunted," she said.
"This crime did not end when the recording stopped."
Chan used delivery job to access victims' homes

Chan came to Canada from Hong Kong as a child. Although Chan's lawyer said the 39-year-old identifies as gender fluid, police referred to Chan using male pronouns and some victims say they saw a man hovering nearby, phone in hand.
Crown prosecutor Paul Cheeseman said Chan worked as an Uber Eats delivery driver, using the job to access apartment building laundry rooms.
"[Police] found thousands of pairs of women's underwear in his house and a number of them were used," Cheeseman told the court.
"So it appears he was stealing women's underwear while he was doing these videos and deliveries."
Chan has a history of secretly recording women; in 2019, Chan was caught filming a woman in a changing room at a Forever 21.

During Chan's recent sentencing, the voyeur apologized to victims but offered little insight into a pattern of prolific offending. The judge said Chan compared it to the rush of "stealing a chocolate bar from a store" and attributed the crimes to "warm weather” in an earlier proceeding.
Saanich police have repeatedly declined to specify where Chan filmed victims, in spite of calls from B.C.'s attorney general to help potential victims know if they could be affected.

According to the court records, more than 400 victims were targeted at Value Village in Victoria, while about 80 were filmed at local Walmart locations. Others were recorded at Greater Victoria businesses, including Indigo Books, Munro's Books, Shoppers Drug Mart, Michaels, Mayfair Shopping Centre, Hillside Centre, and the Bay Centre mall.
A few were sunbathing at what is believed by police to be Willows Beach in Oak Bay.
Five people were recorded through the windows of their homes and apartments, at addresses in the James Bay, Fairfield, and Hillside neighbourhoods of Victoria.
Police also found about 100 hours of other videos Chan recorded of other women at gyms and malls that "don't rise to the level of criminal voyeurism," Cheeseman said.
'A part of my innocence was taken from me'
One victim told CBC News that Saanich police contacted her in January 2025 after an officer she knew recognized her in a video seized from Chan's home.
Until she saw the video, she didn’t know Chan had snuck up behind her in an Indigo Books to film up her dress — though she remembers seeing the voyeur.

"Him being so close to me was like the most icky feeling and thing to think about, like, how did I let someone get so close to me without noticing?" said the woman, whose identity is protected by a publication ban.
"It made me scared to think of, like someone could get that close to me without realizing, like what else could they have done to me?"
For a time after she found out, the woman says she was too afraid to go out alone in public, even to the grocery store.
Just weeks ago, a man in line at a dollar store started talking to her.
"I just like, shut down in my body," said the woman.
In victim impact statements, other women told the judge who sentenced Chan that they have difficulty holding down a job, struggle with mental health, and have changed the clothes they wear.

items: 1st known victim of Saanich voyeur calls for police, court reforms to prevent future offences

blocks.text: Some spend money on Ubers to avoid public transit. One victim said she got off a bus and walked almost an hour, because another passenger had a phone camera pointed her way.
The women said Chan's crimes have affected relationships, eroded their ability to trust others, and left them feeling powerless.
"I feel as though a part of my innocence was taken from me," wrote one victim, who was 17 and days out from her high school graduation when Chan filmed her.

Another victim was underage when Chan recorded her working as an employee at a mall. The incident triggered past trauma and she began to isolate herself. Her grades at a local college suffered, and she had to withdraw.
She said she was unable to maintain a job due to intense anxiety and fear in public spaces.
The woman said she gets counselling and financial support from WorkSafeBC, but the $4,900 she receives a year isn't enough to make ends meet.
"My life has been delayed and derailed, and my future seems uncertain," she said in her statement to the court.
"This offence did not just take away my sense of safety, it took away my independence, my ability to support myself, and my financial stability."
Some recordings still online
Cheeseman said Chan was well known in the online voyeurism community for posting videos, which were downloaded and reposted by other users.
"Mr. Chan has made it available for the entire world to revictimize these people," he said.
While police have gotten some recordings removed from Chan's personal website and Flickr, the prosecutor said officials have faced challenges in getting others taken down.

items: Girls in school uniforms among hundreds filmed by Saanich voyeur, court records reveal

blocks.text: A search of the username Chan used to upload many videos and images of the victims shows many are still easily found online on social media and porn websites.
One of these posts, on Reddit, is tagged "NSFW" — the site's label for explicit content.
Comments on this post, shown in court, ask Chan where to find the videos.
"We're all eager and ready to pay or something man you gotta bless us you got the finest bitches on camera," writes one user.
"Will u sponsor me?" Chan writes back to another, telling a third user the videos are "only open to payers."
Reddit did not respond to questions from CBC News about the post.

Saanich police did not answer questions from CBC News, but Deputy Chief Const. Damian Kowalewich said in a statement that "the scale of this case was unprecedented and the impact on victims cannot be overstated."

"We recognize that once material has been distributed online it may not be possible to remove every copy, which remains an ongoing concern for many victims and represents an additional layer of victimization."
'None of it was your fault,' woman tells other victims
On May 21, the day of Chan's sentencing, Saanich police published a notice announcing the case publicly for the first time.

The victim who spoke to CBC News says it felt strange to see everyone discussing something she'd only told a few of those closest to her, especially as police promised to update her before the case became public — which she says they did not.
At first, she said it felt scary to read what people thought online about the case. But with time, it began to feel validating.

"It kind of made me feel like I was able to then be like, you know what, this was really messed up, and this happened to me, and I am allowed to feel violated by this situation, and I should allow myself time and space to have those feelings," the woman said.
"It doesn't devalue who you are … you didn't do anything wrong to put yourself in this situation, and none of it was your fault."

articles.title: How are northern Sask. schools preparing youth for new mining opportunities?
articles.summary: Schools in northern Saskatchewan are adapting to prepare students to work in a mine that's under construction in the region. It's an unprecedented economic opportunity, but it doesn't come without…

image.caption: Students in northern Saskatchewan schools are thinking about NexGen's mining opportunities. (Don Somers/CBC)

blocks.text: Saskatchewan

Schools in northern Saskatchewan are adapting to prepare students to work in a mine that's under construction in the region. It's an unprecedented economic opportunity, but it doesn't come without concerns for the environment.
Financial literacy, practical skills and environmental protocols are classroom topics
Grade 12 student Landon Moise is part of a cohort of young people who may have a future working at a mine under construction north of their community in a remote part of Saskatchewan.
Moise attends Clearwater River Dene School, a land-based learning school more than 500 kilometres north of Saskatoon and two hours away from a new uranium mine being built by NexGen Energy.
He says the school is adapting its curriculum to prepare students for the big economic and environmental changes on the way.
“I get to learn how to protect the environment and how to work with it,” Moise said. “Along with working and understanding these big corporations that work just in our backyard.”
NexGen’s Rook 1 mine is being built on the traditional territory of the Dene, Cree and Métis people.
The $2.2 billion project is expected to generate nearly 500 full-time jobs and make Canada the world’s largest exporter of uranium.
It’s an unprecedented economic opportunity, and teachers at the school want young people to be ready.
They’re teaching classes like financial literacy, as well as hands-on-skills that are recognized in and out of the classroom.

“[They're] making those connections with industry and finding out that something they can do with the toolset they’re learning in the shop could also provide an income,” said Brien Morgan, the school’s practical and applied arts teacher.
“And then they were able to actually make that connection with the work that’s going on north of us.”
Morgan taught students to make core sampling boxes, which hold soil during mine drilling. He partnered with a local business and sold students' work to mines up north.
These kinds of projects uplift students and make them feel ready to take jobs after graduation, he said.
The school also knows that a mining project of this magnitude will affect the land.
Last year, students had a chance to visit the mine site and plant just over 4,000 seedlings of blueberry, alder and jack pines.
“I think it was great because we got to learn how this stuff grows, how to protect them and how to treat them properly,” Moise said.
Teacher Paul Haynes organized that project and helped start the land-based learning program so students could reconnect with the land and learn in a more traditional setting.
It’s great that students are already signing contracts with NexGen for after graduation, he said.
“Here’s what you’re making in a year. It’s more than twice as much as me, and you just graduated.”
But he’s also worried about how the development will affect the land and traditional food sources.
Sask. mine set to make Canada largest global uranium exporter
“There’s a lot more traffic on the road. That changes things,” Haynes said.
“It affects how you hunt or how you trap. There’s certain spots on the highway [where] I don’t set traps anymore, it’s not safe.”
Haynes said it’s important that students get educated on the environmental pros and cons so they can self-determine their viewpoint on the project.
How is NexGen protecting the environment?
NexGen tells CBC that rigorous environmental protocol is followed daily relating to wildlife, air quality and water.

The company has signed benefit agreements with First Nations and Métis communities near the mine, allow the communities to engage their own environmental consultants and review all of NexGen’s environmental data relating to operations.
NexGen CEO Leigh Curyer said they work in collaboration with the provincial and federal governments to ensure operations are environmentally sensitive.
“In a lot of instances we’re even improving the environment through proactive reclamation,” Curyer said.
Every mining operation in Canada uses surface tailings, which is the most environmentally impactful element of any mining operation, and he wanted this project’s tailings to be different, he said.
“We purposely designed the tailings in underground chambers, which are elite with respect to the environmental consequence of tailing attributes of a mining operation,” Curyer said.
It’s the first time the concept is being executed in Canada.
“It does cost extra from a capital cost and also an operating cost,” Curyer said. “But it's environmentally elite.”

Curyer said the concept has been recognized by the Canadian Nuclear Safety Commission as industry leading, and he hopes it means the traditional land won’t be harmed during the 24-year lifespan of the mine.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Halyna Mihalik is a journalist and weather specialist for CBC Saskatchewan. She holds a degree in journalism from the University of Regina. Halyna enjoys stories about advocacy, local politics and rural communities. Send Halyna news tips at halyna.mihalik@cbc.ca

articles.title: Russia and Ukraine exchange strikes as two killed at Moldova border
articles.summary: Meanwhile, four people, including a child, were killed in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk.

blocks.text: Two people have been killed after Russian drones struck a border crossing between Ukraine and Moldova, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said.

The Starokozache crossing, around 500km (310 miles) south of Kyiv, was closed after the overnight attack. Images from the scene showed several cars left completely scorched, with wreckage and debris strewn across the border post.
Meanwhile, four people, including a child, were killed in the southern Russian city of Novorossiysk in a Ukrainian drone attack, the regional governor said.
Both Russia and Ukraine have stepped up long-range strikes in recent months, despite renewed diplomatic efforts to end the war.
Zelensky renewed calls for international support in the wake of the Starokozache crossing attack, saying "the aggression must be stopped here and now before it spreads any further".
The border link between Ukraine and Moldova was shut after the attack killed two people and injured three others, Odesa regional governor Oleg Kiper said.
A Moldovan driver was also injured, according to the country's foreign ministry.

Moldova has increasingly found itself caught up in the conflict, with Prime Minister Vasile Tofan confirming that 17 drones had struck Moldovan territory in August alone - more than during the whole of last year.
"Those who ignore or downplay these threats - and refuse to name the aggressor - are denying reality," he wrote on social media.
"Russia started this war. Russia alone bears responsibility."

articles.title: Win: Sara Duterte's impeachment trial verdict eyed before December
articles.summary: Senate President Sherwin "Win" Gatchalian and other senators are eyeing to wrap up Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial before December, hoping that a verdict would be reached before the…

blocks.text: Published September 9, 2026 6:50pm

Senate President Sherwin "Win" Gatchalian and other senators are eyeing to wrap up Vice President Sara Duterte's impeachment trial before December, hoping that a verdict would be reached before the year ends.
In an ambush interview at the Senate on Wednesday, Gatchalian said the prosecution's move to drop 15 witnesses has a big impact on the trial's timeline.
"Ang timetable na nakikita namin, hopefully, before December matapos na lahat," Gatchalian said.
(The timetable that we see, hopefully before December, everything is finished.)
Gatchalian stressed that this still depends on the witnesses that the defense will present after the prosecution is finished tackling all four Articles of Impeachment.
However, Gatchalian said the defense has already lessened the number of witnesses they planned to present.
Meanwhile, Senate finance committee chair Senator JV Ejercito said he wanted to get the trial done as soon as possible to allow more time for the budget hearings.

"Sana mapabilis na ito para makabalik na tayo sa normal na pamumuhay. Kasi dami nating kailangan ayusin. Daming problema. Nakaka-apekto rin siyempre 'yung hidwaan sa politika sa overall, sa lahat ng takbo natin ng bansa," Ejercito said.
(I hope the trial progresses faster so we can get back to normal. Because we have so many things to fix. A lot of problems. The political divide is affecting the way that the country is being run.)
The prosecution panel dropped the 15 witnesses in Article 1 of the Articles of Impeachment, hoping to replace them with Duterte instead. Article 1 refers to the alleged misuse of confidential funds.
Senators have previously lamented the prolonged time that the impeachment trial was taking away from other legislative matters. — VDV, GMA News

articles.title: Supreme Court acquits Imelda Marcos in 7 counts of graft
articles.summary: The SC says the prosecution failed to prove Marcos' guilt beyond reasonable doubt

blocks.text: IMELDA. Former first lady Imelda Marcos at Senator Bongbong Marcos rally in Mandaluyong.
Rob Reyes
The SC says the prosecution failed to prove Marcos' guilt beyond reasonable doubt

items: The Supreme Court of the Philippines acquitted Imelda Marcos of graft charges related to Swiss foundations, overturning a previous conviction by the Sandiganbayan.
The Court ruled that the prosecution failed to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt, particularly regarding the authenticity of evidence presented.
The decision emphasized that the prosecution did not establish that the foundations in question constituted 'businesses' as defined under the relevant laws.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.
MANILA, Philippines – The Supreme Court (SC) 1st Division acquitted Imelda Marcos, the mother of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., in her graft cases related to Swiss foundations.
In a decision made public on Wednesday, September 9, the SC division overturned the Sandiganbayan’s November 2018 decision that convicted the 97-year-old former first lady of seven counts of graft.

“Accordingly, the Appeal is granted. The November 9, 2018 Decision of the Sandiganbayan in Criminal Case Nos. 17287, 17288, 17289, 17290, 22867, 22868, and 22869 is reversed and set aside. Accused-appellant Imelda R. Marcos is acquitted for the prosecution’s failure to prove her guilt beyond reasonable doubt for violation of Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019, in relation to Article IX, Section 8 of the 1973 Constitution,” said the 50-page ruling penned by Associate Justice Rodil Zalameda.
Associate justices Ramon Paul Hernando, Henri Jean Paul Inting, Ricardo Rosario, and Jose Midas Marquez all concurred in the ruling.
The Marcos matriarch is acquitted four years into the presidential term of her son, who won the presidency in 2022.
In its decision, the SC division said the prosecution failed to prove Marcos’ guilt beyond reasonable doubt. Beyond reasonable doubt is the threshold needed to convict an accused in criminal cases.
Marcos was charged with alleged violation of Section 3(h), which has the following elements:

items: the accused is a public officer
they have direct or indirect financial or pecuniary interest in any business, contract, or transaction
they either intervened or took part in their official capacity or connection with such interest, or they are prohibited from having such interest by the Constitution or by any law

blocks.text: The SC said it’s undisputed that the first element is present, but the second and third elements are contested. The Office of the Ombudsman presented documentary and testimonial evidence that sought to prove Marcos’ financial interest, but the SC said they were “inadmissible and lack probative weight.”

In Marcos’ case, the Sandiganbayan found that she had a financial and pecuniary interest in the foundations based on the Swiss documents. The documents were retrieved from Swiss banks and had been authenticated in accordance with Swiss legal procedure.
However, the SC said the Sandiganbayan erred when it considered the Swiss documents duly authenticated.

“The Court has emphasized that the rule on authentication, more particularly as to private documents, is in place to prevent the inclusion of spurious documents in the body of evidence. Thus, it is settled that private documents are generally inadmissible in evidence unless they are properly authenticated,” said the ruling, adding that the prosecution was not able to present a credible witness who could have testified to the documents’ authenticity.

In addition, even if the SC would ignore the probative weight of the prosecution’s evidence, Marcos must still be acquitted, said the Court. The prosecution, according to the SC, failed to prove that the alleged pecuniary interest was “covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution.”

“All told, the prosecution failed to establish that the subject foundations are businesses as the term is ordinarily understood. Any financial or pecuniary interest in the subject foundations is not covered by Section 3(h) of Republic Act No. 3019 and Article IX, Section 7 (then Section 8) of the 1973 Constitution. Doubts on the coverage of the term ‘business’ should be resolved against the State and in favor of the accused-appellant,” said the ruling. – Rappler.com

blocks.text: Republicans put Trump center stage for convention in US midterms gamble
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.

Donald Trump is due to address Republicans tonight at the party’s first ever national convention ahead of the crucial midterm elections, with the GOP hoping to energize voters as it fights to hold its narrow congressional majorities.
The two-day gathering takes place in Dallas, marking a break from the longstanding tradition of holding national conventions only during presidential election years.
“It has never been done before, and will be a truly Historic Event,” Trump said in July while announcing the convention, promising the convention would feature “Great Entertainment”.
Trump first floated the idea for a convention last year, arguing that it would provide an opportunity to showcase his administration’s achievements since he returned to the White House in 2024.
More than 100 House members and candidates are expected, with over 50 speakers or presentations scheduled each night.

Trump delivers this evening’s keynote speech and returns for Thursday’s finale after vice-president JD Vance speaks. Cabinet members, congressional leaders and candidates in closely watched House and Senate races are also on the program.
Republicans plan to highlight tax cuts, immigration enforcement, manufacturing and prescription drug prices, while depicting Democrats as dangerously far to the left.
In other developments:

items: Clashing court rulings plunged Missouri’s congressional elections into uncertainty. blocks.text: Trump gave $45,000 to Natalie Harp and other White House aides as holiday gifts
Donald Trump gave sizable holiday gifts to four White House aides, according to new financial disclosures released by the administration, including $45,000 to executive assistant Natalie Harp.

Communications adviser Margo Martin and deputy director of Oval Office operations Chamberlain Harris also received $45,000, while director of Oval Office operations Walt Nauta received a $20,000 gift.

The gifts were noted in the staffers’ annual financial disclosure forms that were published by the administration last week. Harp, Martin and Harris make $150,000 annually and Nauta is paid $175,000 a year, according to the White House’s salary disclosure report to Congress.

A White House official told the Associated Press that Trump “has a longstanding practice of giving Christmas gifts to people in his orbit, including at times employees and aides, both in government and in his time in the private sector.”

The official did not say if any other staffers were given similar gifts from the president, but added that the cash gifts were not related to the “individuals’ official government duties, and therefore are entirely permissible under relevant legal and ethical standards.”
The disclosures of the gifts were first reported earlier on Tuesday by The Washington Post.

articles.title: P6.2 billion slated for fertilizer, fuel aid to ease El Niño impact
articles.summary: On top of this, the Department of Agriculture is asking Congress for an additional P10 billion in its 2027 budget in anticipation of severe El Niño impact

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – The government is set to distribute P6.2 billion worth of fertilizer and fuel assistance to help cushion the impacts of the global oil crisis and El Niño on farmers and fisherfolk.
The fund is under the Unified Package for Livelihoods, Industry, Food, and Transport, or UPLIFT, a comprehensive response to energy security and livelihood needs amid the Middle East conflict.

There is no identified number yet of beneficiary farmers and fishers, according to Department of Agriculture spokesperson Arnel de Mesa. To ensure good yield, much of the fertilizer aid will be distributed to places less affected by El Niño.
“One of the things that DA is really going to do is to maximize yield in areas not affected by El Niño,” De Mesa said in a press briefing on Wednesday, September 9.

De Mesa said the full impact of El Niño on crops and prices will not be felt until the first semester of 2027, and that these measures are preparatory before El Niño develops into a more severe state by the end of 2026.
“If the fund is released in October, it works exactly as support during El Niño,” said De Mesa.
The Department of Agriculture is also requesting an additional P10 billion in 2027 to augment cash assistance for farmers and fishers, in anticipation of El Niño impacts.

The agriculture sector was left reeling from the effects of the southwest monsoon or habagat and past tropical cyclones, incurring production losses worth P4.38 billion. The palay sector lost P2 billion.
“Again, we do not see impact on rice prices because, in terms of volume, this is within our estimated losses every year because of typhoons, flooding, and other calamities,” De Mesa explained.
Estimated losses in rice production ranged from 500,000 to 600,000 metric tons, said De Mesa. The P2 billion worth of damage in the palay sector is “about only 70,000 metric tons of losses.”

In a bid to curb prices and support local production, the DA said it will not allow imports of high-grade rice in the meantime. According to reports, Agriculture Secretary Francisco Tiu Laurel Jr. talked with the rice industry to import only 25% (and above) broken rice. – Rappler.com

“The program highlighted the important role of the youth in addressing environmental concerns, as well as the fact that environmental protection is a global responsibility that knows no nationality,” the DENR said.
Cenro Lipa also emphasized the importance of engaging young people in environmental protection efforts.
“It is important to raise their awareness and encourage their active participation in initiatives aimed at protecting the environment and natural resources,” the DENR said.

The narra, which is the Philippines’ national tree, is a large leguminous tree that can grow 30 to 40 meters tall. It produces fragrant yellow flowers that attract bees and typically blooms from February to May.
The species faces increasing threats from illegal logging, habitat loss, land conversion, and unsustainable harvesting. /mcm

articles.title: No travel tax, no budget: Can TIEZA keep its tourism projects alive?
articles.summary: The pesky travel tax is easy to hate, but abolishing it could leave multi-year tourism infrastructure projects in limbo, especially with TIEZA not getting anything in the proposed 2027 budget

blocks.text: The pesky travel tax is easy to hate, but abolishing it could leave multi-year tourism infrastructure projects in limbo, especially with TIEZA not getting anything in the proposed 2027 budget

Even as the government keeps pitching tourism as a growth priority and jobs engine, the agency tasked with building much of its infrastructure is heading into 2027 with billions’ worth of ongoing projects and a proposed budget of exactly zero.

On top of this, if Congress succeeds in abolishing the travel tax, the Tourism Infrastructure and Enterprise Zone Authority (TIEZA) could also lose the revenue stream that normally pays for almost everything it does.

A source familiar with TIEZA’s budget planning told Rappler that the agency initially sought around P5.2 billion in national government funding for 2027. That request covered infrastructure projects alone and did not yet include personnel services or maintenance and other operating expenses.

Budget Secretary Kim Robert de Leon informed TIEZA that the request could not be favorably considered because of the government’s limited fiscal space, the source said. Consequently, the proposed 2027 budget carries zero subsidy for the agency, compared with P248 million for general administration and support in 2026.
The Department of Budget and Management (DBM) echoed this stance during the budget hearing of the Department of Tourism (DOT).

“TIEZA’s proposal for National Government Subsidy in FY2027 is in view of several legislative measures proposing the abolition of the travel tax. However, as these bills remain under deliberation in the Senate and have yet to be enacted into law, the TIEZA’s requested subsidy was not considered in the FY [2027] NEP,” DBM Assistant Director Lulu Vispo said.

A zero budget may come with consequences on the tourism infrastructure pipeline. TIEZA chief operating officer Mark Lapid told lawmakers during the tourism department’s budget hearing that almost all of its projects are multi-year, with around P5.2 billion needed in 2027 alone to keep them moving.
The DBM, however, pointed to P2.355 billion in supposedly available TIEZA funds: P810.25 million in unobligated allotments as of March 31 and another P1.545 billion in unreleased 2025 appropriations.
“TIEZA may continue to utilize its travel tax collections to fund tourism-related infrastructures or projects,” Vispo added on Monday, September 7.

Meanwhile, TIEZA says that money is not sitting idly. Lapid told lawmakers that the roughly P2 billion cited during the hearing could not simply be used to pay for its infrastructure commitments as it was being used to fund the agency’s payroll.
“The P2 billion is for our personnel services in our office operations. So technically, we wouldn’t have any funds for infrastructure from the amount mentioned,” Lapid told lawmakers in Filipino.

blocks.caption: [In This Economy] Travel tax: Time to go

blocks.text: The problem is that the pesky P1,620 travel tax that travelers love to hate is also what keeps much of TIEZA running.
Congress is now moving to abolish it. The House has already approved House Bill 8464, while Senate President Sherwin Gatchalian said in August that the Senate is targeting abolition within the year.

Under the current setup, 50% of tax collections go to TIEZA, 40% to the Commission on Higher Education, and 10% to the National Commission for Culture and the Arts. TIEZA’s share from those travel taxes makes up roughly 95% of its funding, an agency source told Rappler.

The House bill does anticipate the problem by requiring the national government to replace those funds through the annual budget. The tricky part is timing. TIEZA is being told to prepare for a future in which the travel tax disappears, but it has yet to receive approval for replacement funding.

blocks.caption: Photo from a TIEZA presentation shown during the House budget hearing for the DOT.

blocks.text: The tax cut could also have a very human cost inside the agency that needs consideration. A TIEZA presentation showed that around 300 travel tax personnel may be displaced out of its 1,045-strong workforce. Of those, 115 may have difficulty finding new work because of their age, while some 270 families could be affected.

Lapid told lawmakers that TIEZA cannot simply absorb the workers elsewhere because they are spread across international gateways nationwide and the agency does not have enough plantilla positions at its main office. Some could be terminated, while others may receive separation incentives.
During Monday’s budget hearing, the DOT made its case for Congress to restore an allocation for at least P1.3 billion for five TIEZA projects.
The list obtained by Rappler from a source includes:

items: P328.9 million for improvements of the Banaue Hotel and Youth Hostel complex in Ifugao. The TIEZA-owned property sits on a 5.3-hectare site overlooking the Banaue Rice Terraces and has 81 hotel rooms plus a 15-room youth hostel. TIEZA has been rehabilitating the aging property for years, which has remained temporarily closed.

P301.07 million for the CBDC River Water System in San Vicente, Palawan. This is meant to provide a long-term potable water supply to tourism establishments and communities around Long Beach, one of the main clusters of TIEZA’s San Vicente Flagship Tourism Enterprise Zone.

P400 million for iLIPAD, TIEZA’s airport development program with DOTr. Launched in 2020, the program helps fund upgrades to provincial airports, particularly facilities needed for night operations and greater flight capacity.

P212.2 million for the construction of a waste water treatment facility in Coron. The project is aimed at addressing the environmental strain that tourism and development place on one of Palawan’s busiest destinations.

P63.7 million for the construction of Sky Garden in Barangay Lucap, Alaminos City. The project, which Marcos himself broke ground for in May 2025, is envisioned as another attraction and gateway near Hundred Islands, with elevated gardens, viewing decks, walkways, parking, a commercial center, and a multipurpose hall.

blocks.text: The proposed allocations for the DOT and its attached agencies are not yet final, however, as Congress can still revise the 2027 budget before it is enacted. But so far, lawmakers have appeared receptive to calls for more tourism funding, repeatedly pointing to the country’s infrastructure gaps and the need for greater investment.

After all, one need only look at NAIA to see what years of underinvestment can do to a country’s main international gateway — and how quickly things can begin to turn once fresh capital finally starts pouring in. – Rappler.com

blocks.caption: Two years and billions later, has NAIA finally leveled up?

articles.title: [DECODED] Why gamifying abuse impacts all of us
articles.summary: Gamified abuse scales the way it does not only because of the bad actors that exploit them, but for the lack of accountability from the online platforms in which they thrive

blocks.text: Gamified abuse scales the way it does not only because of the bad actors that exploit them, but for the lack of accountability from the online platforms in which they thrive

items: Rappler's investigation reveals NSFWPH, an online forum exploiting women by sharing non-consensual intimate content, boasting 430,000 members and a gamified system that rewards such behavior.
Members of NSFWPH take pride in manipulating women into sharing intimate photos, viewing their participation as a badge of honor, while the forum's ranking system incentivizes further exploitation.

The model of gamified abuse is not isolated to NSFWPH; similar practices are seen in the 'Grift Economy,' where online communities monetize vulnerability, highlighting a broader issue of accountability among platforms.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

In case you missed it, Rappler published a two-part investigative series over the weekend uncovering an online community that exploits women by sharing their intimate photos and videos without consent. The online forum called NSFWPH, which launched in April 2023, claims to have amassed 430,000 registered members and nearly 9 million posts and comments — all to share and consume voyeur content.

What’s more troubling, apart from the non-consensual sharing of intimate content featuring unwitting women, is that the members of this forum deliberately post and contribute to the forum as a point of pride.

Posts in the forum showed that many of the members of NSFWPH consider their participation a badge of honor, considering the lengths that they go to in order to obtain intimate photos and videos from women they know or interact with.
PART 1: How Filipinas’ intimate moments end up on a 430,000-member forum
Some even shared how they manipulated women into sharing nudes with them, which were in turn rewarded by the other forum members through congratulatory comments.

The forum treats these exploits, betrayals of trust, and, in some cases, content theft, as achievements that catapult a member’s “status” on the platform. The more a user shares and interacts on the platform, the more they get points that place them higher in NSFWPH’s ranking system.
This system has a name: it’s gamified abuse.

Because the higher a member ranks in the forum’s merit system, the more privileges they unlock, such as access to locked content or additional information about the victims, like their names or links to their Facebook and Instagram accounts.
Part 2: Gamified abuse: How a PH forum rewards submissions of non-consensual intimate content
In the case of NSFWPH, Filipinas were the victims. But the same business model is being used by bad actors across our current online ecosystem, targeting everyone vulnerable — including men.

Research and advocacy groups Reset Tech and Equimundo recently published a report called “The Grift Economy,” which examined how male loneliness is being monetized through membership schemes and so-called educational products. The report outlined how those in the “manosphere,” a collection of online communities focused on masculinity, are being pulled in with content that aligns with their ideologies, until they are drawn deeper into grievance-driven communities and, ultimately, monetized.

We see parallels in how the Grift Economy gamifies the exploitation of men’s need for connection to how the NSFWPH gamifies the exploitation of women’s intimate images and videos. Both employ these three mechanisms:

items: Points system turns participation into a game.

blocks.text: The NSFWPH forum gamifies its members’ participation by assigning them ranks. The Grift Economy explains how manosphere communities assign similar status systems in the “brotherhood” system. Such practice keeps members engaged, because they are rewarded through their participation.

items: Online platforms are active financial beneficiaries.

blocks.text: The Grift Economy points to online platforms as “usually the single largest financial beneficiary of any given operation.” This is because they share a portion of advertising income with the creators who run the ads that target vulnerable men.

In NSFWPH’s case, the result is a multi-layered monetization model. “The forum’s gamified system rewards users for uploading intimate content, while traffic and advertising turn exploitation into profit,” Rappler writers Gelo Gonzales and Lance Ariel Bustos said.

items: The problem is not limited to one platform.

blocks.text: Rappler’s investigation found that one of the most prominent members of NSFWPH is diverting the voyeur content he posts on the forum to a separate website where he set up pop-up ads that he can directly earn from, and to his own membership-based channel on Discord, a separate messaging and communication platform. By doing so, he is able to charge for more exclusive content.
The same is true for the Grift Economy. They thrive on different platforms, including YouTube, TikTok, X, Kick, Telegram, Instagram, and Spotify.

This practice makes the entire operation resilient: if one platform goes bust, other online communities will be able to absorb the operation, especially if they have lax policies against abuse and exploitation.

Gamified abuse is a business model, and it scales the way it does not only because of the bad actors that exploit them, but for the lack of accountability from the online platforms in which they thrive.
This makes all of us who spend time online vulnerable. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Family of killed teen call for death penalty in D4vd trial
articles.summary: The parents of Celeste Rivas Hernandez say execution "would be perfect" if D4vd is found guilty.

blocks.text: The lawsuit, lodged at Los Angeles Superior Court and reported by multiple, external US media outlets, external, makes similar claims to those raised by prosecutors in the criminal case against the singer.
Mercedes Martinez and Jesus Rivas allege that Burke caused the wrongful death, false imprisonment and childhood sexual assault of their daughter.
In the court documents, they say Burke and Hernandez first met in November 2023, when she was 13 years old.
Over the next 16 months, they claim, the pair would exchange almost 10,000 texts and have sex several times.

"At all relevant times Burke was an adult who occupied a position of authority over decedent, a minor, and was able to and did exercise undue influence and control over her," the parents say, in papers filed last Friday.

They go on to claim that Burke killed the teenager at his Hollywood Hills home, when she threatened to reveal their relationship, after allegedly sending a message that read: "I will end ur career and ur life".
In addition to Burke, the lawsuit names several of Burke's companies and managers, his mother and a live-in security guard.
Hernandez's parents allege that these people "enabled Burke to isolate" Rivas Hernandez and facilitated his travel, housing and security.
Burke's management company Mogul Vision and finance manager have previously denied knowing about Burke and Rivas Hernandez, the Los Angeles Times, external reported.

In July, a judge found enough probable cause for Burke to stand trial on the murder charge in the criminal case. At the time, the district attorney said he was weighing whether to seek the death penalty.
In a statement on Monday, which would have been Hernandez's 16th birthday, her family demanded that Burke be subjected to execution.

"If the death penalty were activated, it would be perfect for this kind of human being, devoid of feelings and emptiness inside, and without conscience, who only caused pain to our daughter, our family, and the world that supports our precious daughter," read the statement, released via the family's attorney.

Burke again pleaded not guilty to the charges last week and has since parted ways with his celebrity defence attorney. He is now being represented by a public defender and is due back in court on 19 October. His trial has been moved to next year.
Deputy public defender Walid Kandeel has said that Burke was "entitled to a defence that takes his circumstances seriously and carefully examines the evidence".
"We are committed to providing him with that defence," he said.
His office did not immediately provide comment on the civil lawsuit.

articles.title: Conspiracy theories can provide answers, but not peace
articles.summary: Twenty-five years after 9/11, conspiracy theories about the terrorist attacks persist. But even as an attempt to make sense of a tragedy, psychologists say the benefit in conspiracy ideation or…

image.caption: Not even conspiracy theories help us come to terms with the unsettling events of September 11, 2001Image: Diane Bondareff/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Psychology is not an exact science. That may irk a few researchers in the field. But it is important to mention upfront: Researching the psychology of conspiracy theories — why people are drawn to believing them and the effect they have on those people — is a complicated field of research, and conclusions are difficult to derive.
That is due, in part, to one of the basic problems with psychology, whether it's in treatment or in research, and that is that it relies on people's self-awareness.

If we take the example of the 9/11 terrorist attacks, some people continue to maintain it was "inside job", orchestrated by a secretive and powerful club of evil doers in the US government, intent on controlling citizens' lives by fear. And that may be true. But it may also be true that you, as a believer in such a theory, have always felt powerful people — your parents or teachers — have controlled and curtailed your agency in life. You may even have a false memory of how the terrorist attacks evolved on that day in 2001. Then, if someone asked you, "What really happened?", could you really say it for sure? I couldn't.
Self-report data is an issue in conspiracy research
Whether as patients or participants in a study, we may be asked to "self-report" — to look inside ourselves and express how we feel and why.
Self-reporting is an established way of measuring conspiracies, said Neil Dagnall, a professor of psychology at Manchester Metropolitan University, in an interview with DW.
But self-report data are "not perfect," he added.

They can be difficult data to handle because each judgment a person makes about themselves is relative, inherently subjective, and open to outside influence and bias. People's answers can change from day-to-day, especially when they involve emotions or feelings about mental state, depending on a multitude of events and experiences in our lives. In addition, there is no common scale.

Say, for example, you and a friend were asked, "Are you happy?" You may both say "yes," but your reasons for doing so may be completely different and be subject to different variables. The same goes for a question like, "Do you believe in conspiracy theories?"

"The judgment I'm making is a relative one. What's my norm? Am I comparing it to my friends who don't believe in conspiracies or am I in a group of people who do believe in conspiracies? We're always making relative judgments about our psychological propensities," said Dagnall.
Which suggests we're unlikely to ever get a definitive answer. Self-report data suggest correlations, not causation.
In a study on conspiratorial beliefs and well-­being, which Dagnall co-authored and published in May 2026, "self-report data" was specifically highlighted as a limitation.

This makes it very difficult to assess whether "conspiracy belief" or "conspiracy ideation" is good or bad for people and their sense of well-being. Especially as people who seek and believe in conspiracy theories often start out with a skewed view of reality.
Brain health: How to protect mental fitness and memory
Observing behavior can offer clues
There are ways of "triangulating" self-­report data, as the authors of the study put it, to get a more reliable, objective reading of a person's emotional, or psychological, state.

For example, psychologists use behavioral observations, like measuring heart rate variability, or Galvanic Skin Responses such as the electrical conductance of a person's skin, which is affected by sweating under stress. You can also retest participants' self-reported data, and therefore its reliability, by asking the same questions at different points in time.

But there is another factor that complicates research into the psychology of conspiracy theories, and that is that they, and people who believe in them, are more common than we like to think or admit (even when we believe them ourselves).
"The idea that people who believe in conspiracies in general populations are remarkable or different is not true," said Dagnall.
The truth: 'conspiracies theories are common'

Most of us, at some point in our lives, are bound to see something strange or stressful in society and question whether we, as individuals or as a member of a group, accept the accepted truth of how that thing or event came about. It can be a healthy sign of a questioning mind.
There are positive examples of conspiracy theories that happened to kickstart investigations that then revealed the horrible truth of government corruption.
Take Partygate during the COVID pandemic in the UK or — the mother of all conspiracies — Watergate during the Nixon Administration in the US.
And there are other conspiracy theories, such as the one that nobody has ever landed on the moon, which you can either take seriously or laugh about.
It all comes down to "the degree to which we engage in conspiracies generally, and the extent to which they interfere and disrupt our everyday lives," said Dagnall.
For Dagnall, who doesn't believe in the 1969 moon landing, it doesn't seem to disrupt his daily life — at least, that is what he self-reported to DW.
Watergate Anniversary
But for some people, conspiracy theories are disruptive and can lead to a sustained sense of dissatisfaction.

"Ample studies suggest that exposure to conspiracy theories or belief in them might lead to more negative emotions, heightened anxiety, or even paranoid thoughts," said Zuzanna Molenda, a researcher at the Polish Academy of Sciences and lead-author of a 2023 study on emotion dysregulation and belief in conspiracy theories.

Some people may be primed to more readily believe in conspiracy theories because they generally struggle to deal with psychological threat and distress. When they then seek answers in conspiracy theories, their pre-existing negative psychology may be enhanced.

"If anything, the available evidence suggests that rather than help people manage difficult emotions, conspiracy beliefs may be accompanied by or contribute to further distress," wrote Molenda in an email to DW.
No long-term benefit from conspiracy belief
There may be some psychological benefit to conspiracy theories, said Molenda, but only in the short term.

"Conspiracy beliefs can provide people with a sense of explanation and understanding when events feel uncertain or difficult to make sense of. For some people, they might also be a source of entertainment and fun. For others, they can provide a sense of belonging and connection with others who share the same beliefs, and they can be an important part of social identity," Molenda said.
But these potential benefits do not necessarily translate into better well-being in the longer term, said Molenda.
In the end, we're all searching for meaning and purpose in life. If we find a satisfactory answer, it gives us, what psychologists call presense — a direction in life, and that is good.

But if your search only leads to more uncertainty, more anxiety, and more doubt in your purpose in life, then that's bad. "And people who believe in conspiracies are asking questions but not getting answers," said Dagnall.
