Their lack of representation, he says, has left their grievances easier to ignore. “But we will not stop asking questions until the demands and issues we raised are addressed,” he said. “And if the government forgets what citizens expected from this movement, we will continue to hold it to account.”
Even those who joined the protests and survived are wondering whether the movement will actually change their future.

Dhiraj Joshi, a Gen Z protester who took part in talks at the Nepali Army headquarters in the early hours of September 9, said protesters never took to the streets expecting to be injured, killed or rewarded. “No one joins a protest thinking they will be injured, killed or honoured,” he said. “But once people have been killed and injured, the government has a responsibility to honour the commitments it made.”

The movement was ultimately driven by demands for accountability, transparency and an end to corruption, Joshi said. Those in power must also recognise the sacrifices made by the injured and the families of those killed, he added. “A year on, it does not feel like the government is moving towards greater accountability,” Joshi told Kantipur. “The government appears to be falling short on accountability, responsibility and democratic values.”

Law Minister Sobita Gautam said the government was in regular contact with injured protesters and families of those killed and that the Gen Z Council would provide a more formal channel for that engagement.

“It’s not that we have stopped talking to them,” she said. “But it can sometimes be difficult to speak to everyone individually. That is why we want the Gen Z Council to serve as a channel through which their concerns can reach the government.”

She said the government was already in direct talks with the affected families and protesters and acknowledged their frustration over the delays. “Understandably, they feel things are taking too long,” she said. “But we needed time to work out how to implement the agreements and set up the necessary mechanisms. That work is under way, and it should not take much longer.”
Meanwhile, a year after rallying in Kathmandu for a corruption-free Nepal, injured protesters say they are left with little more than frustration and regret.

Mahato, who was shot in the belly and collapsed on the spot, says he is disappointed that the current government hasn’t investigated who shot them and why. He adds he keeps repeating the same question to himself: “When will I be able to stand and walk again?”
Bhandari, who sustained a gunshot in his leg, says he regrets his decision to join the protests. “Sometimes I ask myself why the bullet hit my leg,” he says. “Why didn’t it hit my chest?” /dl

articles.title: Russia, North Korea open first road bridge across border
articles.summary: SEOUL — North Korea called the first road bridge across its narrow border with Russia a concrete sign of tightening bonds, state media reported Tuesday, as the Ukraine war draws the…

blocks.text: SEOUL — North Korea called the first road bridge across its narrow border with Russia a concrete sign of tightening bonds, state media reported Tuesday, as the Ukraine war draws the Western-sanctioned nations closer.
The bridge over the Tumen river, which Russia said is designed to accommodate a projected growth in freight and passenger traffic, adds to the rail and air links between the neighbours.
The ceremony on Monday marking its opening came as Russia and North Korea have heavily boosted military and economic ties since Moscow launched its Ukraine offensive in 2022.

“The completion of the bridge is a significant event adding a new dynamic movement to the overall bilateral cooperation,” North Korean official Pak Thae Song said, according the official KCNA news agency.
Video published by the Russian government showed trucks from both sides crossing the bridge, as crowds lining the road applauded.
“The launch of the first automobile route will further strengthen the connection between our friendly countries,” Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin said in a video link at the ceremony.

KCNA added that the new bridge ensures “safe passage of various forms of transport and the movement of people,” and has “strengthened a key infrastructure component for economic cooperation between North Korea and Russia.”

North Korea dispatched thousands of troops to Russia in 2024 to help ward off a Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region, while Kyiv has accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles in its nightly barrages.
The two countries signed a defence treaty in 2024 that provides for mutual support if either country is attacked.
One of the world’s most isolated and repressive countries, North Korea bars most its citizens from leaving and heavily monitors incoming travellers.
Russian tourism to North Korea has increased in recent years, although Pyongyang sometimes closes its border at short notice.

South Korea’s central bank estimated in July that North Korea’s economy grew more than three percent for a third straight year in 2025, citing it’s expansion of economic cooperation with Russia as a “major drive.”
The bank’s official said North Korea’s gross national income also “received a boost from a sharp rise in foreign currency earnings” linked to the deployment of its troops to Russia.

Ukrainian rights group Truth Hounds, meanwhile, previously warned that the new bridge could become “a direct artery for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, with Russian technology and resources flowing in the opposite direction”. /dl

articles.title: Nepal flood death toll rises to 1,355, nearly 5,000 unaccounted for
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The confirmed death toll from catastrophic flash floods in northern Nepal has risen to 1,355, with 4,996 people still unaccounted for, according to government data released on…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The confirmed death toll from catastrophic flash floods in northern Nepal has risen to 1,355, with 4,996 people still unaccounted for, according to government data released on Monday.

The National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA) said search and rescue teams had recovered 1,355 bodies from eight districts following the late-August floods. Chitwan recorded the highest number of fatalities with 363, followed by Nawalparasi East with 222 and Nawalparasi West with 221.
Of those still unaccounted for, 2,340 are from Nuwakot and 1,967 from Rasuwa. The figure also includes 589 foreign nationals and around 100 security and government personnel.

Emergency teams have rescued 13,396 people so far. More than 21,000 security personnel remain deployed in the worst-hit mountain areas, including 9,287 soldiers from the Nepali Army, 7,912 personnel from the Nepal Police and 4,203 from the Armed Police Force. Preliminary estimates put losses to property, housing and infrastructure at Rs387.5 billion ($2.56 billion).

Helicopters have been crucial in reaching isolated areas of the Himalayas. Military, paramilitary and private operators based in Kathmandu have carried out nearly 1,500 flights to deliver supplies and evacuate survivors.

The government has allocated Rs160 million ($1.06 million) in emergency funds to affected district offices and municipal councils. More than 3,500 displaced people are being housed in 39 holding centers, while medical teams have treated 6,672 injured people.

Restoration of essential infrastructure is under way. Electricity has been restored to more than 78 percent of households in Rasuwa, over 96 percent in Nuwakot and more than 99 percent in Dhading. Telecommunications operators have also restored nearly 98 percent of damaged mobile towers.
Humanitarian agencies say difficult access and damaged roads remain the main obstacles to delivering heavy equipment and sustaining relief operations in remote parts of the affected districts. /dl

articles.title: A flood of bad news leaves Nepal’s tourist hubs eerily quiet
articles.summary: KATHMANDU — The impact of the floods in the Bhotekoshi River is beginning to ripple through Nepal’s tourist industry, with hotels reporting a wave of cancellations just as the peak autumn…

blocks.text: KATHMANDU — The impact of the floods in the Bhotekoshi River is beginning to ripple through Nepal’s tourist industry, with hotels reporting a wave of cancellations just as the peak autumn tourist season gets underway.

Hotels in Pokhara, Chitwan and Lumbini say domestic and foreign tourists have cancelled their bookings following reports that have portrayed Nepal as unsafe in the wake of the August 26 disaster. Domestic travellers have also called off their plans because of difficult road conditions.
As a result, hotels in some of the country’s major tourist destinations are largely deserted during what is normally one of the busiest times of the year.

Sauraha in Chitwan, for instance, would be bustling with tourists at this time of year. This year, however, only a handful of tourists can be seen in the popular jungle destination. The Regional Hotel Association said hotel occupancy has fallen below 5 percent.
“There are hardly any tourists at the moment,” said Suman Ghimire, former president of the Regional Hotel Association Sauraha. “Hotel occupancy is below 5 percent.”

Ghimire’s Jungle Safari Lodge has 34 rooms. But after bookings were cancelled, most of the rooms are now empty, he said. Tourists have stopped travelling to Chitwan by road after the Krishnabhir section of the highway was washed away by floods.
Although the Bhotekoshi flood did not cause any damage in Chitwan, Ghimire said the destination was suffering because negative reports about Nepal had spread through travel advisories.
“There is no problem on the East-West Highway,” he said. “But tourism has been hit because reports have spread internationally portraying the situation in Nepal as disastrous.”

As alternatives to the damaged Mugling-Kathmandu section of the Prithvi Highway, the Hetauda-Kathmandu road, also known as the Kanti Lokpath, the Tribhuvan Highway and the Hetauda-Kulekhani road are operational. Tourists can use these routes to reach Chitwan. There is also no difficulty in reaching Chitwan by air from Kathmandu to Bharatpur.
Royal Tulip Chitwan Hotel, operated by KTM Hospitality, has 65 rooms. Rameshwar Sah, chairman of Royal Tulip, said 80 percent of bookings have been cancelled so far.

“The tourism sector has been severely hit by the floods,” Sah said. “Although the destinations themselves have not been affected by the floods, rumors and misleading reports about the situation have had a significant impact.”
Sauraha has 125 small and large hotels with a combined capacity to accommodate 8,000 tourists a day.
Gunaraj Thapaliya, vice-president of the Regional Hotel Association, said the impact was particularly visible in Sauraha.
“Except for a handful of Chinese tourists, there are no visitors in Sauraha at the moment,” he said.

Large hotels in Patihani and Meghauli are also waiting for tourists to return. At the Soaltee Westend Chitwan Resort in Patihani, Bharatpur, the number of guests has dropped sharply since the floods, said Choplal Pandey, general manager of the hotel.

“We are receiving messages from foreign tourists cancelling their bookings one after another,” he said. “Forty percent of bookings have already been cancelled. We became more concerned when guests also began cancelling bookings made through November.”
Pokhara, the tourist city in Kaski district, has also not escaped the impact.
Hari Bhujel, chairman of the Tourism Council, said the Bhotekoshi floods and damage to the Prithvi Highway at Krishnabhir have added to the challenges facing tourism in Pokhara.
“The tourist season for foreign visitors has begun,” he said. “But up to 30 percent of hotel bookings have been cancelled at present.”

He said the closure of the Prithvi Highway, increased airfares, inadequate flights between Pokhara and Kathmandu and the continued charging of dollar-denominated fares to foreign tourists have directly affected tourism in Pokhara.
The damage at Krishnabhir has also affected the arrival of Indian tourists travelling from Sunauli to Pokhara, then to Muktinath and on to Pashupatinath, he said.

“With the recent increase in fuel prices making airfares more expensive, the arrival of domestic tourists is also expected to decline,” he said. “However, it is necessary to convey the message to foreign tourists that destinations other than the areas affected by the floods are safe.”
Lumbini, the birthplace of Buddha, has also begun to see fewer tourists.

Lilamani Sharma, president of the Lumbini Hotel Association, said foreign tourists travelling to Lumbini via Kathmandu have been cancelling their hotel bookings. Bookings made for the main October-November season are also being cancelled, he said.
He said bookings were being cancelled because information was being circulated abroad in a way that made it appear that Nepal as a whole had been affected by the floods.
“The problem travelling to and from Kathmandu is because one or two sections of the Mugling-Kathmandu road have been damaged,” he said. “Even that situation is gradually improving.”

Khim Shrestha, operator of Hotel Suramma in Lumbini, said the government should take the initiative to communicate through foreign diplomatic missions in Nepal and international media that the situation in the country is improving and that Nepal is eager to welcome foreign visitors.

Bhavishwar Adhikari, operational manager of Hotel Hokke, a four-star boutique hotel in Lumbini, said 100 room-nights booked on various dates over a two-month period have been cancelled. He said the tourism sector would be badly affected if the government failed to immediately communicate internationally that the situation in the country was normal.
Prakash Bhattarai, operator of Shakya Guest House, said the problem was being compounded by the failure to communicate accurate information.

“One or two problems seen on the roads should not be exaggerated,” he said. “The local and federal governments should prioritise both information dissemination and repair and maintenance work to revive the tourism sector.”

Chandra Prakash Shrestha, president of Hotel Association Nepal’s Lumbini Province chapter, said Indian tourists arriving on package tours through border points such as Belahiya to visit various destinations have also been affected.

Indian tourists come to visit religious sites in the high Himalayan region. Following reports that the Himalayan region had been devastated by floods, they are understood to have cancelled their bookings.
Although tourists continue to visit border towns and nearby destinations for short stays, Shrestha said there had been a sharp decline in tourists travelling on package tours.
The tourist bus park at Mustang Chowk in Pokhara, which normally sees a steady flow of passengers from morning until night, is now deserted.
Twenty-four buses used to leave the bus park for Kathmandu in the morning and eight at night.

According to Buddhi Sagar Paudel, an employee at the Mustang Chowk branch of Prithvi Highway Bus Operators Company, 14 tourist buses used to leave from Prithvi Chowk, eight from Lamachaur, two from Hemja and two from Zero Kilometre.
At present, only tourist buses travelling to Chitwan and Lumbini are operating.
The Nepal Association of Tour and Travel Agents (NATTA) Gandaki also inspected an alternative route to bypass Krishnabhir on Saturday.

Sangita Paudel, president of NATTA Gandaki, said the association studied a route that involves crossing a suspension bridge from Krishnabhir to reach Jyāmire on the opposite side and then travelling 11 kilometres to reach Benighat.

“A diversion is currently being constructed at Krishnabhir and it is expected to come into operation within a week,” Paudel said. “But it is uncertain how long it will remain operational. If it cannot operate for a long period, the Jyamire-Benighat route could serve as an alternative.”

She said an alternative was being sought because large vehicles cannot travel along the Tribhuvan Highway from Hetauda to Naubise. The disruption to tourist vehicles has directly affected nearly 1,000 business operators and workers, Paudel said.
Meanwhile, the Lumbini Development Trust has said Lumbini, the birthplace of peace, remains completely safe and open despite the difficult situation in the country caused by the Bhotekoshi floods.

In a statement issued on Sunday, the trust said Lumbini had not been affected by the floods or the disaster and that, at a time when people were engaged in relief, rescue and assistance efforts, the Buddhist values of compassion, loving-kindness and harmony remained equally relevant. Visiting Lumbini, it said, could be meaningful for those seeking a sense of peace and spiritual energy.

“The recent floods have not affected the greater Lumbini area,” said Himal Upreti, acting member-secretary of the Lumbini Development Trust. “Lumbini, Kapilvastu, Devdaha, Ramgram and other major tourist destinations remain open to visitors.”

“The Bhotekoshi flood has created a negative message that the entire country is experiencing fear and hardship,” he said. “That is why we have to reassure the international community that Lumbini is safe and accessible.” /dl

articles.title: DILG chief to visit France for red notice bid vs Zaldy Co
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla will also be visiting France to follow up with the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) on the Philippine…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla will also be visiting France to follow up with the International Criminal Police Organization (Interpol) on the Philippine government’s request for a red notice against resigned Ako Bicol party-list Rep. Zaldy Co.

Remulla made the announcement in a press briefing in Camp Crame on Tuesday, a day after his brother, Ombudsman Jesus Crispin Remulla, likewise said he would be flying to France to work with the authorities there to find Co.

Co was again the subject of an arrest warrant issued by the Sandiganbayan, alongside Leyte 1st District Rep. Martin Romualdez, in connection with a plunder charge for over P7 billion worth of alleged kickbacks in various government projects
Romualdez was arrested at the Cardinal Santos Medical Center in San Juan City on Monday night. /gsg

articles.title: Praying for rain as fires, haze plague Indonesian Borneo
articles.summary: PONTIANAK, Indonesia — Wildfires ravaging the Indonesian part of Borneo island are choking communities as far away as Malaysia with putrid haze, testing the resources and resolve of those…

blocks.text: PONTIANAK, Indonesia — Wildfires ravaging the Indonesian part of Borneo island are choking communities as far away as Malaysia with putrid haze, testing the resources and resolve of those having to endure them.

Blamed partly on one of the worst episodes of the drought-inducing El Nino weather phenomenon in decades, the disaster threatens millions of people’s access to necessities such as clean water and air — even education.
Here is the situation as seen from the perspective of three community leaders in Indonesia’s West Kalimantan province, one of the worst-affected regions:
The teacher
Syarifah Hatifah, the 57-year-old vice principal of a junior high school in provincial capital Pontianak, fears some of her nearly 600 pupils may be falling behind.
They are in the third week of the second school closure this fire season. It’s the longest closure Syarifah can remember in her 30-year career.
Hundreds of schools have been closed indefinitely in West Kalimantan due to air pollution, with about 200,000 pupils learning from home, according to the provincial education ministry.
The kids are being kept home for their health, Syarifah told AFP in a classroom empty but for two teachers presenting classes online, both with dozens of pupils scattered across their screens.
“The hope is that at home, in terms of health, they can be protected… because they are inside the house. They don’t have to go through roads full of dust and smoke,” she said.
But Syarifah said not every child has stable internet or access to a computer, making live sessions difficult for some.
“Sometimes… there is a power outage at their home, or they forget to charge their phones”, and some students live in faraway areas with patchy connectivity, she said.
The school’s teachers have been showing up every day as usual, giving lessons online in classrooms with no air purifiers. They work maskless so students can understand them clearly.
Syarifah said the school would offer extra lessons for free once in-person learning resumes.
“We hope that this haze will pass quickly. Usually after the rain falls, the haze will disappear,” she said.
West Kalimantan’s wetter season usually starts around October or November.
The health official
Iwansyah, head of the Kubu Raya regency’s health agency, is responsible for the welfare of some 700,000 people spread over 123 villages, served by one general hospital and 21 clinics.
His staff focus on efforts to prevent illness caused by “the unhealthy air people inhale every day”.
So far in September, more than 1,400 people in the regency have been treated or hospitalised for acute respiratory infections, said Iwansyah, who like many Indonesians has one name.

blocks.caption: An aerial view shows the Ampera Bridge over the Musi river shrouded in haze caused by forest fires in Palembang, South Sumatra on September 3, 2026. Agence France-Presse

blocks.text: In August, the number was 6,396.
“We distribute masks to the public every day, about one thousand masks per day. Of course our stock is starting to run low,” the official told AFP.
Iwansyah said the agency had requested additional masks from the provincial government, and was encouraging people to buy their own.
The agency also monitors cases of diarrhoea brought on by reduced access to clean water due to the drought, with 225 cases so far this month.

With Indonesia’s BMKG weather agency warning of little respite in the weeks ahead, “we will have to work even harder on mitigation and preparing for a potentially very severe situation”, said Iwansyah.
This includes stocking up on medicines and equipment at clinics and intensifying surveys of water and air quality.
“Hopefully there will be rain between now and November,” Iwansyah said.
The hamlet head
For Yonas, deputy head of the Lintang Batang hamlet outside Pontianak, the priority is firefighting equipment.

“The residents here even pooled money to buy a (water pump) machine and hoses, and other equipment,” he told AFP on Sunday night while battling a peatland fire that had been raging for four days, emitting acrid smoke.
“We’re still short of hoses, which makes it hard for us to extinguish this fire.”

Volunteer firefighters were using “whatever we have. Sometimes we use buckets, and even those aren’t enough”, said Yonas, adding that the teams were also in need of food and protective gear, including masks.
He said the smoke posed a danger especially for children, pregnant women, the elderly and people with asthma.
Scientific observations show the haze contains levels of toxic small particle pollution far exceeding the World Health Organization’s recommended safe limit.
“It’s very hazardous to the health of us who live in this village,” said Yonas. /dl

articles.title: Prosecutors ask ICC to examine documents linking ex-Pres Duterte to DDS
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines – International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors have asked Trial Chamber III to examine documents submitted by a witness that may link former President Rodrigo Duterte to the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines – International Criminal Court (ICC) prosecutors have asked Trial Chamber III to examine documents submitted by a witness that may link former President Rodrigo Duterte to the Davao Death Squad or DDS.

According to the document made public Monday, Acting Prosecutor Mame Mandiaye Niang filed a request on August 31 seeking permission for the witness, identified as “P-1100,” to submit a statement instead of testifying in person.

The prosecution cited Rule 68 of the ICC Rules of Procedure and Evidence, which allows parties to invoke prior recorded testimony before a witness’s scheduled testimony. However, such submissions remain subject to cross-examination and questioning by the Trial Chamber.
“The Prior Recorded Testimony of P-1100… is particularly relevant to the policy to ‘neutralise’ through violent crimes, including murder, alleged criminals in the Philippines,” Niang wrote.
He continued: “It also provides evidence of the Davao Death Squad’s modus operandi as well as [Duterte’s] criminal responsibility, including in relation to his knowledge and intent.”
Primarily, the prosecution reasoned that the request is to expedite Duterte’s proceedings, “having the health of [Duterte] in mind.”
Niang also wrote that, should the request be granted, the length of the witness’ direct examination would be reduced from seven hours to two hours.

Duterte is facing two counts of murder as crimes against humanity, and one count of attempted murder and murder as a crime against humanity for his supposed role in the drug war as president of the Philippines and as Davao City mayor.
His trial is scheduled to commence on November 30, 2026. /jpv

articles.title: Nepal says big polluters must ‘wake up’ as it calls for climate compensation over flood disaster
articles.summary:
Foreign minister Shisir Khanal tells the Guardian the world’s biggest economies need to help Nepal, which contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions

Nepal is demanding…

blocks.text: Nepal is demanding $20m in climate compensation for the recent devastating floods, as a senior minister called on the world’s most polluting countries to “wake up” and accept shared responsibility for a disaster that led to the death or disappearance of more than 6,000 people.

Scientists believe the climate crisis had a role to play in the floods, which were triggered when a melting glacier partially collapsed and set off a deadly landslide and flash flooding through Chinese-controlled Tibet and Nepal in late August. So far, more than 1,300 are confirmed dead and more than 5,500 still missing, with hopes of their survival diminished after 12 days of rescue operations.

Speaking to the Guardian, Nepal’s foreign minister, Shisir Khanal, was forthright in his call for climate justice and said it was imperative the world’s biggest economies stepped up to help Nepal recover and rebuild after the catastrophic floods.

Nepal contributes less than 0.1% of global greenhouse gas emissions, while its neighbours India and China are among the world’s biggest emitters. The mountains of the Himalayas – which span across India, China, Nepal and Bhutan – have been warming at a rate nearly 50% faster than the global average.
In 2023, the UN said Nepal’s mountains had lost close to a third of their ice in just over 30 years due to global heating.

Khanal emphasised that the recent disaster was far more extreme than any flooding regularly seen during the monsoon season, and said the magnitude of damage was on par with the 2015 earthquake that left much of the country in ruins.

blocks.caption: An excavator repairs a damaged road in Nepal near the Trishuli River on Monday. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

blocks.text: “This felt like a tsunami that was coming from the Himalayas,” he said. “We experienced waves as high as 60, 70 feet, which were mixed with debris, mud, stones, rocks, and came at the speed of almost 180km per hour. Towns, villages and highways were completely wiped out and there are some areas still disconnected.”

Khanal confirmed that Nepal’s ministry of finance and ministry of environment had written a joint letter to the UN’s fund for responding to loss and damage – which was set up in 2022 in line with the Paris climate agreement – to request $20m in climate-related damages.

“We have contributed so little to climate change,” he said. “It is imperative for those in the global community who benefit from larger, much more polluting economies, and whose historical contribution to greenhouse gases is much bigger than ours, to accept a shared responsibility. This affects all of humanity.”
For Nepal, the disaster was particularly worrying because it was “one of the strongest warning signals that we’ve experienced of what’s to come”, he said.

“The global community should not see this as one-off disaster; it should be viewed in the context of the changing climate in the Himalayas,” he said. “We know it is going to be a recurring scenario that more and more communities, not just in Nepal but around the world, will have to face.”

Khanal acknowledged that the compensation amount Nepal has requested from the UN was “obviously not nearly enough to cover the damage that we have sustained”. According to some estimates, the total damage caused by the floods will be upwards of $5bn, though Khanal said it could be even higher.

Upwards of 20,000 homes will probably have to be rebuilt, as well as the main highway. Villages built in vulnerable areas along the river, some of which washed away entirely, may have to be relocated to higher, safer ground.

While Khanal initially singled out India and China as countries that should step in to help – while avoiding mention of the US, which is the world’s biggest polluter – he rowed back on those comments, saying: “It is not just about shifting the blame to one or the other country, it’s about us all working together.”

blocks.caption: Damaged buildings on the banks of the Trishuli River. Photograph: Anushree Fadnavis/Reuters

blocks.text: He emphasised that the compensation demand was also meant to act as a “wake-up call for the global community to establish a more robust mechanism to help vulnerable and small economies like Nepal”.

The UN has admitted the loss and damage fund is already facing a “significant financing gap”. The fund has already received requests totalling $2.8bn from about 119 countries, but so far only around $400m has been given by the international community. The US has given just $17m, after Donald Trump withdrew from the Paris agreement.
Khanal acknowledged there were “political challenges” in getting Nepal the climate compensation it was demanding.
“Yes there always will be people who may not agree to our perspective or deny there is climate change, but there are also people who deny that the Earth is round,” he said bluntly.
He emphasised the importance of funds being made available not just for immediate disaster response but also for preparedness and mitigation for climate-related risk.

Khanal rebuffed allegations that China had failed to give an adequate warning or share data with Nepal about the impending floods. He said he was in discussion with China about enhancing coordination and data sharing for the Himalayan region.
“With the benefit of hindsight, we can now see that this glacier was fragile and had been receding in the past six months,” he said.

“But before the floods hit, there was no knowledge on our part, or on the part of Chinese scientists, that this particular collapse was imminent. I do not believe any of us had any idea of the threat until it happened.”

articles.title: Second-hand smoke causes to nearly 1.7M deaths globally – study
articles.summary: PARIS — More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published Tuesday…

blocks.text: PARIS — More than 2.7 billion people including children have been exposed to second-hand smoke globally, contributing to nearly 1.7 million deaths in 2023, according to study published Tuesday in The Lancet.

Tobacco remains a leading cause of disease globally, the study said, noting many “non-smokers exposed to second-hand smoke” were among the estimate total of 8 million people who died in 2023 of smoking-related illnesses.
“Exposure to second-hand smoke is a globally recognized health risk, with no safe level of inhalation,” it said.

By reviewing studies published in the US National Institutes of Health database PubMed along with population surveys, Tuesday’s study sought to estimate the prevalence of exposure to second-hand smoke and quantify the burden of disease in 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023.
Among the approximately 2.7 billion people exposed to second-hand smoke in 2023 were 767 million children aged 0 to 14, the study found.

This exposure is estimated to have resulted in 1.66 million premature deaths and causing premature disability and illness, leading with ischemic heart disease, a heart condition caused by insufficient oxygen supply to the heart muscle.
In children, exposure to second-hand smoke is estimated to have caused 5.2 million respiratory tract infections in 2023, it said.
People in proximity to someone lighting up are exposed to both the “sidestream smoke” from the burning tobacco product and smoke exhaled by the active smoker, the study explained.

“The sidestream component, which dominates the air non-smokers breathe, is unfiltered… carrying higher per-unit concentrations of the toxic and carcinogenic compounds” than that being inhaled by the active smoker, it said.

Despite significant declines in smoking prevalence globally since 1990, the absolute number of people exposed has remained stable due to population growth and increased exposure in Africa and the Middle East.
Women are also disproportionately affected by second-hand smoke, particularly in regions where smoking prevalence among women is low, it noted.
“Despite this substantial burden, (second-hand smoke) exposure remains rarely acknowledged as a major risk factor for female health,” it said.
The study called for governments to implement stronger tobacco controls in public places and in homes in order to better protect women and children from second-hand smoke. /dl

articles.title: A food safety officer has become a social media star in India - why?
articles.summary: Tukaram Mundhe has gone viral after a series of aggressive inspections of restaurants to detect hygiene lapses.

blocks.text: The images are hard to ignore.
Cockroaches scurry across kitchen floors. Spider webs cling to walls. Spoiled vegetables rot in corners, while food counters show signs of pest infestation.
One might assume these scenes belong to a struggling restaurant. But the photos are from a members-only club in Mumbai - India's financial capital and the capital of its richest state Maharashtra.

They are among dozens of photos and videos that have gone viral since May, after Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration (FDA) began a series of inspections at restaurants, cafes and other food businesses across the state.
At the centre of the crackdown is 51-year-old civil servant Tukaram Mundhe, the state's new food commissioner.
Since taking charge in May, Mundhe has overseen thousands of inspections and says food safety laws must be enforced regardless of a business's size, influence or reputation.

His department has suspended the licences of several quick-commerce warehouses and sent notices to Bollywood celebrities for doing advertisements suspected of indirectly promoting restricted products.
"These actions are taken in public health interest. We will continue to take them against violations," Mundhe told the BBC.
The campaign has made Mundhe a recognisable face across India, rare for a civil servant.
Videos of his inspections and press briefings circulate widely on social media, where reels and podcasts have turned him into an unlikely celebrity.
But the spotlight - and the controversy that often comes with it - is nothing new to him.

An officer in the Indian Administrative Service, Mundhe has more than two decades of experience and has been transferred so often that reports say the number exceeds his years in service, though he declines to confirm it.
"I have stopped counting my transfers," he told the BBC.
Admirers see the transfers as evidence of his uncompromising style. Critics argue that this confrontational approach has put him at odds with colleagues and elected representatives.

In the past decade, Mundhe has won praise for his handling of the Covid pandemic outbreak during his time as Nagpur city's municipal commissioner and earlier for his work on water conservation in Maharashtra's drought-prone regions.

"When he was transferred out of Nagpur during the pandemic, thousands showed up outside his home to bid him farewell. It took him an hour just to reach his car," says Shafi Pathan, a journalist who's written Mundhe's biography in the local Marathi language.
But his food-safety crackdown has brought him the most attention yet.
The scale of India's food-safety problem is serious and numbers presented to the parliament in July offer a glimpse of just how widespread the issue is.
Of 223,808 food samples tested across India in 2025 and 2026, nearly one in five, external were found to be "non-conforming" - which means the samples were either unsafe, substandard or mislabelled.
And Mundhe has responded with an unusually aggressive enforcement drive.
By the end of July, his department had carried out more than 3,100 inspections across the state - a number he expects has since crossed 4,000.
Around 300 licences had been suspended and more than 1,000 improvement notices issued. A new complaints portal had also received more than 16,000 complaints in its first three months, Mundhe said.
"Hygiene has always been a problem here," Pawan Agarwal, former chief of India's food regulator, told the BBC. "What Mundhe has done differently is make it visible".

Consumers have responded positively to that visibility, Agarwal says. Unlike in India's conventional system, where food safety cases and consumer complaints can take years to move through regulators and courts, enforcement actions are now playing out in public.
The campaign has also made Mundhe a social media star - he now has more than 3.8 million followers on Instagram.
However, even as consumers welcome the speed and visibility of his actions, many in the food industry are less enthusiastic.
Restaurant associations allege the official has been bypassing a statutory process, while courts have termed some of his actions "high-handed".

Under India's food safety laws, businesses are usually given time to fix violations before regulators suspend or cancel their licences. Regulators can suspend licences immediately only in urgent public health situations but must record their reasons.

"While compliance is non-negotiable, high-handed approaches - like public naming-and-shaming, instant suspensions over minor procedural or rectifiable issues and treating administrative oversights with harsh penal measures - create panic rather than reform," said Niranjan Laxman Shetty, legal chairman of hospitality association Indian Hotel and Restaurant Association.

Responding to the criticism, Mundhe said his raids are lawful and that suspensions are only for extreme cases. However, some businesses have publicly claimed that they've been shut over minor violations, without warning or a chance to improve first.
His actions have also faced legal challenges. In some cases, courts have overturned licence suspensions, ordered compensation for affected businesses and criticised the regulator's approach.

In August, for instance, the Bombay high court ordered, external Mundhe's department to pay 500,000 rupees ($5,291; £3,893) in compensation to a sweets shop whose licence remained suspended even after a reinspection found it 98% compliant with the law.
The court said the regulator's intentions were "laudable" but that it had "gone overboard".
The judges also raised a question - was the regulator applying the same scrutiny to government establishments as it was to private businesses?
Within a day of that criticism, Mundhe's team inspected canteens in the state's high court complex and flagged violations.
For Mundhe, it is proof that the rules apply equally to everyone.
"Had the food business operators or establishment complied with existing regulations, I would not be needed to take those actions," Mundhe told the BBC.
He also insists that they are not trying to shut down businesses but only ensure safety.

"We are not here to close down or suspend every licensee," he said at an event last week. "We are here to ensure food is safe, food is not substandard, it is not misbranded and it is good for consumption."
The restaurant inspections - which dominate social media - are only a part of his work.
Mundhe has enforced bans on using newspapers to wrap food, synthetic dyes and banned analogue paneer - non-dairy cottage cheese substitutes.

Its focus has now shifted to schools. The department has ordered canteens, hostel kitchens and midday meal suppliers to obtain proper licences, and banned the sale of food high in fat, sugar or salt within 50m of schools.
But the bigger question is what happens once Mundhe moves on to his next post.
"The efforts of Mundhe have created a nationwide awareness about food safety, both amongst businesses and consumers, which is desirable - but not sustainable," says Agarwal.
The challenge is to build systems that outlast an individual officer, he adds.
For now, however, the effects are being felt even on the streets.

Yuvraj Yadav, who sells sandwiches in a Mumbai suburb, says he used to wrap them in discarded newspapers, despite concerns that chemicals in the printing ink can leach into food. He recently switched to greaseproof paper after hearing about the ban.
"We started this a few months ago after newspapers were not allowed for packing as it's bad for health," he says.

articles.title: Canada’s retaliatory US tariffs set to take effect as trade dispute grows
articles.summary:
Counter-measures covering several sectors come after Trump announced 50% tariffs on Canadian goods

Canada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American…

blocks.text: Canada is set to impose retaliatory tariffs on billions of dollars’ worth of American imports early on Tuesday, escalating a trade fight with its largest trading partner as tensions between US president Donald Trump and Canadian prime minister Mark Carney intensify.

The tariffs, which take effect at 12.01am on Tuesday, will range from 15% to 50% and apply to products covering C$27.6bn in imports from the US. The measures will target sectors including steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper, and electronics – industries that have been most affected by US tariffs.
The retaliatory tariffs come “as a result of the United States’ decision to impose a 50% tariff on $27.6bn of Canadian goods effective August 22”, the Canadian government said.
“Canada’s counter-measures do not apply to US goods that are in transit to Canada on the day on which they come into force,” it added.

Tensions between Canada and the US have intensified in recent weeks, with Carney last week urging the Trump administration to “start being serious” as the trade dispute has increasingly spilled into broader diplomatic tensions.

Trump and senior US officials have repeatedly criticized Canada and its leadership, while Trump has taken a series of symbolic digs at Canada including signing an executive order renaming Lake Ontario “Lake America” – which Canadians have rejected.
US vice-president JD Vance has also reportedly mocked Carney, apparently saying the Canadian prime minister “comes in and puffs his chest out and says: ‘I’m going to, like, out-tough Donald Trump.’”
Last month, Trump announced a new 50% tariff on cars and raw materials from Canada. He accused the country of “ripping off” the US “for years”, adding: “We don’t need Canada, they need us!”

Carney said last month Canada would not accept a US trade deal that weakened French-language protections, saying American negotiators viewed the measures as an “irritant”, while “in Quebec, these are rights”.

Quebec has long maintained laws aimed at protecting French and preserving its distinct cultural identity. Those measures have become a sticking point in the trade talks between the two countries, with American negotiators raising concerns about rules they say can disadvantage US businesses.

articles.title: AI cancer cures slowed by chip shortage, says UK's biggest tech boss
articles.summary: The head of chip designer Arm says modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer cannot be done now, but computers are "going to solve it".

blocks.text: The boss of the biggest UK-headquartered tech firm has said that artifical intelligence will find a cure for cancer that humans cannot in our lifetimes.

Rene Haas, chief executive of Cambridge-based chip designer Arm Holdings, said while modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer was currently "too complex" a problem, computers are "going to solve it" in the future.

Haas also told the BBC that AI would lead to widespread humanoid robots in the next five years, but that its current rapid growth was being held up by a shortage of chips needed to build data centres.
However, he was sceptical about the idea chips could be manufactured in the UK in the future.
Arm designs the brains or CPUs of microchips already used in hundreds of billions of phones, cars, smartwatches and gadgets across the globe.
Earlier this summer, the company's peak share price amid the AI boom made it, in cash terms, the most valuable UK-based company in history.

Haas, who stepped down from the board of British pharmaceutical giant AstraZeneca in April, told the BBC's Big Boss Interview podcast: "AI is going to... find a cure for cancer that today you and I, other humans [could] not in our lifetimes. I believe in our lifetime, AI will help cure cancer.
"Modelling a cell, modelling a human, modelling how a DNA marker is impacted by cancer - it's too complex a problem, not only for humans today, but the computers that run AI.

"However, going forward, as we feed more and more of the models into these computers, and the computers get more sophisticated to run the models, they're going to solve it," said Haas, who also holds a key role in Arm's main owner, the Japan-based Softbank, which has a range of investments in tech including in OpenAI.
Prof Chris Bakal, from the Institute of Cancer Research, London, and CEO of Sentinal4D, said the real question was no longer whether we use AI, it's what we feed it.
He said in labs like his, they are training AI on data generated themselves from patient samples.

"It is not scraped from the internet. It does not need a giant data centre to run. The future of medical AI will not belong to whoever builds the biggest computer. It will belong to whoever has the right measurements.
"That kind of prediction could cut years from the time it takes to develop new treatments. This is where AI delivers real benefit to patients."

In a wide-ranging interview, Haas said the chips Arm designs would fuel self-learning AI robots "in a very large way" in manufacturing, cleaning, security, building bridges, and doing repairs within a decade.

"With artificial intelligence, these robots can see, learn, and essentially be reprogrammed for new tasks. So, in the service industry, the robot that was programmed to make a bed can also learn how to arrange the towels in a room, or clean the dustbins, or whatever you want to go off and do."

Addressing concerns that AI would lead to mass job losses, Haas said while there would be some change for workers, "the estimates of jobs going away and being completely replaced by machines is a bit overstated" and outweighed by new opportunities.
He also said fears over a correction in the remarkable rise in the stock market value of AI companies were overstated, because of the long-term demand for AI.
Arm's power-efficient technology was now being used in half of AI data centres worldwide, he said.

This has led to a significant evolution in its business in recent months, selling its own microchips. Facebook-owner Meta asked Arm to develop the Arm AGI chip and "demand has been off the charts", according to Haas, with more than $2bn worth of demand since it was launched in March.
There have, however, been challenges in the supply of many types of chips, which Haas believes is holding back the roll-out of AI and data centres.
He pointed to plans for massive "multi-gigawatt" data centres in France and the US as well as plans to put them in space.
"We are absolutely in a supply-constrained environment. Can you get enough chips? We need more fabs [chip factories] before we can put a data centre in space."

But he does not believe that manufacturing, currently centralised around Taiwanese giant TSMC, could eventually occur in the UK, despite the government holding talks with the industry about the possibility of bringing parts of the physical chip supply chain over here.

"I don't think it's necessary for the UK to [build] fabs. Fabs are very expensive. They take a lot of specialised workers. They take a lot of natural resources, and there's a pretty broad ecosystem for those."
As the great hope of UK tech for decades, some government ministers have lamented Arm's sale to Japanese investors in 2016 and subsequent partial flotation on New York's Nasdaq rather than in London.
But Haas maintained that half of Arm's employees remain in the UK and said the company was "by far and away the largest employer in Cambridge".

articles.title: Social media posts reveal wider habitat of Philippine tarsiers
articles.summary: With their huge eyes and bodies small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, Philippine tarsiers are among the best-known inhabitants of the country’s tropical forests. The tiny nocturnal primates are…

blocks.text: With their huge eyes and bodies small enough to fit in the palm of a hand, Philippine tarsiers are among the best-known inhabitants of the country’s tropical forests.

The tiny nocturnal primates are closely associated with the central island of Bohol, a popular tourist destination, but researchers have found evidence that their range is far more extensive than previously documented.

A study by researchers at the University of the Philippines Diliman found reports of Philippine tarsiers in 29 provinces, more than double the 14 provinces previously identified as habitats by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN).
The findings were based largely on an unlikely source: Facebook.

Graduate student Simeon Bejar, 30, and fellow researcher Maria Tabeta, 25, examined more than 1,000 Facebook posts dating back to 2006, gathering information on tarsier sightings and analyzing where photographs of the animals had been posted.
More habitats
The IUCN had previously identified tarsier habitats in just 14 of the Philippines’ 82 provinces.
They also found numerous sightings in northern Leyte and indications that forests there may have tarsier population densities comparable to those in protected areas in Bohol.
“I think it’s really appropriate to do it here because a lot of Filipinos use Facebook,” Bejar said.
More than 80 percent of the Philippine population is estimated to use Facebook, giving the researchers a vast pool of information posted by people across the archipelago of more than 7,000 islands.

The Philippine tarsier, an endemic species measuring little more than 10 centimeters in body length, is difficult to find because of its small size and nocturnal habits. Much about its ecology remains unknown.
It is classified as “Near Threatened” on the IUCN Red List.
The study also highlighted shortcomings in efforts to protect the animals.
On Bohol, where ecotourism is a major attraction, the Department of Environment and Natural Resources and local authorities have stepped up management of forests inhabited by tarsiers.
Protected areas open to tourists have also introduced rules aimed at minimizing stress on the animals, including asking visitors to keep their voices down.
But the researchers found signs of problems elsewhere.
“Some of the Facebook posts featured photographs of tarsiers being inside cages, which is illegal. Some are leashed … some were dead,” Bejar said.
Illegal trafficking
Illegal trafficking for the pet trade is one of the main threats facing Philippine tarsiers, and poaching appears to be taking place in areas beyond the reach of authorities.
Bejar and Tabeta have set up a dedicated Facebook page for their research and hope to expand the scale of the study.
“If maybe we get another student who can work with us or a project where we can use funds to focus on this, then we’ll try to scale up what we are doing right now,” Bejar said.—KYODO NEWS

articles.title: Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward to ban vacation rentals
articles.summary: Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward plans to ban, as a general rule, vacation rentals such as Airbnbs in residential areas and areas near schools, local officials said on Monday. The ward in central Tokyo hosts…

blocks.text: Tokyo’s Shinjuku Ward plans to ban, as a general rule, vacation rentals such as Airbnbs in residential areas and areas near schools, local officials said on Monday.
The ward in central Tokyo hosts the largest concentration of vacation rentals in the country. The policy will also apply to existing properties, the officials said.

There were 3,775 registered short-term rental properties in the ward as of July 15, according to the Japan Tourism Agency. The ward estimates that approximately 2,000 of them may have to cease operations under the plan.

The agency and other relevant bodies notified local governments in July that they could effectively ban short-term rentals in specific areas through local ordinances if the properties were found to be harming the residential environment, citing a series of incidents.
The ward plans to solicit public comments in October and submit an amendment to its short-term rental ordinance at the first regular session of the ward assembly in February next year.
According to the officials, the ban will apply to areas zoned for residential use only or designated as cultural and educational districts.
Exceptions will be made for vacation rentals that meet certain requirements, such as those whose owners live on-site and manage the properties appropriately. —KYODO NEWS

articles.title: Senate OKs five international resolutions on third reading
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday approved, on its third and final reading, five international resolutions on aviation security, criminal justice cooperation, space activities, higher…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Senate on Monday approved, on its third and final reading, five international resolutions on aviation security, criminal justice cooperation, space activities, higher education, and taxation.
In a roll call vote, 19 senators, with no abstentions or objections, approved the following resolutions aimed at strengthening the Philippines’ participation in international agreements:

items: Senate Resolution No. 622, which seeks concurrence in the accession to the Protocol to Amend the Convention on Offenses and Certain Other Acts Committed on Board Aircraft, strengthening the legal framework for offenses committed aboard aircraft.

Senate Resolution No. 624, providing concurrence in the ratification of the Philippine-India Treaty on Mutual Legal Assistance in Criminal Matters, which establishes mechanisms for cooperation in investigating, prosecuting, and preventing crimes between India and the Philippines.

Senate Resolution No. 625, concurring in the ratification of the Convention on International Liability for Damage Caused by Space Objects, providing a framework for liability and compensation for damage caused by space objects.

Senate Resolution No. 626, which seeks concurrence in the Philippines’ accession to the Asia-Pacific Regional Convention on the Recognition of Qualifications in Higher Education, facilitating the recognition of Filipino academic qualifications abroad.

Senate Resolution No. 628, concurring in the ratification of the Philippines–Cambodia Agreement on the Elimination of Double Taxation and the Prevention of Fiscal Evasion with respect to Taxes on Income, which seeks to prevent double taxation and strengthen bilateral economic ties.

blocks.text: The approval of these measures is expected to improve the country’s cross-border cooperation while also supporting the country’s economic, educational, and security interests. /cb

articles.title: Alleged killers of Australian surfers and American friend go on trial in Mexico
articles.summary:
Three men on trial for killing Jake and Callum Robinson and Jack Carter Rhoad in Baja California in 2024

The alleged killers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing…

blocks.text: The alleged killers of two Australian surfers and an American at a Mexican surfing hotspot in 2024 have gone on trial in the border resort where the three were murdered.

The Australian brothers Jake and Callum Robinson, aged 30 and 33, respectively, and their 30-year-old American friend Jack Carter Rhoad were shot dead after being robbed in Mexico’s violence-hit Baja California.
They were camping in a remote beachside area when they were attacked. Their bodies were found hidden on a cliff.
The Robinsons’ parents travelled to the port city of Ensenada for the start of the trial.
“It’s about representing our sons, being here for them. I know they want us to be here,” Martin Robinson told reporters as he entered the court with his wife, Debra.
“We want to find out what happened. We want to find out why,” he said.

blocks.caption: Jake (left) and Callum (right) with their parents, Debra and Martin Robinson. Photograph: Callum and Jake Robinson Foundation

blocks.text: Three men are on trial for homicide.
The girlfriend of one of the accused was sentenced to 20 years in prison last year after admitting she had instigated the robbery.
The crime sparked outrage and sadness in Australia and the United States.
Callum Robinson played professional lacrosse in the US. His brother Jake was pursuing a career in medicine. Rhoad was killed a few months before he was due to marry.
Other foreign tourists have previously been targeted in criminal attacks on Mexico’s Pacific coast.
Two Australian surfers were murdered in 2015 while traveling through the north-western state of Sinaloa.
Their bodies were later burned.

articles.title: 26 Filipino seafarers awaiting repatriation after Ukraine attack
articles.summary: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the…

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines—The 26 Filipino crewmen of the bulk carrier Gingo are awaiting repatriation to the Philippines after safely disembarking following an attack while it was docked in Ukraine, the Department of Migrant Workers (DMW) said in a statement Monday.
The DMW said that as of Sept. 4, the 26 Filipino seafarers safely disembarked from the vessel. The seafarers are currently awaiting transit to Moldova before their repatriation to the Philippines.

The DMW said it is coordinating with the Department of Foreign Affairs (DFA), Philippine Embassy in Warsaw, Philippine Consulate General in Kyiv and Migrant Workers Office (MWO) in Prague to monitor the seafarers’ condition and facilitate their “safe and immediate” return, including the processing of their travel documents with Moldovan authorities and the ship owner.
Labor Attaché Llewelyn Perez said the Philippine diplomatic posts were working with Moldovan authorities and the shipowner to complete the documents needed for the crew’s return.

“The Philippine Embassy and the Philippine Consulate in Kyiv are coordinating with the relevant authorities, in partnership with the shipowner, to facilitate the processing of their travel documents,” Perez said.
The DMW said it is also coordinating with the licensed manning agency and the ship owner to address the seafarers’ immediate needs following their disembarkation.

“The DMW assures the families of the affected seafarers that it, together with its MWOs, Philippine embassies, and consulates, is facilitating the necessary arrangements for their safe return to the Philippines.” /gsg

articles.title: Russia and North Korea open first road bridge across their shared border
articles.summary:
Connection across Tumen River is further sign of closer ties between the two countries since start of war in Ukraine

Russia and North Korea have opened

blocks.text: Russia and North Korea have opened the first road bridge across their shared border, in the latest sign of the rapidly deepening ties between the two countries since the start of the war in Ukraine.

The one-kilometre bridge spans the Tumen River between Khasan in Russia’s far east and Tumangang in North Korea, along a remote and sparsely populated stretch of the countries’ shared border just a few miles from the coast.

Speaking by video link during the bridge’s opening ceremony on Monday, Russia’s prime minister, Mikhail Mishustin, said the new crossing would spur development in a range of areas, including tourism, while creating new jobs

“I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation,” Mishustin said.
The road bridge is named after the Soviet officer Yakov Novichenko, who is credited with saving North Korea’s founding leader, Kim Il-sung, from an assassination attempt by a pro-South Korean group.
After the opening ceremony, convoys of vehicles crossed the bridge from both sides.
Russia and the secretive North Korea regime are already connected by a railway bridge across the Tumen, as well as regular flights between Vladivostok and Pyongyang.
Ukrainian human rights groups have warned that the bridge may be intended to provide a discreet military logistics corridor between the two countries.

Truth Hounds, a Ukrainian human rights organisation, has described it as a likely future corridor for moving North Korean troops, construction brigades and military officials into Russia, while allowing Russian technology and resources to travel in the opposite direction with less risk of detection.

Ties between Moscow and Pyongyang have strengthened dramatically since Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. North Korea has sent thousands of troops to Russia’s Kursk region to help Moscow repel a Ukrainian incursion launched there in 2024.
In return, Russia is believed to have provided North Korea with air-defence missiles, electronic warfare equipment, drones and spy-satellite technology, according to South Korean intelligence.

Russian and North Korean officials have also touted North Korea as a new holiday destination since the country reopened to Russian tourists in 2024, with thousands of Russians visiting its newly opened beach resorts and ski slopes since then.
Russia’s increasingly close embrace of totalitarian North Korea has raised eyebrows even in Moscow.

During an interview with the Russian broadcaster RBC last month, a reporter asked Sergei Lavrov, Russia’s longtime foreign minister, how the country had “ended up” with just “two allies – North Korea and Iran”.
Lavrov pushed back against the premise, saying there was “nothing wrong” with such company.
At the same time, some of Russia’s traditional partners have shown growing frustration with Moscow’s continuing war in Ukraine and the fallout it has caused across the region.

During a meeting in July, Kazakhstan’s president, Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, a longtime ally of Moscow, told the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, that he was hearing from leaders of many countries who questioned why Russia was still waging the war.
“The nature of the conflict isn’t entirely clear for many, including us,” Tokayev told Putin.

articles.title: Weather tracker: Typhoon Saudel causes mass evacuations in south-east China
articles.summary:
Torrential rain causes widespread damage; while north-west South Africa hit by thunderstorms and central-southern US faces oppressive heat

Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to…

blocks.text: Typhoon Saudel brought days of torrential rain to the Zhejiang, Jiangxi, Fujian and Guangdong provinces in south-east China last week. The city of Putian, in Fujian province, recorded 416.5mm of rain in a 24-hour period between Thursday and Friday, with surrounding villages recording more than 500mm in the same period. In Fujian, authorities estimate that almost 600,000 people were evacuated from high-risk, flood-prone areas. A further 128,000 people in 53 counties were also affected across Jiangxi, with emergency evacuations affecting 9,000 people.

Flooding, landslips and infrastructure damage were reported widely in the region. More than 2,500 teachers and students were trapped in a school compound in the Zhejiang city of Wenzhou on Wednesday after extreme rainfall caused flash floods in low-lying areas. At least 1,260 people reportedly had to be rescued in Putian after a river embankment collapsed on Thursday, flattening 100 homes. On Saturday, a landslip in a village of Suichuan county, in Jiangxi province, killed three people and nine others remaining missing.
This is the seventh typhoon to affect China this year, and Saudel arrived shortly after Typhoon Narra dumped heavy rain on Guangdong, Hainan and Guangxi late last month.

The South African Weather Service implemented several thunderstorm warnings late last week, covering a large swathe of the northern and western provinces. Disruptive rainfall, damaging winds, excessive lightning and hail were all reported, with rainfall totals expected to have reached at least 75-100mm for parts of the Northern Cape and North West provinces over the weekend. In Johannesburg, eight families were evacuated from an apartment building after strong winds tore off a significant part of its roof.

Oppressive heat in the US affected states across the central-southern plains and the Mississippi valley this weekend, with maximum temperatures easily reaching the high 30s (Celsius; high 90s Fahrenheit). However, with high humidities, the heat indices in this region have been closer to 40-43C (105–110F). The unrelenting temperatures will continue across the midwest and southern US this week, with maximum temperatures continuing to reach the high 30s.

articles.title: Japanese woman goes viral for giving birth to 7th child
articles.summary: A woman in Japan went viral and captured the public’s attention after announcing the birth of her seventh child, amid the country’s falling birth rate. Japanese writer and former political candidate…

blocks.text: A woman in Japan went viral and captured the public’s attention after announcing the birth of her seventh child, amid the country’s falling birth rate.

Japanese writer and former political candidate Kotoe Hashimoto announced on social media platform X on Aug 29 that she had given birth to her seventh child, thanking the medical staff who attended to them.
The post, which includes a photo of Hashimoto cradling her newborn, has been viewed 27 million times on X and received 10,800 likes on Facebook.
In a follow-up post later the same day, she also thanked the public for their congratulatory messages.
“I believe that now is the time for Japanese women to have children,” she said. “The rise and fall of our nation depends on the active role of women.”
Her post struck a chord among the Japanese.

“I think you’re absolutely right. I feel that the key to changing the current state of Japan, which is heading towards (demographic) collapse, is precisely the conscience of Japanese women,” Facebook user Etsugaku Kankou replied to her post.
Another user, Hideto Umegaki, said: “It’s a national treasure to give birth to seven children.”

Hashimoto, who ran as a candidate under the Party of Hope during the 2017 general election, has used her social media accounts to discuss the country’s demographic challenges and advocating for Japanese women to have more children.
She was not elected, and the conservative party, which was founded by Tokyo Governor Yuriko Koike, disbanded in October 2021.
The baby’s birth comes as Japan’s fertility rate fell to a fresh record low in 2025, extending a decade-long slide despite years of government efforts to reverse the trend.

The total fertility rate – the average number of children a woman is expected to have over her childbearing years – slipped to 1.14 from 1.15 a year earlier, according to data by the country’s Welfare Ministry.
The reading was the lowest since comparable records began in 1947.

Japan, one of the world’s oldest societies, faces mounting demographic pressures. A shrinking workforce and rising social security costs are placing strain on public finances at a time when the government is also seeking to fund higher defence spending and other growth initiatives. /dl

articles.title: Man given 6 months to live; spends it finding home for autistic son
articles.summary: SINGAPORE — Jeon Gyeong-cheol, the author widely known as the “Peter Pan Dad” for documenting his search for a home where his disabled son could live after his death, died Saturday.…

blocks.text: SINGAPORE — Jeon Gyeong-cheol, the author widely known as the “Peter Pan Dad” for documenting his search for a home where his disabled son could live after his death, died Saturday. He was 64 and had been fighting late-stage liver cancer.

Jeong Yu-jin, head of the Developmental Disabilities Support Expert Forum, announced Jeon’s death on social media Sunday, saying the funeral would be held without a formal wake, in accordance with his wishes.
“He is currently at the hospital, and no separate memorial hall will be set up. We extend our deepest condolences,” she wrote.
Jeon spent more than two decades as the sole caregiver for his son, who is now 27 and has autism, with his developmental level assessed as that of a 2- or 3-year-old.

After receiving a terminal diagnosis of late-stage liver cancer in April last year, Jeon traveled across the country, reaching out to nearly 1,000 care facilities in hopes of finding a place that could look after his son once he was gone. Few, however, were able to take him in.

Jeon later began writing about his search on the content publishing platform Brunch, and his accounts struck a chord with many readers. His story soon reached a wider audience through television programs including MBC’s “True Story Expedition” and tvN’s “You Quiz on the Block.”
Jeon later compiled his writings on Brunch into the essay collection “Annyeong, Peter Pan,” published in June.

Readers moved by his story raised some 80 million won ($59,000) in donations, and with growing nationwide support, Je-won was able to move into a community village for people with profound developmental disabilities.

“I want to tell him to forget about his dad and live happily. But I don’t want him to forget me completely. I hope he remembers me with a faint sense of longing, as an old man who once looked at him with warmth,” Jeon said on “You Quiz on the Block” last month.
Jeon also sought to help families facing struggles similar to his own, working to establish a welfare foundation for adults with severe autism-related disabilities, like his son.

On Aug. 26, shortly before his death, he announced the launch of a preparatory committee for the foundation. With the committee now in place, its members are expected to carry on Jeon’s efforts and continue discussions on launching the foundation, according to news reports. /dl

articles.title: Water levels at San Roque Dam, Pangasinan rivers remain under close watch
articles.summary: PANGASINAN---San Roque dam continued to release water Monday morning as several rivers in Pangasinan remained above normal levels, including one that remained above the critical level. As of 5 a.m.…

blocks.text: (Photo via Liezle Inigo)
PANGASINAN---San Roque dam continued to release water Monday morning as several rivers in Pangasinan remained above normal levels, including one that remained above the critical level.
As of 5 a.m. on Sept. 7, the dam’s water level was at 279.79 meters above sea level (masl), with an inflow of 338 cubic meters per second (cms) and a combined outflow of 746 cms.
Two gates were opened at the dam. Gate No. 2A was opened to 1.0 meter, while Gate No. 2B was opened to 1.5 meters. The Low Level Outlet was also releasing 125 cms.
The elevated discharge comes as authorities continue to monitor river conditions downstream, particularly communities located near waterways and flood-prone areas.

At 6 a.m., the Marusay River in Calasiao was above the critical level, while the Sinucalan River in Sta. Barbara, Pantal River in Dagupan City, and Agno/Bañaga River in Bugallon were above normal levels.
The Camiling River in Camiling, Tarlac was at normal level. No level reading was indicated in the monitoring report for the Bued/Cayanga River in San Fabian and Balingcaguing River in Mabini.
Residents near rivers and low-lying communities are urged to remain alert, monitor advisories, and follow evacuation or other safety directives when issued.
